meta.textbook: Potter & Perry, Fundamentals of Nursing, 12th ed.
meta.notes: Each question supports two views. The default view explains why the key is correct: 'takeaway' is the clinical rule and each option carries its own rationale. The strategy view uses 'elimination', which names the test-taking strategies in play, walks the options out one at a time, and ends with the verdict. Both views describe the same question, so a student who is short on content can still reason to the answer. All fields are plain text with no markup, so render 'strategy' in italic with CSS rather than expecting tags. Every chapter and skills section carries an 'exam' field naming the exam it belongs to; meta.exams lists the sections in each. Filter on 'exam' to build a single exam's bank. The top-level 'chapters' and 'skills' arrays stay flat and hold every exam, so anything reading them without filtering still sees the whole course. Chapters carry both 'id' (unique key) and 'chapterNumber' (the number to display); they match except for The Endocrine System and Diabetes Mellitus, which displays as 56 and uses id 1056 because two different chapters in this course are numbered 56. Daily sets: questions written for a given day carry a 'dailySet' field holding that date (YYYY-MM-DD). Only one daily set exists at a time. Generating a new one strips 'dailySet' from every question that has it, then applies it to the new batch. meta.currentDailySet mirrors the active date and ids. Filter on the presence of 'dailySet' to pull today's set; questions keep their chapter membership and stay in the bank permanently after the tag is removed. 'source' is Potter or Iggy. Chapter numbers repeat across the two books, so 'id' is the unique key: Potter chapters use id = chapter number, Iggy chapters use id = 1000 + chapter number. Question ids are prefixed ch<n>- for Potter and ig<n>- for Iggy. Display chapterNumber with source, never id. Chapter groups: chapters taught from the same PowerPoint share a 'group' id on the chapter, and meta.chapterGroups lists each group with its title, exam and member chapter ids in display order. Chapters without a 'group' field stand alone.

questionTypes.multiple_choice: one correct option; answer is a string
questionTypes.sata: select all that apply; answer is an array and is scored all or nothing

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate absolutes
optionStrategies.cue: always, never, all, none, only, every
optionStrategies.note: Absolutes are usually wrong because medicine rarely deals in certainties.

optionStrategies.name: Favor qualifiers
optionStrategies.cue: usually, generally, often, may, approximately, most
optionStrategies.note: Qualifiers make a statement realistic. Not automatically right, but worth a second look against an absolute.

optionStrategies.name: Opposite pair, look closely
optionStrategies.cue: increase vs decrease, before vs after
optionStrategies.note: Often one of the pair is correct. Sometimes both are distractors, so treat it as a flag for attention.

optionStrategies.name: Global or umbrella option
optionStrategies.cue: one option covers two or more others
optionStrategies.note: If one option encompasses the others it is often the most complete answer.

optionStrategies.name: Patient-centered option
optionStrategies.cue: asks, involves, or respects the patient
optionStrategies.note: Options that involve the patient beat options that decide for them.

optionStrategies.name: Duplicate facts
optionStrategies.cue: a wrong fact shared by two or more options
optionStrategies.note: One shared wrong fact eliminates several options at once.

optionStrategies.name: Eliminate options that deny patient feelings
optionStrategies.cue: don't worry, it's nothing, most people are fine
optionStrategies.note: Therapeutic communication reflects feelings and invites more.

optionStrategies.name: Odd man wins
optionStrategies.cue: three options share an idea, one stands apart
optionStrategies.note: When most options point one way, the different one is often correct.

optionStrategies.name: Negative polarity
optionStrategies.cue: avoid, except, not, least, contraindicated, requires further teaching
optionStrategies.note: You are hunting the wrong option. Identify polarity before reading the choices.

optionStrategies.name: Priority key word
optionStrategies.cue: priority, immediate, first, best, most, least
optionStrategies.note: More than one option may be true. The key word decides how to choose among them.

optionStrategies.name: Apply the ABCs
optionStrategies.note: In ordering and priority questions, airway, breathing, and circulation come first, then safety, then comfort.

optionStrategies.name: Assessment before intervention
optionStrategies.cue: assess, check, determine versus administer, apply, notify
optionStrategies.note: When the stem asks what comes first and an assessment option is present, assessment usually precedes action.

optionStrategies.name: Treat each option as true or false
optionStrategies.note: Work each option independently. Partial credit means a wrong selection costs you, so only select what the scenario supports.

questions.stem: A nurse with four years on a medical unit is asked by a provider to insert a device she has never placed. He offers to talk her through it. Two colleagues say they have done it here before. The hospital policy manual does not mention the procedure. Which factors determine whether she may legally perform it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Her state nurse practice act
options.rationale: State law, and the outer limit of what any nurse there may do. If the procedure is not within it, nothing else on this list can make it lawful.

options.text: Her demonstrated competence to perform it safely
options.rationale: The act permitting something does not mean she can do it today. Competence is hers to declare, and she has never placed one.

options.text: Agency policy and procedure
options.rationale: Policy can narrow the practice act but never widen it. The manual being silent is a reason to check before proceeding, not a green light.

options.text: The provider offering to supervise her
options.rationale: Supervision feels like cover and confers no legal authority. She answers for what she does, supervised or not.

options.text: The patient consenting to her performing it
options.rationale: Consent covers whether the care happens, not who is permitted to perform it.

options.text: That other nurses on the unit have done it
options.rationale: Common practice is not proof of permission. They could all be working outside their scope without anyone having noticed.

questions.takeaway: Three things decide scope and they stack: the practice act sets the limit, policy may narrow it, and competence is yours to declare.
questions.strategy: More than one option describes something reassuring. Reassurance is not legal authority.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The state practice act, and nothing overrides it.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse notices that four patients over two weeks received their scheduled 0800 insulin after 0930. She reported each delay to the charge nurse and each time was told the unit was short-staffed. Which action best reflects a Standard of Professional Performance?

options.text: Continue reporting each late dose to the charge nurse as it happens
options.rationale: Correct, and it is what she has already done four times without effect. Repeating an action that has not worked is not a standard.

options.text: Stay past her shift to give the insulin herself when the unit is short
options.rationale: The compassionate answer and the worst one. It fixes tonight and hides the problem, so the data that would drive a change never appears.

options.text: Bring the pattern to the unit practice council with a proposed change
options.rationale: Quality of practice is a Standard of Professional Performance. Four events is a pattern, and a pattern belongs where practice gets changed.

options.text: Ask the provider to move the insulin to a later administration time
options.rationale: Changes the order to fit a staffing failure, which puts the problem in the prescription instead of in the process.

questions.takeaway: Standards of Professional Performance cover how you conduct yourself as a professional, including quality of practice.
questions.strategy: One option is what she has already tried. One is kind and conceals the problem. Ask which one changes anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reporting, four times, with no change.
Fixes one shift and hides the pattern.
Adjusts the prescription to a staffing problem.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the practice council: take the pattern where practice changes.

questions.stem: A nurse administers a dose of heparin that a colleague drew up and left at the bedside during a busy round. The syringe held five times the ordered dose and the patient bleeds. The colleague states she drew it correctly, and leaving prepared syringes is routine on this unit. Which statement describes the administering nurse's position?

options.text: The colleague is accountable, because she prepared the dose
options.rationale: The colleague answers for her own preparation error. That does not subtract from the nurse who gave it.

options.text: She is accountable, because the nurse who gives a medication answers for it
options.rationale: Drawing up and administering are separate acts and each carries its own answerability. Once she picked up the syringe, verifying it became hers.

options.text: Both share accountability equally, because both handled the syringe
options.rationale: Accountability is not divided between them. Each answers fully for her own act.

options.text: This is a system failure, because the unit routinely leaves syringes out
options.rationale: A genuine system problem, and system problems do not erase an individual act.

questions.takeaway: Accountability follows administration. It does not transfer to whoever prepared the dose, or to the system that made the error likely.
questions.strategy: Three options name something genuinely true. Only one describes her own position.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the shared and transferred options

steps.detail: Real, and it does not erase what she did.

elimination.verdict: That leaves her own accountability for administering it.

questions.stem: A nurse finds a systematic review supporting mobilization within 12 hours of abdominal surgery. Her patient, six hours post-operative, says he fell at home last month and is frightened of falling again. He declines to get up. Which action best reflects evidence-based practice?

options.text: Document the refusal and try again tomorrow
options.rationale: Respects his wish and abandons the evidence. A day's delay after abdominal surgery carries real risk.

options.text: Follow the review and mobilize him today as the evidence directs
options.rationale: Research without values. High-quality evidence applied over a patient's stated position is not evidence-based practice.

options.text: Ask the provider for an order requiring ambulation
options.rationale: An order does not resolve fear, and it moves a nursing decision to someone else.

options.text: Explore what is behind the fear and adapt how mobility is introduced
options.rationale: Evidence-based practice is research, clinical expertise, and what matters to the patient, together. Dropping any one of the three is not EBP.

questions.takeaway: Evidence-based practice needs all three legs: research, clinical expertise, and what matters to the patient.
questions.strategy: Each wrong option keeps one leg of the triad and drops another. The fall last month is what makes his refusal reasonable rather than obstinate.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hands the decision to someone else.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring the fear and adapting the plan.

questions.stem: For each action, indicate which professional role the nurse is performing.

rows.text: Weighs him and assesses for peripheral edema
rows.rationale: Direct care delivered to the patient.

rows.text: Shows him how to read a food label for sodium
rows.rationale: Building a capability he will use after discharge.

rows.text: Arranges a meeting so he can put his questions about the catheterization to the provider
rows.rationale: Creating the opportunity for his voice to reach the decision.

rows.text: Reassigns the assistive personnel so the two heaviest patients are not bathed at the same hour
rows.rationale: Organizing people, time and workload.

rows.text: States his wish not to proceed clearly during the team discussion
rows.rationale: Carrying his stated position when he is not in the room. Advocacy is not one action.

questions.takeaway: Five roles: caregiver, educator, communicator, advocate, manager. Autonomy and accountability run underneath all five rather than forming a sixth.
questions.strategy: Two rows are both advocate. Advocacy is anything that keeps the patient's own position in play, whether or not he is present.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two rows protect his stated position.
One is hands-on, one is teaching, one is workload.

elimination.verdict: Caregiver, educator, advocate, manager, advocate.

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for a patient newly diagnosed with heart failure across one shift. He is alert, anxious about a recommended cardiac catheterization, and his wife is at the bedside.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews her unit's fall rate for the past quarter, finds it at 4.2 per 1,000 patient days against a benchmark of 3.4, trials an hourly rounding protocol for 60 days, and re-measures at 2.9. Which QSEN competency does this best demonstrate?

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Falls are a safety issue, so safety is genuinely involved. The question asks what she did, and what she did was run an improvement cycle.

options.text: Informatics
options.rationale: She used data, and informatics concerns the systems that manage information rather than the improvement cycle itself.

options.text: Evidence-based practice
options.rationale: Hourly rounding is evidence-based, so this is also genuinely present. It describes where the intervention came from, not the method she used.

options.text: Quality improvement
options.rationale: She measured against a benchmark, changed something, and measured again. That closed loop is what quality improvement means.

questions.takeaway: Quality improvement is the measure, change, re-measure cycle. The subject matter of a project is not the competency.
questions.strategy: More than one competency is genuinely involved. Choose the one that names what she actually did.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The topic of the project, not the method.
One is the source of the intervention, one is the systems.

elimination.verdict: That leaves quality improvement.

questions.stem: A patient in a rural clinic needs her hypertension managed, her medication adjusted, and someone to follow her over the coming year. No physician is on site four days a week. Which advanced practice role is prepared to manage her care independently, including diagnosing and prescribing?

options.text: Certified nurse-midwife
options.rationale: An advanced practice role with a defined population, and hypertension follow-up in a rural clinic is outside it.

options.text: Clinical nurse specialist
options.rationale: Also an advanced practice nurse with deep expertise. The role centers on improving practice and consulting to staff and systems rather than carrying a caseload.

options.text: Nurse practitioner
options.rationale: Carries an independent caseload with diagnostic and prescriptive authority, which is exactly what this patient needs.

options.text: Certified registered nurse anesthetist
options.rationale: Advanced practice confined to anesthesia care.

questions.takeaway: Four APRN roles: clinical nurse specialist, nurse practitioner, certified nurse-midwife, certified registered nurse anesthetist.
questions.strategy: All four are advanced practice. Ask which one manages a general caseload over time.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Consults to practice rather than carrying patients.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the nurse practitioner.

questions.stem: A preceptor discusses scope with a new graduate in her third month. Which statement by the new graduate indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If the provider writes the order, the responsibility for giving it rests with him."
options.rationale: A written order does not transfer accountability for administration. The nurse who gives a drug answers for having given it.

options.text: "My state nurse practice act sets the outer limit of what I may legally do."
options.rationale: Accurate. The act is the boundary and nothing widens it.

options.text: "Agency policy can narrow my practice but cannot widen it beyond the act."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the reason a permissive employer cannot authorize something the act excludes.

options.text: "Competence is my own responsibility, so I should say when I have not done something before."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is the declaration that protects both her and the patient.

questions.takeaway: An order authorizes the drug. It does not transfer answerability for administering it.
questions.strategy: Three statements are correct as written. The one needing correction moves responsibility off the person who acts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement handing responsibility to the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse moves to a neighboring state and is told a wound procedure she performed routinely is outside her scope there. She holds the same national certification she held before. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Scope is set by each state's practice act, and certification does not expand it
options.rationale: Certification demonstrates expertise within a scope. The state defines the scope, so crossing a line changes what the same credential permits.

options.text: Her certification lapses when she practises in a different state
options.rationale: Certification is national and travels with her. What changed is the legal boundary around it.

options.text: She needs employer approval before the procedure returns to her scope
options.rationale: An employer can narrow scope and never widen it past the practice act.

options.text: The procedure requires an additional state-specific certification
options.rationale: Another credential does not help when the act itself excludes the procedure.

questions.takeaway: Licensure permits practice and is state-governed. Certification demonstrates expertise and does not widen scope.
questions.strategy: Every distractor offers a way to get the procedure back. Ask who defines scope in the first place.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the state act, with certification not expanding it.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel tells a nurse she gave eye drops routinely at her previous hospital and offers to give a patient's drops now. The nurse has watched her work all week and considers her careful. Which consideration determines the answer?

options.text: What the state practice act permits assistive personnel to perform
options.rationale: Scope for unlicensed staff is set in law. Being careful and having done it elsewhere cannot place a task inside a scope the act excludes.

options.text: Whether the nurse has observed her perform the task competently
options.rationale: Competence is one of the five rights of delegation and it only matters for a task that is delegable in the first place.

options.text: Whether the previous employer permitted it
options.rationale: Another state or another employer's practice has no authority here. This is the same error as a nurse assuming her old scope travels.

options.text: Whether the patient consents to the assistive personnel giving the drops
options.rationale: Consent covers whether care happens, not who may lawfully perform it.

questions.takeaway: Check whether a task may be delegated before asking whether this person can do it. Scope first, competence second.
questions.strategy: Two options describe genuine considerations that come later. Ask what has to be true before any of them matter.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: May it be delegated, then can she do it.
Both matter only after scope allows it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves what the state act permits.

questions.stem: A unit adopts an artificial intelligence tool that flags patients at risk of deterioration. It alerts on a patient whose pulse has risen from 74 to 108 and whose blood pressure has fallen to 94/56. The nurse had already noticed both changes. Which statement about her responsibility is accurate?

options.text: The tool assumes responsibility for identifying deterioration once implemented
options.rationale: Technology supports judgment and does not hold it. Nothing about implementing a tool moves accountability.

options.text: She remains accountable for her own assessment and for acting on her findings
options.rationale: A tool can surface a pattern. It cannot assess, and it cannot be answerable for what happens next.

options.text: Alerts from the tool may be documented in place of nursing assessment
options.rationale: An alert records what an algorithm noticed, not what a nurse found.

options.text: She should defer to the tool when her assessment disagrees with it
options.rationale: Her assessment is primary. A disagreement is a reason to look harder, not to stand down.

questions.takeaway: Emerging technology supports clinical judgment. Accountability for assessment and action stays with the nurse.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you she had already noticed. Ask what the tool actually changed about her obligations.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She had seen both changes herself.
Her assessment is the primary source.

elimination.verdict: That leaves her own accountability, unchanged by the tool.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A 34-year-old with no chronic conditions sees her family nurse practitioner for a sore throat and to discuss contraception. She is receiving [[1]].

A 58-year-old is admitted directly to intensive care after a myocardial infarction, needing continuous monitoring and intravenous medication. He is receiving [[2]].

Three weeks after a stroke, a patient enters a facility for daily physical and occupational therapy with the goal of going home. This is [[3]].

An 84-year-old with advanced dementia lives in a residential facility receiving help with all activities of daily living. Her condition is not expected to improve. This is [[4]].

options.text: primary care
options.rationale: First contact for a routine problem, with no specialist involved and an ongoing relationship.

options.text: secondary care
options.rationale: Secondary is hospital treatment for an acute episode, not a clinic visit for a sore throat.

options.text: tertiary care
options.rationale: Tertiary is highly specialized care for complex conditions.

options.text: preventive care
options.rationale: Preventive reduces risk factors before disease. She came with a symptom.

options.text: tertiary care
options.rationale: Intensive care is the specialized end of hospital treatment, which is what tertiary names.

options.text: secondary care
options.rationale: Close, and the near-miss. Secondary is admission for an acute episode; intensive care is the tertiary level of it.

options.text: restorative care
options.rationale: Restorative recovers function that has been lost. He is still in the acute event.

options.text: primary care
options.rationale: Primary is first contact and continuity, not an intensive care admission.

options.text: restorative care
options.rationale: Function was lost and is expected to return. Restorative exists to recover it.

options.text: continuing care
options.rationale: Continuing supports needs not expected to change. His are expected to improve.

options.text: acute care
options.rationale: The acute event was three weeks ago and he is medically stable.

options.text: tertiary care
options.rationale: Describes specialization, not the recovery of function.

options.text: continuing care
options.rationale: Needs are ongoing and not expected to improve, which is what continuing care is for.

options.text: restorative care
options.rationale: The near-miss. Both happen in facilities; only restorative expects improvement.

options.text: secondary care
options.rationale: No acute episode is being treated.

options.text: preventive care
options.rationale: Nothing here is aimed at preventing disease.

questions.takeaway: Six levels: preventive, primary, secondary, tertiary, restorative, continuing. Restorative and continuing are separated by the trajectory, not the setting.
questions.strategy: Two pairs get confused. Secondary versus tertiary is how specialized; restorative versus continuing is whether function is expected to return.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what is expected to happen
steps.detail: Improvement, or a stable ongoing need.
Admission is secondary; intensive care is tertiary.
Recovery is restorative; permanent need is continuing.

elimination.verdict: Primary, tertiary, restorative, continuing.

questions.stem: A patient with type 2 diabetes has not filled his insulin for two months and his A1C has risen from 7.4% to 10.2%. He works two jobs, has no car, and the pharmacy is a 40-minute bus ride each way with one change. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Reinforce teaching about the consequences of untreated diabetes
options.rationale: A correct nursing action that assumes the barrier is knowledge. Nothing here suggests he misunderstands; he cannot reach the pharmacy.

options.text: Ask the provider to simplify the insulin regimen
options.rationale: A reasonable move for a complex regimen. Simplifying a prescription he cannot collect changes nothing.

options.text: Document nonadherence to the medication regimen
options.rationale: Feels like doing something and is a label. Nonadherent places the failure in him and closes a question the stem has already answered.

options.text: Explore the transportation and pharmacy options available to him
options.rationale: The A1C rise proves the problem is real and worsening. The two jobs, no car and the bus route name the obstacle, and the obstacle is what can be acted on.

questions.takeaway: When a patient is not doing what the plan asks, the plan usually met a barrier it cannot pass. Find the barrier.
questions.strategy: One option names him rather than the obstacle. Labels close a problem instead of solving it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two jobs, no car, 40 minutes each way.
Assumes a knowledge gap the stem does not show.
One labels him, one changes a prescription he cannot collect.

elimination.verdict: That leaves exploring transport and pharmacy options.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old is discharged after abdominal surgery needing a daily dressing change for 14 days. The wound is 6 cm with moderate serous drainage. He lives alone, has never changed a dressing, and his daughter works weekdays. Which actions belong in the discharge plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Arrange home health services before he leaves
options.rationale: The daughter works weekdays and he has never done this. Someone skilled has to cover the days nobody is available.

options.text: Confirm by return demonstration that whoever will perform it can
options.rationale: Watching the skill performed is the only way to know it can be done. Saying it is understood is not evidence.

options.text: Provide written instructions in plain language
options.rationale: Something to refer to on day nine, when the teaching session is a memory.

options.text: Verify he can actually obtain the supplies
options.rationale: A perfect teaching session is worthless if the dressings never arrive.

options.text: Document that discharge teaching was completed
options.rationale: Records the nurse's action rather than his capability, and it makes no dressing change happen.

options.text: Schedule a surgeon follow-up in two weeks
options.rationale: Appropriate and it is thirteen days after the first dressing change is due.

questions.takeaway: Discharge planning asks four things: who will do it, can they demonstrate it, is the information usable, and are the supplies in place.
questions.strategy: Two options are reasonable things to do, and neither makes the dressing change happen tomorrow morning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask who does it on day one
steps.detail: Not him, and not his daughter on a weekday.
Records your action, not his capability.
Thirteen days too late for the first change.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.scenario: A 79-year-old is admitted with a wound infection. It is his third admission in four months, each for the same wound. He tells the nurse he has been changing the dressing himself because the home health visits stopped when his insurance changed. He has no car, and his daughter visits at weekends.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Refer to social work for insurance and home health options
options.rationale: The interruption is an access problem with an administrative cause, and social work is who resolves that.

options.text: Confirm who will perform the dressing change at home and verify they can
options.rationale: Three admissions say nobody competent is doing it. Establishing who, and checking they can, is what breaks the cycle.

options.text: Teach the dressing change again before discharge
options.rationale: A correct nursing action aimed at the wrong problem. He has been doing it for months; repeating the teaching changes nothing about why it is failing.

options.text: Document that he has been changing the dressing himself
options.rationale: Records the finding without addressing it, and he will return a fourth time.

options.text: Interrupted access to skilled care after an insurance change
options.rationale: He tells you the cause outright. The visits stopped for an administrative reason, not a clinical one.

options.text: Nonadherence to the wound care regimen
options.rationale: Blames him for something he did not choose. He has been doing the dressing himself precisely because nobody is coming.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about wound care
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he misunderstands. Assuming a knowledge gap is what produces the wrong action.

options.text: Lack of family support
options.rationale: Closer to true and still wrong. The daughter visits; the gap is skilled care on weekdays.

options.text: Whether home health visits have actually restarted
options.rationale: Measures whether the referral worked, which is the thing that was changed.

options.text: Whether he is readmitted within 30 days
options.rationale: The outcome the whole intervention exists to prevent, and the pattern that brought him in.

options.text: Whether the wound is smaller at the next visit
options.rationale: A real wound outcome, and it does not tell you whether the access problem was solved.

options.text: Whether he can name the signs of infection
options.rationale: Measurable, and it evaluates teaching nobody identified as the problem.

questions.takeaway: Access failures look like nonadherence. When a patient tells you why the plan stopped working, that is the problem statement.
questions.strategy: Two problem options blame the patient. Evaluate the thing you actually changed, not a related outcome that would move anyway.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The visits stopped when the insurance changed.
You referred and you verified, so measure those.

elimination.verdict: Refer and verify, for interrupted access, evaluated by restarted visits and readmission.

questions.stem: A nurse manager audits the unit after complaints that decisions were made without patients. Which staff actions reflect person-centered care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Involving the patient in decisions about the plan of care
options.rationale: Respect for the patient's values, preferences and expressed needs, which is the first of her eight dimensions.

options.text: Asking what matters most to the patient about this admission
options.rationale: Surfaces the preferences the rest of the plan has to fit around.

options.text: Including the family the patient designates in discussions
options.rationale: Involvement of family and friends, on the patient's terms rather than the institution's definition.

options.text: Sharing information in a form the patient can use
options.rationale: Information and education. Information he cannot use has not been shared.

options.text: Applying the same standardized plan to every patient with the diagnosis
options.rationale: Efficient, evidence-based, and the opposite of individualized.

options.text: Completing the plan before the admission interview to save the patient's time
options.rationale: Sounds considerate and produces a plan made without him, which is the complaint that started the audit.

questions.takeaway: Person-centered care: respect for values, coordination, information, physical comfort, emotional support, family involvement, continuity, and access.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses efficiency as the reason for excluding the patient, dressed as courtesy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Produces exactly the complaint being audited.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A hospital preparing a Magnet application must show how it measures the quality of nursing care specifically. Its dashboard reports 30-day readmission after myocardial infarction, surgical site infection after colorectal surgery, time from emergency arrival to provider, and fall rate with injury. Which measure serves the application?

options.text: Fall rate with injury
options.rationale: Falls track assessment, rounding, toileting schedules and environment, all of which are nursing work. The number moves when nursing care moves.

options.text: Surgical site infection after colorectal surgery
options.rationale: Reported and tracked, and driven substantially by operative technique and prophylaxis.

options.text: Thirty-day readmission after myocardial infarction
options.rationale: A genuine quality measure driven largely by medical management and what happens after discharge.

options.text: Time from emergency arrival to provider evaluation
options.rationale: A throughput measure reflecting staffing and capacity rather than nursing care.

questions.takeaway: A nursing-sensitive outcome is one that changes when nursing care changes. Falls, pressure injuries and line infections are the classic three.
questions.strategy: All four are real quality measures the hospital genuinely reports. Only one isolates nursing's contribution.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does this number move when nursing care moves?

steps.action: Cut the medical and surgical measures

elimination.verdict: That leaves fall rate with injury.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches a community group about where to go for different needs. Several participants describe using the emergency department for routine problems. Which statement by a participant indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "An immunization clinic is preventive care, because it stops me getting ill."
options.rationale: Accurate. Preventive care reduces and controls risk factors before disease appears.

options.text: "The emergency department is the same as seeing a primary provider."
options.rationale: The emergency department treats acute episodes. It offers no continuity, no prevention, and no relationship over time, which is what primary care is for.

options.text: "Rehabilitation after a stroke is restorative care, because the goal is getting function back."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the reason restorative is separate from continuing care.

options.text: "Being admitted for intravenous antibiotics is secondary care."
options.rationale: Accurate. Secondary care is hospital treatment for an acute episode.

questions.takeaway: Primary care is first contact plus continuity and prevention. An emergency department provides none of the last three.
questions.strategy: Three statements are accurate as spoken. The fourth is the behavior the session set out to change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Treating the emergency department as a provider.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the emergency department statement.

questions.stem: A nurse manager presents to the board on the challenges facing nursing over the next decade. Which set of factors matches what the profession identifies?

options.text: An aging patient population, rising costs, and falling patient satisfaction scores
options.rationale: Costs and satisfaction are genuine issues in health care delivery. They are consequences of the workforce problem rather than its drivers.

options.text: Physician shortages, expanded advanced practice scope, and growth in telehealth
options.rationale: Names one real factor and pairs it with two developments that relieve workforce pressure rather than cause it.

options.text: An aging baby boomer generation, physician shortage and uneven distribution, nurse retirements, and uncertainty over health care reform
options.rationale: Demand and supply move against each other: the boomers reach their years of heaviest health care use exactly as the nurses who would care for them retire.

options.text: Nurse retirements, competency concerns, and variation in prelicensure preparation
options.rationale: Retirements belong on the list. Competency and preparation are separate professional issues.

questions.takeaway: Four challenges: the aging baby boomer generation, physician shortage and uneven distribution, the rate of nurse retirements, and uncertainty over health care reform.
questions.strategy: Every distractor contains at least one true factor. Ask which set names drivers rather than consequences.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Costs and satisfaction result from the shortage.
Expanded scope and telehealth ease pressure.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the four the profession names.

questions.nursesNote: 1015: Patient is 71, discharged home four days ago after a hip replacement. Lives alone in a two-story house with the bathroom upstairs. Daughter visits at weekends. Reports she has not been able to shower since coming home and has been sleeping in a downstairs chair. Physical therapy was arranged twice weekly but no visit has taken place. Says she is eating 'whatever is easy to reach'. Wound is clean and dry with no redness. Pain is 3 of 10 and controlled with acetaminophen. Temperature 36.8 C, blood pressure 128/76.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate the discharge plan has failed.

segments.text: Lives alone in a two-story house with the bathroom upstairs
segments.rationale: The environment was never matched to her mobility. She cannot reach her own bathroom.

segments.text: Has not been able to shower since coming home
segments.rationale: A direct consequence of the environment, and an unmet basic need four days in.

segments.text: Sleeping in a downstairs chair
segments.rationale: She has no accessible bed. This raises risks for skin, sleep and further deconditioning.

segments.text: Physical therapy arranged twice weekly but no visit has taken place
segments.rationale: Arranging a service is not the same as the service happening. Nobody verified it started.

segments.text: Eating whatever is easy to reach
segments.rationale: Nutrition has become a function of what she can physically get to, which is a mobility problem presenting as a dietary one.

segments.text: Wound is clean and dry with no redness
segments.rationale: A normal finding. The wound is the part that is going well.

segments.text: Pain is 3 of 10 and controlled with acetaminophen
segments.rationale: Controlled pain on a simple analgesic four days after joint replacement is an expected finding.

segments.text: Daughter visits at weekends
segments.rationale: A fact about her support, and it was known before discharge. It is context rather than a failure.

questions.takeaway: Discharge planning fails at the point where the plan meets the home. Arranging a service is not the same as confirming it happened.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal or expected and they are there to be left alone. Ask which findings describe a plan that did not survive contact with her house.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the clinical from the situational
steps.detail: The wound and the pain are fine.
That she could reach a bathroom and that therapy would start.
The daughter's schedule was known beforehand.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s5: environment, hygiene, sleep, missing therapy, and reachable food.

questions.scenario: Maria is 68 with well-controlled hypertension. She takes her medication daily, gardens, volunteers at her church, and says she feels healthy and happy despite occasional knee pain.
questions.stem: For each model of health, indicate whether it would judge Maria healthy or not healthy.

rows.text: Clinical model
rows.rationale: Health is the absence of disease. She has a diagnosis and knee pain, so this model calls her unhealthy regardless of how she lives.

rows.text: Role performance model
rows.rationale: She fulfills her roles: she gardens and volunteers. Function is what this model measures.

rows.text: Adaptive model
rows.rationale: She has adapted to a chronic condition and manages it daily. Adaptation is the measure.

rows.text: Eudaimonistic model
rows.rationale: She reports satisfaction and meaning through her volunteering. Self-actualization is the measure.

questions.takeaway: Only the clinical model says a person with a chronic condition cannot be healthy. The other three judge function, adaptation, or fulfillment.
questions.strategy: One model disagrees with the other three, and the reason is that it looks only at the diagnosis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only one is looking at her blood pressure.
She functions, adapts, and finds meaning.

elimination.verdict: Clinical says no. The rest say yes.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has stopped attending the choir he sang with for twenty years because of breathlessness. He manages his inhalers correctly and says he no longer feels like himself. Which model of health best captures what he has lost?

options.text: Clinical, because his lung disease is progressing
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem says the disease has worsened. He describes a loss that the clinical model cannot see.

options.text: Adaptive, because he has failed to adjust to his diagnosis
options.rationale: He uses his inhalers correctly and has changed his activity. That is adaptation, not failure to adapt.

options.text: Role performance, because he cannot perform his usual activities
options.rationale: The near-miss, and singing in a choir is not a societal or work role. What he lost was meaning rather than function.

options.text: Eudaimonistic, because meaning and life satisfaction have gone
options.rationale: He is managing the disease and performing daily tasks. What has gone is the thing that made his life feel like his own.

questions.takeaway: Eudaimonistic health is self-actualization: satisfaction, meaning, and growth. It is the model that sees what the others miss.
questions.strategy: Two options describe things he is actually doing well. The near-miss turns a source of meaning into a role.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he is still doing

steps.detail: A choir is meaning, not a societal role.

elimination.verdict: That leaves eudaimonistic.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses two patients with the same diagnosis and the same severity whose management of it differs greatly. Which variables influence health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Genetics and age
options.rationale: Both named, and both non-modifiable.

options.text: Environment and lifestyle
options.rationale: Two of the seven, and the ones nursing intervention most often reaches.

options.text: Culture and socioeconomic status
options.rationale: Culture shapes what health means to a person; socioeconomic status shapes what is available to them.

options.text: Access to health care
options.rationale: The last of the seven. A plan a patient cannot reach does not work.

options.text: The severity of the diagnosis itself
options.rationale: The stem holds severity constant between the two patients, so it cannot explain the difference between them.

options.text: The nurse's own health beliefs
options.rationale: They shape the encounter and are not a variable influencing the patient's health.

questions.takeaway: Seven variables influence health: genetics, age, environment, lifestyle, culture, socioeconomic status, and access to health care.
questions.strategy: The stem holds two things constant on purpose. Anything that does not vary cannot explain a difference.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: It cannot explain a difference it does not vary with.
About the nurse, not the patient.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old develops crushing chest pain while mowing the lawn. He sits down, tells his wife it is indigestion, and takes an antacid. Which stage of illness behavior does this represent?

options.text: Assumption of the sick role
options.rationale: Stage two, where a person accepts being ill and seeks relief from usual duties. He is minimizing rather than accepting.

options.text: Medical care contact
options.rationale: Stage three, and he has contacted nobody.

options.text: Symptom experience
options.rationale: Stage one. He has noticed something is wrong and is interpreting it, which is exactly what this stage is.

options.text: Dependent patient role
options.rationale: Stage four, where the person accepts care from others. He has not entered the system at all.

questions.takeaway: Five stages: symptom experience, assumption of the sick role, medical care contact, dependent patient role, recovery and rehabilitation.
questions.strategy: Every distractor is a later stage. Ask how far into the sequence he has actually travelled.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Noticed a symptom and named it something harmless.
He has told nobody and accepted nothing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves symptom experience.

questions.stem: A self-employed builder has had a persistent cough for six weeks. He tells the nurse he has been calling it a chest cold because he cannot afford to lose a week of work. Which concept explains his delay in seeking care?

options.text: Assumption of the sick role
options.rationale: Stage two, where a person accepts being ill. He is doing the opposite.

options.text: Illness behavior
options.rationale: Illness behavior is how a person monitors, interprets, and responds to symptoms. Calling a six-week cough a chest cold is the interpretation; not seeking care is the response.

options.text: Perceived severity
options.rationale: A Health Belief Model construct about how serious he judges it to be. It is one input into illness behavior rather than the concept itself.

options.text: The dependent patient role
options.rationale: Stage four, where care from others is accepted. He has not entered care.

questions.takeaway: Illness behavior is influenced by culture, family, education, and past experiences.
questions.strategy: Three options name a specific stage or construct. Ask which term covers the whole pattern of interpreting and responding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Interpreting a symptom and deciding not to act.
He has neither accepted the sick role nor entered care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves illness behavior.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse plans care for a community with a high rate of cardiovascular disease.

Running a school program that teaches children never to start smoking is [[1]].

Offering blood pressure checks at a community event is [[2]].

Running a cardiac rehabilitation group for people who have had a myocardial infarction is [[3]].

Teaching a patient with diabetes how to inspect his feet is [[4]].

options.text: primary prevention
options.rationale: Acts before any disease exists, in people who are currently well.

options.text: secondary prevention
options.rationale: Secondary looks for disease that is present but not yet symptomatic.

options.text: tertiary prevention
options.rationale: Tertiary limits complications in people who already have the disease.

options.text: health promotion
options.rationale: The near-miss. Health promotion is broad and aimed at wellbeing; this targets one specific disease, which makes it prevention.

options.text: secondary prevention
options.rationale: Screening detects disease early, before symptoms bring someone in.

options.text: primary prevention
options.rationale: Primary acts before disease occurs. A screening looks for disease already present.

options.text: tertiary prevention
options.rationale: Tertiary manages a disease already diagnosed.

options.text: secondary care
options.rationale: A level of the health care system, not a level of prevention. Same word, unrelated systems.

options.text: tertiary prevention
options.rationale: The disease has happened. Rehabilitation limits further damage and loss of function.

options.text: secondary prevention
options.rationale: Detection is past. The diagnosis is established.

options.text: restorative care
options.rationale: A level of care rather than a level of prevention.

options.text: primary prevention
options.rationale: Far too late for primary, which acts before disease.

options.text: tertiary prevention
options.rationale: He already has diabetes. Foot inspection exists to prevent ulceration and amputation.

options.text: primary prevention
options.rationale: The disease is present, so nothing here prevents it occurring.

options.text: secondary prevention
options.rationale: The near-miss. He is looking for early skin changes, and the frame is a complication of a known disease rather than detection of a new one.

options.text: health education
options.rationale: It is health education, and the question asks which level of prevention it serves.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevents disease occurring. Secondary detects it early. Tertiary limits complications once it exists.
questions.strategy: Ask one question of each: does the person have the disease yet? No is primary, maybe is secondary, yes is tertiary.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Secondary prevention is screening; secondary care is hospital treatment.

elimination.verdict: Primary, secondary, tertiary, tertiary.

questions.stem: A 47-year-old smoker whose father died of lung cancer at 60 tells the nurse he knows smoking is dangerous but does not believe it will happen to him. Which Health Belief Model construct does this reflect?

options.text: Low perceived severity
options.rationale: Severity is how serious he judges the outcome to be. He watched his father die of it, so he is unlikely to underrate its seriousness.

options.text: Low perceived benefits
options.rationale: Benefits concern whether he thinks quitting would help. He has not said quitting would not work.

options.text: Low perceived susceptibility
options.rationale: He accepts the risk exists and does not accept it applies to him. That gap is susceptibility.

options.text: High perceived barriers
options.rationale: Barriers are what stands in the way, such as cost or withdrawal. He has named none.

questions.takeaway: Health Belief Model: perceived susceptibility, perceived severity, perceived benefits, perceived barriers.
questions.strategy: The family history is placed to rule one option out. Someone who watched a parent die of a disease knows how serious it is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That it will happen to him.

elimination.verdict: That leaves low perceived susceptibility.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a patient who wants to lose weight and has not managed to change anything in six months. Which barriers to behavior change should the nurse assess? Select all that apply.

options.text: Cost of the changes involved
options.rationale: A named barrier, and gym fees or fresh food can make a plan unreachable.

options.text: Time available to make the change
options.rationale: Named, and it is why plans built for someone with free evenings fail.

options.text: Fear about what change might involve
options.rationale: Named, and it includes fear of failing again.

options.text: Health literacy
options.rationale: Named. A plan he cannot read or interpret is not a plan he can follow.

options.text: His motivation to change
options.rationale: Motivation is one of the four requirements for change, not a barrier. The stem already tells you he wants to.

options.text: His genetic predisposition to weight gain
options.rationale: A non-modifiable risk factor. It affects the difficulty of the goal rather than standing between him and starting.

questions.takeaway: Change requires motivation, knowledge, resources, and support. Barriers include cost, time, fear, and health literacy.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a requirement for change rather than a barrier, and the stem has already established it is present.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He wants to; that is given.
Non-modifiable, and not a barrier to starting.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse plans a program for a workplace. Which activity is health promotion rather than illness prevention?

options.text: An on-site influenza vaccination clinic
options.rationale: Illness prevention with a specific focus: one disease, one intervention.

options.text: Mammography screening arranged for eligible staff
options.rationale: Specific and aimed at detecting one disease early.

options.text: A campaign encouraging seatbelt use in company vehicles
options.rationale: Illness prevention. It targets a specific harm, and her slide lists seatbelts under primary prevention.

options.text: A stress management and exercise program open to all staff
options.rationale: Health promotion is broad and aimed at increasing wellbeing and maximizing health potential. It targets no single disease.

questions.takeaway: Health promotion improves wellness and has a broad focus. Illness prevention targets a specific disease or harm.
questions.strategy: Three options name one disease or one harm each. Ask which one has no particular target.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the one with no target

elimination.verdict: That leaves the stress and exercise program.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a 52-year-old's risk factors: he smokes 20 a day, drinks heavily at weekends, is sedentary, has a body mass index of 34, has a father who died of myocardial infarction at 55, and is of an ethnicity with raised cardiovascular risk. Which of his risk factors are modifiable? Select all that apply.

options.text: Smoking 20 cigarettes a day
options.rationale: Named as modifiable, and the single change with the largest effect here.

options.text: Heavy alcohol use
options.rationale: Alcohol and drug use are named as modifiable.

options.text: Being sedentary
options.rationale: Activity level can be changed, which makes it modifiable.

options.text: A body mass index of 34
options.rationale: Weight is named as modifiable.

options.text: His father's death from myocardial infarction at 55
options.rationale: Family history is genetics, and genetics is non-modifiable. It raises the urgency of changing the others.

options.text: His ethnicity
options.rationale: Named as non-modifiable, and it is never a target for intervention.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable: smoking, diet, alcohol and drug use, weight. Non-modifiable: age, genetics, biological sex, ethnicity.
questions.strategy: Two of his risk factors are real and cannot be changed. They alter how urgent the others are, not whether they are targets.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he could change tomorrow

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse on a busy oncology unit finds herself irritable with colleagues, dreading her shifts, and no longer moved by patients' distress. She has worked twelve-hour shifts without a break for three months. Which is she most likely experiencing?

options.text: Compassion fatigue
options.rationale: Emotional and physical exhaustion from prolonged caregiving. The decreased empathy alongside irritability and cynicism is the recognizable picture.

options.text: A normal adjustment to a demanding specialty
options.rationale: Normalizes a set of findings her slide names as a syndrome, and it is how the problem goes unaddressed.

options.text: Ineffective coping with the patients' diagnoses
options.rationale: Closer, and it locates the problem in her response to individual patients rather than in cumulative exposure.

options.text: An underlying mood disorder requiring referral
options.rationale: Possible, and the occupational pattern and timing point first to compassion fatigue. Assessment precedes that conclusion.

questions.takeaway: Compassion fatigue: emotional exhaustion, irritability, cynicism, decreased empathy, burnout. Prevention is boundaries, self-care, peer support, mindfulness, debriefing, and counselling when needed.
questions.strategy: One option normalizes it. One reaches for a diagnosis before assessing. Ask what the three months of unbroken shifts adds.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Irritability, dread, lost empathy, no breaks.
These are named findings, not adjustment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves compassion fatigue.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what makes the WHO definition of health different from earlier definitions. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: It defines health as the ability to fulfill societal and work roles
options.rationale: That is the role performance model, not the WHO definition.

options.text: It defines health as the ability to adapt to environmental change
options.rationale: That is the adaptive model.

options.text: It defines health as a fixed state a person either has or does not have
options.rationale: Reverses a central point. Health is dynamic and constantly changing, and it sits on a continuum.

options.text: It defines health as complete physical, mental, and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease
options.rationale: The phrase not merely the absence of disease is what makes it broader, and it is why a person with a chronic condition can still be healthy.

questions.takeaway: WHO: complete physical, mental, and social wellbeing, not merely the absence of disease. Six dimensions: physical, emotional, intellectual, social, spiritual, environmental.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are models of health offered as the definition. One contradicts the continuum.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Not merely the absence of disease.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the WHO definition.

questions.nursesNote: 1100: Patient is 61, attends for a routine review. Reports sleeping four to five hours most nights since being moved to night shifts six months ago. Has gained 8 kg in that time. Says he eats from vending machines at work because nothing else is open. Blood pressure 152/94, up from 128/80 a year ago. Smokes 15 a day, unchanged for 20 years. Walks his dog twice daily. Says he has stopped seeing friends because his hours no longer match theirs. Temperature 36.6 C. Attends his annual review every year without fail.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that represent modifiable risks the nurse can address.

segments.text: Sleeping four to five hours most nights
segments.rationale: Sleep hygiene is named under health promotion, and short sleep affects weight, blood pressure and mood.

segments.text: Gained 8 kg in six months
segments.rationale: Weight is a named modifiable risk factor, and the rate of gain makes it recent and reversible.

segments.text: Eats from vending machines because nothing else is open
segments.rationale: Diet is modifiable, and he has named the barrier himself, which is what makes it addressable.

segments.text: Blood pressure 152/94, up from 128/80 a year ago
segments.rationale: A change from his own baseline, and it is the consequence the other findings are producing.

segments.text: Smokes 15 a day
segments.rationale: The first named modifiable risk factor, and unchanged does not mean unchangeable.

segments.text: Has stopped seeing friends because his hours no longer match theirs
segments.rationale: Social isolation affects the social dimension of health and removes the support systems that behavior change requires.

segments.text: Walks his dog twice daily
segments.rationale: Something he is already doing well. It is a strength, not a risk.

segments.text: Temperature 36.6 C
segments.rationale: A normal finding, included to be left alone.

segments.text: Attends his annual review every year without fail
segments.rationale: A health-seeking behavior and another strength. It is why you are able to catch this at all.

questions.takeaway: Modifiable risks are the ones nursing can act on. Strengths matter too, and they are not risks.
questions.strategy: Two findings describe things he is doing right, and one is normal. A strength offered among risk factors is there to be left alone.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The dog walk and the attendance are strengths.
Night shifts changed sleep, food, weight and pressure.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s6: sleep, weight, diet, pressure, smoking, isolation.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares discharge teaching for a patient newly diagnosed with heart failure. Which content is the priority before he leaves?

options.text: The pathophysiology of how heart failure develops
options.rationale: Interesting and it does not change what he does on Tuesday when his weight is up two kilograms.

options.text: When to notify the provider and how to recognize the signs that matter
options.rationale: Health education exists so patients can make informed decisions. Knowing when to seek help is what prevents the readmission.

options.text: A complete list of his medication side effects
options.rationale: Medication instruction is named content, and an exhaustive list without priorities is not usable at home.

options.text: The names and roles of the team members who cared for him
options.rationale: Courteous, and it does not prevent a complication.

questions.takeaway: Health education asks what the patient needs to know before discharge to stay healthy and prevent complications. When to seek help sits at the top.
questions.strategy: Three options contain real information. Ask which one he will act on at home.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what he does with each
Cut the exhaustive list and the team names

elimination.verdict: That leaves when to notify the provider.

questions.stem: A patient with a new diagnosis of type 2 diabetes attends a follow-up having learned to adjust his diet, check his glucose, and plan around his work shifts. He says it has become routine. Which model of health evaluates him most favorably?

options.text: The clinical model, because his glucose is being monitored
options.rationale: The clinical model measures absence of disease. He has diabetes, so this model does not judge him healthy.

options.text: The adaptive model, because he has adjusted to the change
options.rationale: Adaptive health is the ability to adapt flexibly. Coping with a new diagnosis is her own example of it.

options.text: The role performance model, because he keeps working
options.rationale: Plausible, and the stem emphasizes how he adjusted rather than what roles he fulfills.

options.text: The eudaimonistic model, because he has found meaning
options.rationale: He describes routine, not meaning or growth. This model would need more than competent management.

questions.takeaway: Adaptive health is resilience and flexible adjustment. Her examples are coping with a new diagnosis and adjusting after an amputation.
questions.strategy: The stem emphasizes one particular thing about him. Ask what word describes what he did.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Adjusted his life around a new condition.
One is function, one needs meaning.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the adaptive model.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a community where many residents have no supermarket within three miles, limited bus services, and high unemployment. Rates of diabetes are well above the national average. Which concept explains the link?

options.text: Social determinants of health
options.rationale: Non-medical conditions where people live, learn, work and age, which shape daily wellbeing and life expectancy. Transportation, food security and employment are her examples.

options.text: Non-modifiable risk factors
options.rationale: Genetics, age, sex and ethnicity. The conditions described are features of a place, and places can change.

options.text: Illness behavior
options.rationale: How individuals monitor and respond to symptoms. The stem describes conditions before anyone becomes symptomatic.

options.text: The clinical model of health
options.rationale: A way of defining health, not an explanation of why a population's rates differ.

questions.takeaway: Social determinants of health are non-medical conditions with major effects on health, daily wellbeing, and life expectancy.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats a feature of a neighborhood as though it were fixed like genetics.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut illness behavior and the clinical model
steps.detail: One is about symptoms, one is a definition.

elimination.verdict: That leaves social determinants of health.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what Healthy People 2030 sets out to do. Which answer is accurate?

options.text: Improve health and wellbeing, eliminate disparities, promote healthy environments, and increase health equity
options.rationale: The four aims, and the key focus areas run through social determinants, preventive care, community health, and health literacy.

options.text: Set clinical treatment standards for the management of chronic disease
options.rationale: It sets population objectives rather than clinical protocols.

options.text: Define the scope of nursing practice across the states
options.rationale: That is the Nurse Practice Acts, which are state law.

options.text: Establish the accreditation requirements for health care organizations
options.rationale: Accreditation is the work of bodies such as The Joint Commission.

questions.takeaway: Healthy People 2030: improve health and wellbeing, eliminate disparities, promote healthy environments, increase health equity.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real functions performed by other bodies entirely.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what kind of document it is

elimination.verdict: That leaves the four aims.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses health and wellness with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Someone with a chronic illness can still be healthy under most models."
options.rationale: Accurate. Only the clinical model says otherwise.

options.text: "Health sits on a continuum rather than being present or absent."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it runs from high-level wellness through neutral health and illness to death.

options.text: "Learning to manage my blood pressure now counts as primary prevention."
options.rationale: Managing a diagnosed condition is tertiary prevention. Primary acts before disease exists, and hers already does.

options.text: "Illness affects the family as well as the patient."
options.rationale: Accurate. Caregiver burden, financial stress, role adjustment, and emotional distress.

questions.takeaway: Primary prevents disease occurring. Secondary detects it early. Tertiary manages an established condition to limit complications.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her key takeaways correctly. The fourth misplaces a level of prevention.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chronic illness, continuum, family impact. All accurate.
Management of an existing condition is tertiary.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the primary prevention statement.

questions.scenario: A 44-year-old attends a follow-up three months after being told she has prediabetes. She has not started the exercise plan or changed her diet. She says she understands why it matters, works two cleaning jobs with a two-hour commute, and that the recommended gym costs more than her weekly food budget. Her weight is unchanged and her fasting glucose has risen from 112 to 119 mg/dL.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Build a plan around activity that costs nothing and fits her existing day
options.rationale: Cost and time are the two barriers she has named. A plan that avoids both is one she can actually start.

options.text: Connect her with community food and activity resources she can reach
options.rationale: Advocating for resources is part of the nursing role in risk reduction, and it addresses the barrier rather than the behavior.

options.text: Re-teach the risks of progressing from prediabetes to diabetes
options.rationale: Correct teaching aimed at the wrong problem. She has told you she understands why it matters.

options.text: Document that she has not adhered to the recommended plan
options.rationale: Records the outcome and calls it her failure. The stem has already named what stood in the way.

options.text: Barriers of cost and time preventing a plan she is motivated to follow
options.rationale: Motivation and knowledge are both present. What is missing is resources and time, which are two of the four requirements for change.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about diabetes prevention
options.rationale: She states she understands. Assuming a knowledge gap is what produces more teaching and no change.

options.text: Lack of motivation to change her health behaviors
options.rationale: Blames her for a plan that never fit her life. Nothing in the stem suggests she does not want to.

options.text: Non-modifiable risk factors driving her rising glucose
options.rationale: Her risks here are diet and activity, both modifiable. Naming them fixed would end the intervention.

options.text: Whether she has started and sustained any of the agreed activity
options.rationale: Measures whether the redesigned plan was actually usable, which is what changed.

options.text: Her fasting glucose at the next visit
options.rationale: The outcome the whole intervention exists to move, and it is already trending the wrong way.

options.text: Whether she can state three complications of diabetes
options.rationale: Tests knowledge she already has, and it evaluates teaching nobody identified as the problem.

options.text: Whether she attends her next appointment
options.rationale: Worth noticing, and attendance does not tell you whether the plan worked.

questions.takeaway: Change requires motivation, knowledge, resources, and support. When the first two are present and nothing happens, look at the last two.
questions.strategy: Two problem options blame her motivation or her knowledge. She has told you she has both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Motivation yes, knowledge yes, resources no, time no.
Knowledge deficit and lack of motivation.
You redesigned the plan, so measure whether she started.

elimination.verdict: Redesign and connect resources, for cost and time barriers, evaluated by uptake and glucose.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to explain why health is described as dynamic. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: A person moves along a continuum from high-level wellness through neutral health and illness
options.rationale: Health is constantly changing, and the same person occupies different points at different times.

options.text: Health changes only when a new diagnosis is made
options.rationale: Ties health to diagnosis, which is the clinical model rather than the continuum.

options.text: A person is either well or ill, with no state in between
options.rationale: Neutral health sits between wellness and illness on her continuum.

options.text: Health improves steadily with age as a person adapts
options.rationale: Nothing suggests a direction. Movement along the continuum goes both ways.

questions.takeaway: The continuum runs from high-level wellness through neutral health to illness and death, and a person moves along it in both directions.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat health as a fixed state. One invents a direction of travel.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves movement along the continuum.

questions.stem: Two nurses complete identical admission assessments on a patient with pneumonia. The first works quickly, says little, and leaves. The second introduces herself, sits at eye level, explains each step, and asks what worries the patient most today. Both assessments are clinically complete. What distinguishes the second nurse's care?

options.text: The second nurse gathered more assessment data
options.rationale: Identical assessments. Asking what worries her is presence rather than an extra data point, though it may well produce one.

options.text: The second nurse was more clinically competent
options.rationale: The stem states both assessments were complete. Competence is not what separates them.

options.text: How the care was delivered, which is as much a part of caring as what was done
options.rationale: Caring involves both what nurses do and how they do it. The assessment data is identical; the experience of being assessed is not.

options.text: The second nurse spent longer with the patient
options.rationale: Time is a consequence rather than the distinction. Sitting at eye level and introducing yourself cost seconds.

questions.takeaway: Caring is what nurses do and how they do it. Two technically identical encounters can differ entirely in whether the patient feels cared for.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you both were competent and both were complete. Whatever separates them is not clinical.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves how the care was delivered.

questions.stem: A hospital reviews patient comments to learn which nursing behaviors patients describe as caring. Which behaviors do patients most often name? Select all that apply.

options.text: Listening carefully
options.rationale: The behavior patients name most, and the one that costs nothing but attention.

options.text: Explaining procedures
options.rationale: Named directly, and it turns something done to a patient into something done with them.

options.text: Treating them with dignity
options.rationale: Named, and it is the thread running through the bathing and hygiene examples.

options.text: Responding promptly
options.rationale: Named. A call light answered quickly says something before anyone speaks.

options.text: Protecting privacy
options.rationale: Named, and it is what makes an exposing task tolerable.

options.text: Completing tasks without disturbing the patient
options.rationale: Efficient and it is the first nurse in her scenario. Minimal disturbance is not the same as caring.

options.text: Withholding difficult information until the patient seems ready
options.rationale: Protective in intention and closer to false reassurance than to caring. Patients name honesty and explanation.

questions.takeaway: Patients name: listens carefully, explains procedures, treats with dignity, responds promptly, shows kindness, includes family, protects privacy, advocates.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe things a nurse might do out of consideration. Ask whether patients actually name them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Listen, explain, dignity, promptness, kindness, family, privacy, advocacy.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A patient with a new cancer diagnosis says she does not know how she will tell her children. The nurse has six other patients and a medication round due. Which response demonstrates presence?

options.text: Offer to arrange a referral to the social worker
options.rationale: An appropriate referral, and offered now it moves her distress to someone else instead of meeting it.

options.text: Say you will come back after the medication round and follow through
options.rationale: Better than dismissing her, and it still asks a frightened woman to hold it for an hour. Presence is a few minutes now.

options.text: Tell her many families find a way and she will too
options.rationale: False reassurance. It is meant kindly and it closes the conversation she has just opened.

options.text: Sit down, put the tasks aside for a few minutes, and let her talk
options.rationale: Presence means full attention. Sitting signals you are not about to leave, and sometimes the most therapeutic intervention is simply being present.

questions.takeaway: Presence: sit at eye level, make eye contact, minimize distractions, listen without interrupting, validate feelings.
questions.strategy: Three options are things a considerate nurse might genuinely say. Ask which one meets her now.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both move it elsewhere or later.

elimination.verdict: That leaves sitting down with her.

questions.stem: A patient with heart failure has not been taking his diuretic. Which question reflects Caritas Coaching?

options.text: "Would it help if I explained how the medication works?"
options.rationale: Offers teaching before knowing whether teaching is what is needed.

options.text: "What makes taking the water tablet difficult?"
options.rationale: Opens with the obstacle and assumes he has a reason. Caritas Coaching partners rather than instructs, and it helps patients find their own solutions.

options.text: "Do you understand why the water tablet matters?"
