options.rationale: Checks knowledge and implies the problem is his understanding. It also invites a defensive yes.

options.text: "Did you take your medication this week?"
options.rationale: Her own example of the closed question Caritas Coaching replaces. It produces a yes or no and stops there.

questions.takeaway: Caritas Coaching listens first, asks open-ended questions, encourages reflection, supports the patient's goals, builds confidence, and partners.
questions.strategy: One distractor is the exact question her slide contrasts against. Ask which one cannot be answered with a single word.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Test each for a one-word answer
steps.detail: Three can be answered yes or no.
Assumes the gap before finding it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking what makes it difficult.

questions.scenario: A nurse cares for a patient admitted with pneumonia over one shift.
questions.stem: For each statement the nurse makes, indicate whether it is therapeutic or a communication block.

rows.text: "I can see this is difficult."
rows.rationale: Validates the feeling without judging it, and it invites him to say more.

rows.text: "Everything will be fine."
rows.rationale: False reassurance. It is meant kindly and it tells him the subject is closed.

rows.text: "What concerns you the most today?"
rows.rationale: Open-ended, and it lets him set the agenda rather than the nurse.

rows.text: "Try not to worry about it."
rows.rationale: Dismisses the worry rather than exploring it, and it asks him to manage his feeling alone.

rows.text: "Tell me more."
rows.rationale: The shortest way to keep someone talking, and it commits the nurse to listening.

rows.text: Finishing his sentence when he pauses to catch his breath
rows.rationale: Interrupting, and in a breathless patient it also takes away the time he needs to speak.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic: I can see this is difficult, tell me more, what concerns you most, how can I help. Blocks: false reassurance, don't worry, interrupting.
questions.strategy: The blocks all sound kind. Ask whether the statement opens the conversation or ends it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does he say more, or stop?
Fine and don't worry both close it.

elimination.verdict: Three therapeutic, three blocking.

questions.stem: A nursing student says caring means being kind to patients. Which response by the preceptor is most accurate?

options.text: Caring includes competence, so a nurse who is warm but cannot perform the skill is not providing caring care
options.rationale: The definition names compassion, respect, presence, empathy and competence together. Professional competence and caring work together.

options.text: Kindness is the central element and the clinical skills follow from it
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship. Neither one produces the other, and both are required.

options.text: Kindness matters most with patients who are frightened or distressed
options.rationale: Makes caring conditional on the patient's state, and it applies to every interaction.

options.text: Caring is an attitude, while competence is a separate professional obligation
options.rationale: Separates what her slide joins. Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction.

questions.takeaway: Caring is intentional concern for wellbeing through compassion, respect, presence, empathy, and competence. Competence is part of it, not a separate track.
questions.strategy: Three options treat caring and competence as two different things. Ask what the definition actually contains.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Caring is not reserved for distress.

elimination.verdict: That leaves competence being part of caring.

questions.stem: A nurse performs a bed bath for a patient who is embarrassed about needing help. Which actions demonstrate caring during this skill? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explain each step before doing it
options.rationale: Turns something done to him into something he can anticipate and consent to.

options.text: Keep him covered except for the area being washed
options.rationale: Protecting privacy and promoting dignity, which is her own example for bathing.

options.text: Ask what he would prefer to do himself
options.rationale: Preserves what independence he has, and it treats him as a participant.

options.text: Close the door and the curtain before starting
options.rationale: Privacy is named among the caring behaviors patients value.

options.text: Work quickly so the embarrassing part is over sooner
options.rationale: Sounds considerate and produces the first nurse in her scenario: efficient, minimal conversation, no presence.

options.text: Tell him there is nothing to be embarrassed about
options.rationale: Dismisses the feeling rather than validating it. His embarrassment is real whether or not it is necessary.

questions.takeaway: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction. For bathing, that means privacy and dignity specifically.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are kindly meant. One rushes, one tells him how to feel.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse administering an intravenous antibiotic explains what it is for, what side effects to report, and answers the patient's questions while the infusion runs. Which principle does this demonstrate?

options.text: Caring behaviors are most important during invasive procedures
options.rationale: Ranks the skills, and her slide names vital signs, medication, bathing, and wound care alike.

options.text: Medication administration requires verbal consent for each dose
options.rationale: Explaining is not the same as obtaining consent, and no such requirement is described.

options.text: Patient education should be scheduled separately from procedures
options.rationale: Reverses her point. Teaching while administering is her own example.

options.text: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction
options.rationale: Caring is not a separate activity performed when there is time. The medication round became teaching and presence without adding a task.

questions.takeaway: Caring should be present during every skill. Vital signs, medication, bathing and wound care are all opportunities.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes caring a separate scheduled activity. One reserves it for the invasive tasks.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing, other than how she did it.
Teaching while administering is the example.

elimination.verdict: That leaves every skill being a caring interaction.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reflects on her practice after a shift.

Sitting at eye level and listening without interrupting demonstrates [[1]].

Asking a patient what makes taking his medication difficult, rather than whether he took it, is [[2]].

Saying "don't worry, everything will be fine" is an example of [[3]].

According to Watson, caring is best described as [[4]].

options.text: presence
options.rationale: Full attention, given deliberately. Sitting, eye contact, minimizing distractions, and not interrupting.

options.text: empathy
options.rationale: The near-miss. Empathy is understanding what he feels; presence is the behavior that makes room for him to say it.

options.text: advocacy
options.rationale: Acting on his behalf with others.

options.text: competence
options.rationale: The skill to perform care safely.

options.text: Caritas Coaching
options.rationale: Partnering instead of instructing, and helping him find his own solution. Her exact contrast.

options.text: health teaching
options.rationale: Teaching supplies information. The question supplies nothing and asks for his.

options.text: therapeutic silence
options.rationale: Silence gives time to think. This is an open question.

options.text: motivational reassurance
options.rationale: Not a named technique, and reassurance is something Caritas Coaching avoids.

options.text: false reassurance
options.rationale: Named among the things to avoid, alongside don't worry and interrupting.

options.text: validating feelings
options.rationale: Validating names the feeling and stays with it. This dismisses it.

options.text: offering self
options.rationale: Offering self is being available. This tells him not to feel what he feels.

options.text: giving information
options.rationale: No information is given. It is a prediction nobody can make.

options.text: the essence of nursing, and both an art and a science
options.rationale: Watson's position, and the art and science pairing is why competence sits inside caring.

options.text: an additional skill applied once clinical tasks are complete
options.rationale: Reverses her point. Every skill is a caring interaction.

options.text: a personality trait some nurses have and others do not
options.rationale: Makes caring innate rather than practised, which would make the whole theory pointless.

options.text: the emotional component of care, separate from the technical
options.rationale: Separates what Watson joins. Mind, body and spirit are treated as one.

questions.takeaway: Presence is the behavior. Caritas Coaching is the partnership. False reassurance is the block. Watson calls caring the essence of nursing, art and science together.
questions.strategy: Blank 1 has a real near-miss: empathy is the understanding, presence is what you visibly do.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Empathy is internal; presence is visible.
An open question that asks for his reason.

elimination.verdict: Presence, Caritas Coaching, false reassurance, essence of nursing.

questions.stem: A nurse asks a patient what has been hardest about managing his diet since his diagnosis. He describes his shift pattern and the food available at work. Together they agree he will eat his main meal before his shift rather than during it. Which describes what the nurse has done?

options.text: Negotiated a compromise between his preference and the plan
options.rationale: Closer, and nothing was traded away. The dietary goal is unchanged; only the timing moved.

options.text: Partnered with him so he could find a solution that fits his life
options.rationale: Caritas Coaching helps patients discover their own strengths and solutions. The plan came from his information, not from a leaflet.

options.text: Assessed his adherence to the prescribed regimen
options.rationale: Adherence assessment asks whether he is doing it. She asked what was in the way, which is a different question.

options.text: Provided health teaching about dietary management
options.rationale: She supplied no dietary information. The content came from him.

questions.takeaway: Caritas Coaching: listen first, ask open questions, encourage reflection, support the patient's goals, build confidence, partner.
questions.strategy: The near-miss calls it a compromise. Check whether anything clinical was actually given up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask where the plan came from

steps.detail: She supplied nothing and checked nothing.

elimination.verdict: That leaves partnering so he found the solution.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews what professional caring includes beyond compassion. Which elements are part of it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Named directly, and it is why caring cannot exist without competence.

options.text: Cultural sensitivity
options.rationale: Named, and it is how respect for the whole person is enacted.

options.text: Confidentiality
options.rationale: Named, and protecting privacy is one of the behaviors patients identify.

options.text: Advocacy
options.rationale: Named, and it appears in both the professional caring list and the behaviors patients value.

options.text: Ethical practice
options.rationale: Named, and it is what keeps caring from becoming personal preference.

options.text: Emotional involvement in each patient's situation
options.rationale: Empathy is understanding what a patient feels. Becoming emotionally involved is not a professional element and it leads toward compassion fatigue.

questions.takeaway: Professional caring: compassion, respect, accountability, cultural sensitivity, confidentiality, advocacy, ethical practice.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds like the most caring option on the list and is the one that harms the nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Compassion, respect, accountability, sensitivity, confidentiality, advocacy, ethics.
Not on the list, and not sustainable.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse taking a patient's vital signs enters, applies the cuff, records the readings, and leaves without speaking. The readings are accurate. Which principle has been missed?

options.text: The readings should be verified with the patient before recording
options.rationale: No such requirement, and verification is not what was missing.

options.text: Caring should be present during every skill, including routine ones
options.rationale: Her example for vital signs is to introduce yourself and explain what you are doing. The task was done and the interaction was not.

options.text: Vital signs should be explained because patients have a right to their results
options.rationale: A reasonable position and not the principle here. The point is the interaction, not the disclosure.

options.text: Routine tasks may be delegated so the nurse can focus on caring
options.rationale: Treats caring as something that happens elsewhere, when the point is that it happens here.

questions.takeaway: Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction. For vital signs, introduce yourself and explain what you are doing.
questions.strategy: One distractor suggests delegating the routine work so caring can happen separately, which inverts the whole principle.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the results and verification options

steps.detail: Moves caring away from the task.

elimination.verdict: That leaves caring during every skill.

questions.nursesNote: 1430: Patient is 54, admitted three days ago with pancreatitis. Sitting on the edge of the bed facing the window. Answers questions in single words. Has not touched the lunch tray. Says he is 'fine' when asked, then adds that his wife has not visited since admission. Wound site clean and dry. Pain reported as 2 of 10. Declines to discuss discharge planning, saying there is no point. Vital signs stable. Ambulated in the corridor this morning with the physiotherapist.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate a need for therapeutic presence.

segments.text: Sitting on the edge of the bed facing the window
segments.rationale: Turned away from the room and from people. Nonverbal behavior is part of what you assess.

segments.text: Answers questions in single words
segments.rationale: Withdrawal from conversation, and it is the finding that tells you asking more questions will not work.

segments.text: Has not touched the lunch tray
segments.rationale: A change in a basic behavior, and in this context it belongs with the withdrawal rather than with his pancreatitis.

segments.text: Says he is 'fine', then adds that his wife has not visited since admission
segments.rationale: He offered something after saying he was fine. That second sentence is an opening, and it is the one to stay with.

segments.text: Declines to discuss discharge planning, saying there is no point
segments.rationale: There is no point is a statement about hopelessness rather than about discharge. It needs exploring, not rescheduling.

segments.text: Wound site clean and dry
segments.rationale: A normal finding. The physical recovery is going well.

segments.text: Pain reported as 2 of 10
segments.rationale: Controlled pain, and it rules out discomfort as the explanation for the withdrawal.

segments.text: Ambulated in the corridor this morning with the physiotherapist
segments.rationale: He is participating in his physical care. A strength, included to be left alone.

questions.takeaway: Presence is indicated when a patient is saying something the clinical findings cannot explain. Listen for the sentence that comes after 'I'm fine'.
questions.strategy: Three findings are normal or positive, and one of them actively rules out the easy explanation. If his pain is 2 of 10, the withdrawal is not about pain.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Wound, pain and ambulation are fine.
It rules out discomfort as the cause.
He volunteered the part about his wife.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s5: posture, single words, untouched tray, the wife, and no point.

questions.stem: A nurse hears a colleague tell a frightened preoperative patient that there is nothing to worry about and the surgeon is the best in the hospital. What is the problem with this response?

options.text: It gives the patient unrealistic expectations of the surgical outcome
options.rationale: A fair concern about the specific claim, and the broader fault is what the response does to the exchange.

options.text: It breaches confidentiality by discussing the surgeon's reputation
options.rationale: No confidential information is disclosed. The problem is what it does to the patient's ability to speak.

options.text: It is false reassurance, which closes the conversation the patient was trying to start
options.rationale: Named among the things to avoid. It sounds supportive and it tells the patient the subject is finished.

options.text: It should have been delivered by the surgeon rather than the nurse
options.rationale: Addressing fear is squarely nursing work. Handing it to the surgeon avoids it.

questions.takeaway: Avoid: everything will be fine, don't worry, interrupting, and false reassurance.
questions.strategy: One distractor criticizes the content of the claim. Ask what the response does to the patient's next sentence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves false reassurance.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked why caring is described as improving outcomes rather than simply being pleasant. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Caring improves trust, communication, and treatment adherence, which change clinical results
options.rationale: Research consistently shows caring relationships improve both patient and nurse outcomes. The mechanism runs through trust and communication.

options.text: Caring improves patient satisfaction scores, which affect hospital reimbursement
options.rationale: True and it is an institutional consequence rather than a clinical one.

options.text: Caring compensates for gaps in clinical competence
options.rationale: Competence is part of caring, not something caring substitutes for.

options.text: Caring reduces the time nurses spend answering questions
options.rationale: The opposite of what presence involves, and efficiency is not the argument.

questions.takeaway: Caring improves trust, communication, healing, satisfaction, emotional wellbeing, treatment adherence, and the nurse-patient relationship.
questions.strategy: One distractor gives a real institutional benefit as though it were the clinical argument.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trust and communication change what patients tell you and do.
One inverts presence, one excuses incompetence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves trust, communication and adherence.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses Watson's theory with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Caring is something I can do once I have finished my clinical tasks."
options.rationale: Treats caring as a separate activity. Every nursing skill is also a caring interaction, which means it happens during the tasks rather than after them.

options.text: "Watson describes caring as both an art and a science."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is why scientific knowledge sits alongside caring in the Caritas Processes.

options.text: "Caring means respecting the whole person, mind, body and spirit."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her wording.

options.text: "Caritas Coaching helps patients find their own solutions rather than giving instructions."
options.rationale: Accurate. Partnering rather than directing.

questions.takeaway: Caring is the essence of nursing and happens within every skill, not after the work is done.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth makes caring a separate item on the list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Art and science, whole person, coaching.

elimination.verdict: That leaves caring as something done afterwards.

questions.stem: A nurse applies Watson's Caritas Processes while caring for a patient having a wound dressing changed. Which actions reflect those principles? Select all that apply.

options.text: Explaining each step as the dressing is changed
options.rationale: Teaching and learning together, which involves the patient in his own care rather than performing it on him.

options.text: Ensuring his pain is controlled before starting
options.rationale: Creating a healing environment that promotes comfort, dignity and safety.

options.text: Asking what this wound has meant for him
options.rationale: Recognizing the spiritual and personal meaning of health, illness and healing.

options.text: Using current evidence to select the dressing
options.rationale: Using scientific knowledge alongside caring and clinical judgment, which is why competence is inside the theory.

options.text: Working in silence so the procedure finishes faster
options.rationale: Efficiency offered in place of presence, and it is the first nurse from her pneumonia scenario.

options.text: Telling him the wound looks much better than it does
options.rationale: Kindly meant and it is false reassurance, and it also breaches the honesty that trust depends on.

questions.takeaway: The Caritas Processes cover loving kindness, authentic presence, honoring beliefs, supporting healing, scientific knowledge, a healing environment, teaching together, addressing needs, and personal meaning.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are things a nurse might do to be efficient or to be kind. Neither is in the theory.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.scenario: A 58-year-old with newly diagnosed heart failure is readmitted three weeks after discharge with fluid overload. He tells the nurse he stopped weighing himself because the scale 'just made him feel worse'. He can recite the discharge instructions accurately. He lives alone and says his daughter phones but he does not like to bother her with it. He has not mentioned any of this to his provider.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Ask what the daily weight has come to mean to him
options.rationale: Recognizing the personal meaning of illness. The scale is not a measurement problem, and you cannot solve it until you know what it represents.

options.text: Work with him to agree a monitoring plan he is willing to follow
options.rationale: Caritas Coaching partners rather than instructs, and a plan he helped build is one he may actually use.

options.text: Re-teach the importance of daily weights before discharge
options.rationale: Correct teaching aimed at the wrong problem. He can already recite the instructions.

options.text: Reassure him that many patients find self-monitoring difficult
options.rationale: Normalizes it and closes the conversation, which is false reassurance in a gentler form.

options.text: The monitoring carries a meaning that makes him avoid it
options.rationale: He told you the scale made him feel worse. That is about what the number represents, not about whether he understands it.

options.text: Knowledge deficit regarding heart failure self-management
options.rationale: He can recite the instructions accurately. Assuming a knowledge gap produces more teaching and no change.

options.text: Nonadherence with the prescribed monitoring regimen
options.rationale: Describes what happened and explains nothing. It also puts the failure in him.

options.text: Lack of social support at home
options.rationale: His daughter phones, and he chooses not to raise it. The support exists; something stops him using it.

options.text: Whether he is recording weights in the way he agreed
options.rationale: Measures whether the plan he helped design is one he can use.

options.text: Whether he raises a change in weight with anyone before it becomes an admission
options.rationale: The behavior the whole intervention exists to produce, and the one that prevents the next readmission.

options.text: Whether he can state his target weight range
options.rationale: Tests knowledge he already has, and it was never the problem.

options.text: Whether his daughter attends the next appointment
options.rationale: Might help, and it evaluates her behavior rather than anything that was changed for him.

questions.takeaway: When a patient knows exactly what to do and does not do it, the obstacle is usually what the task means to him.
questions.strategy: Two problem options name knowledge or adherence. He can recite the instructions, which rules the first out and makes the second a description rather than an explanation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The scale made him feel worse.
You asked about meaning and agreed a plan.

elimination.verdict: Ask about meaning and agree a plan, for an avoided task, evaluated by use and by disclosure.

questions.stem: A nurse finishes a difficult conversation with a family and notices she has been thinking about it for two days. Which Caritas principle addresses this?

options.text: Being authentically present with patients and families
options.rationale: She was present, which is part of why the conversation stayed with her.

options.text: Honoring each person's beliefs, values and emotions
options.rationale: Directed at the patient's beliefs rather than at the nurse's own state.

options.text: Creating a healing environment for patients
options.rationale: Concerns the patient's surroundings, comfort, dignity and safety.

options.text: Practicing loving kindness toward yourself as well as others
options.rationale: The first Caritas Process names both directions. A nurse who extends nothing to herself has nothing left to extend.

questions.takeaway: The first Caritas Process is loving kindness toward yourself and others. Self-directed care is inside the theory, not outside it.
questions.strategy: Three options are genuine Caritas Processes directed outward. Ask who this one is about.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the one that includes her
steps.detail: Loving kindness toward yourself and others.

elimination.verdict: That leaves loving kindness toward yourself.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what patients remember about their hospital stay. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Patients remember the nurses who completed tasks most efficiently
options.rationale: Efficiency is rarely what is described. Patients name listening, explaining, and dignity.

options.text: Patients most accurately recall the clinical details of their treatment
options.rationale: Recall of clinical detail is generally poor, particularly during acute illness.

options.text: Patients may forget what was done and remember how it made them feel
options.rationale: Her closing line, and it is why caring behaviors have outcomes beyond the encounter itself.

options.text: Patients remember the amount of time each nurse spent with them
options.rationale: Presence is not measured in minutes. Sitting down for two minutes is remembered differently from standing for ten.

questions.takeaway: Patients may forget exactly what you did and they remember how you made them feel.
questions.strategy: Two distractors measure caring in efficiency or minutes. Neither is what patients report.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves how you made them feel.

chapters.title: Caring for Patients with Chronic Illness

questions.scenario: Two patients attend the same clinic, both diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis four years ago and both with comparable joint damage on imaging.
questions.stem: For each finding, indicate whether it describes the chronic disease or the chronic illness.

rows.text: Joint erosion visible on radiographs
rows.rationale: The clinical process in the body, measurable and objective.

rows.text: One patient has stopped attending her book group because of her hands
rows.rationale: The social experience of living with the condition. No test shows this.

rows.text: Inflammatory markers remain elevated despite treatment
rows.rationale: A laboratory value reflecting the underlying process.

rows.text: The other patient describes constant fatigue that nobody can see
rows.rationale: An invisible symptom, which her slide names specifically as part of the illness experience.

rows.text: The diagnosis has lasted longer than one year and needs ongoing medical management
rows.rationale: Her definition of chronic disease, almost word for word.

rows.text: One patient says she has learned to plan her week around her stiffest mornings
rows.rationale: How she feels, adapts and manages daily life. Adaptation belongs to the illness experience.

questions.takeaway: Chronic disease is the clinical process: diagnosed, lasting a year or more, needing medical management. Chronic illness is how the person feels, adapts and lives.
questions.strategy: Ask whether a test could show it. If a number or an image captures it, it belongs to the disease.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fatigue nobody can see is illness.
Planning around stiff mornings is living with it.

elimination.verdict: Three disease, three illness.

questions.stem: Two patients have the same diagnosis of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease with comparable lung function. One works full time and travels; the other rarely leaves the house. Which principle does this illustrate?

options.text: Care must be patient-centered rather than disease-centered, because no two patients are the same
options.rationale: Physical effects, functional limitations, and ability to perform daily activities all vary between patients with the same condition. Individual assessment is essential.

options.text: One patient is adhering to treatment better than the other
options.rationale: An assumption the stem does not support, and it puts the difference in the patient's behavior rather than in the illness experience.

options.text: The lung function measurement is unreliable in chronic disease
options.rationale: The measurement is fine. It describes the disease, and it does not predict the life.

options.text: The second patient requires a psychiatric referral for possible depression
options.rationale: Depression is a genuine psychosocial concern in chronic illness, and concluding it from this comparison alone skips the assessment.

questions.takeaway: The same condition produces different symptoms, limitations, and daily function in different people. Individual assessment is essential.
questions.strategy: Two distractors explain the difference by something wrong with the second patient. Ask what the stem holds constant.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Nothing in the stem supports it.

elimination.verdict: That leaves patient-centered rather than disease-centered care.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses the health risk of a 68-year-old woman who has cared for her husband with Alzheimer disease in their shared home for the past three years. Which factors place her at risk for poor health? Select all that apply.

options.text: Providing care for more than one year
options.rationale: Named directly, and three years is well past the threshold.

options.text: Being 65 years of age or older
options.rationale: Named, and at 68 she meets it.

options.text: Caring for a family member with significant needs
options.rationale: Named, and dementia care is among the most demanding.

options.text: Caring for someone with Alzheimer disease or dementia
options.rationale: Named separately from significant needs, because the burden is distinct.

options.text: Living with the care recipient
options.rationale: Named, and it removes the respite that living apart provides.

options.text: Having no formal training in caregiving
options.rationale: A real difficulty and not one of the five named risk factors. Training does not shorten the hours or the years.

questions.takeaway: Five caregiver risk factors: more than one year of care, age 65 or older, a family member with significant needs, Alzheimer disease or dementia, and living with the care recipient.
questions.strategy: This patient meets all five, which is the point. One distractor names a genuine difficulty that is not on the list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a 62-year-old with heart failure. Which finding should prompt the nurse to assess the family caregiver as well?

options.text: His wife has provided all of his personal care at home for the past two years
options.rationale: Family caregivers are themselves at risk for poor health, and they belong in the nursing assessment and the care plan rather than only in the history.

options.text: He takes nine medications daily
options.rationale: Polypharmacy is a real concern for him. Whoever administers them may also need assessing, and the stem does not say anyone else does.

options.text: His ejection fraction has fallen since his last admission
options.rationale: A clinical deterioration that concerns his management. It says nothing directly about his wife.

options.text: He has been admitted three times this year
options.rationale: Points to a problem with the plan, and the caregiver is one possible part of that rather than the finding itself.

questions.takeaway: Family caregivers are at risk for poor health and should be included in nursing assessment and care planning.
questions.strategy: Three options describe real findings about the patient. Ask which one tells you about someone else.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask who each finding is about
Find the person in the room
steps.detail: Two years of personal care by his wife.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the wife providing all his care.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A clinic redesigns its care for patients with diabetes using the Chronic Care Model.

Teaching patients to interpret their own glucose readings and act on them addresses [[1]].

Linking patients with a walking group run by the local library addresses [[2]].

Building a registry that flags who is overdue for a foot check addresses [[3]].

Giving clinicians access to current treatment guidelines at the point of care addresses [[4]].

options.text: self-management support
options.rationale: The component nursing most directly owns: helping patients manage the condition themselves between visits.

options.text: decision support
options.rationale: The near-miss. Decision support helps the clinician decide; self-management support helps the patient.

options.text: delivery system design
options.rationale: How care is organized and who does what.

options.text: clinical information systems
options.rationale: The data infrastructure behind the care.

options.text: community
options.rationale: One of two components sitting outside the clinic entirely, and the one students most often forget.

options.text: self-management support
options.rationale: Close, and this is a resource outside the health system rather than a skill built in the patient.

options.text: health system
options.rationale: Refers to the organization delivering care and how it prioritizes chronic illness.

options.text: delivery system design
options.rationale: How the clinic itself arranges appointments and roles.

options.text: clinical information systems
options.rationale: A registry is data organized so that gaps in care become visible.

options.text: decision support
options.rationale: Guidance on what to do. A registry tells you who needs it, not what to do.

options.text: community
options.rationale: Resources outside the health system.

options.text: health system
options.rationale: The organization's priorities and leadership.

options.text: decision support
options.rationale: Evidence and guidelines put where the clinician makes the decision.

options.text: clinical information systems
options.rationale: The near-miss. Both involve information; one holds patient data, the other holds clinical evidence.

options.text: self-management support
options.rationale: Directed at the patient rather than the clinician.

options.text: delivery system design
options.rationale: The structure of appointments and roles.

questions.takeaway: Six components: community, health system, self-management support, delivery system design, decision support, clinical information systems.
questions.strategy: Two pairs are easily confused. Self-management supports the patient, decision support supports the clinician. Information systems hold patient data, decision support holds evidence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Find the one outside the clinic

elimination.verdict: Self-management, community, information systems, decision support.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old with hypertension, arthritis and heart disease becomes confused two days after a medication change. Her daughter says she is 'just getting old'. Which nursing consideration applies?

options.text: Confusion is expected in a patient managing three chronic conditions
options.rationale: Multimorbidity raises complexity and does not make confusion expected.

options.text: The daughter's observation should guide the assessment, since she knows the baseline
options.rationale: Family knowledge of the baseline is valuable and does not substitute for assessing a change that began two days after a medication change.

options.text: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness, so the medication change needs assessing
options.rationale: Overlapping symptoms are a named consideration. Confusing a medication effect with normal aging is her own example.

options.text: Cognitive change is an expected part of aging after 70
options.rationale: Dismissing cognitive shifts as aging is precisely the error her slide warns against.

questions.takeaway: Age-related changes can mask signs of chronic illness. Confusing medication effects with normal aging, or dismissing cognitive shifts, is the named trap.
questions.strategy: Two distractors normalize the confusion. One hands the assessment to the family.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Two days after a medication change.
Her view is data, not the assessment.

elimination.verdict: That leaves assessing the medication change.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the prevalence of chronic conditions among older adults. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Nearly 80% of older adults manage two or more concurrent chronic conditions
options.rationale: Multimorbidity is the norm rather than the exception, which is why single-disease management plans so often fail.

options.text: Multimorbidity becomes common only after the age of 85
options.rationale: Places the threshold far too late, and it would leave most patients unassessed for it.

options.text: Most older adults manage a single well-controlled chronic condition
options.rationale: Reverses the picture. Two or more is the common situation.

options.text: Chronic conditions affect a minority of adults over 65
options.rationale: Hypertension, arthritis and heart disease affect the majority.

questions.takeaway: Nearly 80% of older adults manage two or more concurrent chronic conditions. Hypertension, arthritis and heart disease affect the majority.
questions.strategy: Three distractors understate how common multimorbidity is. Ask what proportion the figure describes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the minority and the 85 threshold

elimination.verdict: That leaves nearly 80%.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a 55-year-old newly diagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Which factors contribute to the multifactorial nature of chronic disease? Select all that apply.

options.text: Genetic influence and family history
options.rationale: Named, along with genetic screening and how genetics interacts with other factors.

options.text: Environmental factors
options.rationale: Named as a category in their own right.

options.text: Tobacco use
options.rationale: Named under lifestyle and risk factors.

options.text: Alcohol consumption
options.rationale: Named alongside tobacco under lifestyle.

options.text: Nutrition
options.rationale: The third lifestyle factor named.

options.text: The patient's level of education about the disease
options.rationale: Education affects how well she manages the condition. It is not among the factors contributing to the disease developing.

questions.takeaway: Chronic disease is multifactorial: genetic, environmental, lifestyle, physical, and psychosocial factors.
questions.strategy: One distractor names something that affects management rather than causation. The question asks what contributes to the disease.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old with Crohn disease tells the nurse the hardest part is that people cannot see anything wrong, so they assume she is exaggerating. Which aspect of chronic illness is she describing?

options.text: Poor adherence to her treatment regimen
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem concerns her treatment. She is describing how others respond to her.

options.text: Progression of the underlying disease process
options.rationale: Describes the disease. She is describing the experience of living with it.

options.text: A knowledge deficit among her family and colleagues
options.rationale: Closer, and framing it as their knowledge gap misses that this is her experience of the illness.

options.text: Invisible symptoms and the social changes that follow from them
options.rationale: Invisible symptoms are named as part of the illness experience, and navigating social changes is named alongside them.

questions.takeaway: Chronic illness includes invisible symptoms, mental health impacts, fatigue, and navigating social changes.
questions.strategy: One distractor relocates the problem into other people's knowledge. The question asks what she is experiencing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Symptoms nobody sees, and being disbelieved.
Moves it away from her experience.

elimination.verdict: That leaves invisible symptoms and social change.

questions.nursesNote: 1000: Patient is 71, attends a routine review for type 2 diabetes and osteoarthritis, both diagnosed nine years ago. Reports she has stopped going to her weekly swim because getting changed takes too long and she is embarrassed. Has not seen friends in four months. Says she is tired 'all the time' but nobody believes her because she looks well. Blood glucose diary is complete and within range. Attends every appointment. Weight stable. Sleeps poorly and wakes with joint stiffness. Says there is not much point planning ahead any more.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that reflect the chronic illness experience rather than the disease process.

segments.text: Stopped going to her weekly swim because getting changed takes too long and she is embarrassed
segments.rationale: A social change driven by the condition, and embarrassment is part of the experience rather than the pathology.

segments.text: Has not seen friends in four months
segments.rationale: Social isolation, which is a named psychosocial need in chronic illness.

segments.text: Tired all the time but nobody believes her because she looks well
segments.rationale: An invisible symptom, named specifically, and the disbelief is part of what makes it hard to live with.

segments.text: Says there is not much point planning ahead any more
segments.rationale: Points toward depression or hopelessness, which are named psychosocial impacts and need exploring rather than recording.

segments.text: Blood glucose diary is complete and within range
segments.rationale: Describes the disease and it is well controlled. A strength, not a finding to act on.

segments.text: Attends every appointment
segments.rationale: A health-seeking behavior and another strength.

segments.text: Weight stable
segments.rationale: A clinical measure describing the disease process, and a reassuring one.

segments.text: Wakes with joint stiffness
segments.rationale: A physical symptom of the disease process rather than the lived experience of it.

questions.takeaway: Disease is what a test shows. Illness is the isolation, the invisible fatigue, and the loss of a future worth planning for.
questions.strategy: Her disease is well controlled, which is the point. Good numbers and a difficult life can coexist, and only one of them shows up in the chart.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a test would show
Note that the disease is controlled

steps.detail: Swim, friends, fatigue, no point planning.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s4: the four findings no test captures.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for a patient with chronic kidney disease who will manage a fluid restriction, a diet, and four medications at home. Which Chronic Care Model component does teaching him to recognize and act on early fluid overload address?

options.text: Clinical information systems
options.rationale: The data infrastructure that shows who needs what.

options.text: Decision support
options.rationale: Evidence and guidance for the clinician, not for the patient.

options.text: Delivery system design
options.rationale: How care is organized and who does what within the service.

options.text: Self-management support
options.rationale: Building the patient's capability to manage the condition between visits, which is the component nursing most directly owns.

questions.takeaway: Self-management support builds the patient's own capability. It is the component that distinguishes chronic care from acute care.
questions.strategy: One distractor also contains the word support. Ask who is being supported to make a decision.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The patient, at home, between visits.

elimination.verdict: That leaves self-management support.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old with three chronic conditions has attended no appointments in eight months. When contacted he says he gave up because every clinic told him something different and he could not keep track. Which Chronic Care Model component has failed?

options.text: Self-management support, because he stopped managing his conditions
options.rationale: Describes the outcome. He stopped because the system was incoherent, not because he lacked the skill.

options.text: Delivery system design, because the care was never organized around him
options.rationale: Delivery system design determines how care is arranged and who does what. Three services working separately is a design failure, not a patient failure.

options.text: Community, because he lacks local resources
options.rationale: Nothing in the stem concerns community resources. The problem is inside the health service.

options.text: Clinical information systems, because his records were incomplete
options.rationale: Plausible and not stated. What he describes is conflicting advice rather than missing data.

questions.takeaway: Delivery system design organizes care around the patient. Fragmented services produce exactly the disengagement described here.
questions.strategy: One distractor names what happened to him as though it were the cause. Ask what produced it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Every clinic told him something different.

elimination.verdict: That leaves delivery system design.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease at a routine review. Which assessments does her slide identify as nursing implications in chronic illness? Select all that apply.

options.text: Adherence to the treatment plan
options.rationale: Named first, and it is where most chronic disease management succeeds or fails.

options.text: Symptom management
options.rationale: Named, and symptoms in chronic illness need managing rather than curing.

options.text: Tobacco use
options.rationale: Named specifically, and it is modifiable.

options.text: Alcohol consumption
options.rationale: Named specifically alongside tobacco.

options.text: Lifestyle
options.rationale: Named as the fifth area, covering activity, diet and daily routine.

options.text: The patient's prognosis and expected survival
options.rationale: A medical determination. It shapes goals of care and it is not among the nursing assessments named.

questions.takeaway: Nursing implications in chronic illness: adherence, symptom management, tobacco use, alcohol consumption, and lifestyle.
questions.strategy: One distractor names something clinically important that belongs to medical management rather than to this list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a community where a large employer closed two years ago and the nearest supermarket is eight miles away. Rates of type 2 diabetes have risen sharply. Which nursing action reflects the role in public policy?

options.text: Focus teaching on individual dietary choices within each consultation
options.rationale: Correct clinical teaching and it addresses individuals while the conditions producing the rise stay in place.

options.text: Refer affected patients to a specialist diabetes service
options.rationale: Appropriate for individuals who need it, and it treats a population problem one person at a time.

options.text: Understand the environmental factors involved and support screening and prevention efforts
options.rationale: Her slide names awareness of policies affecting chronic disease prevention, recognizing environmental influences, and encouraging screening and prevention.

options.text: Document the rising incidence and report it to the clinic manager
options.rationale: Records the pattern without acting on it, and it stops at the clinic door.

questions.takeaway: The nurse's role in public policy: be aware of relevant policies, recognize environmental influences, use reputable sources, provide education, and encourage screening and prevention.
questions.strategy: Three options are appropriate individual-level actions. Ask which one operates at the level the problem does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what level the problem is at
steps.detail: A whole community, after an employer closed.
Teaching and referral treat one at a time.

elimination.verdict: That leaves environmental awareness with screening and prevention.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old with cystic fibrosis has begun missing treatments since starting a new school. Which nursing consideration is most relevant?

options.text: Adolescents typically lack the cognitive ability to manage complex regimens
options.rationale: Underestimates him. He managed the regimen until the school changed, so ability is not the variable.

options.text: The treatment plan should be simplified to improve adherence
options.rationale: May be reasonable eventually, and it acts before understanding why the missing started.

options.text: His parents should resume responsibility for the treatments
options.rationale: Removes the independence appropriate to his age, and it addresses the treatments rather than the reason.

options.text: Growth and developmental needs are age-specific and shape how the illness is experienced
options.rationale: Her slide names growth and developmental considerations with age-specific needs. Adolescence makes visible difference the central problem.

questions.takeaway: Growth and developmental considerations are age-specific. What a chronic illness costs a person depends on where they are in life.
questions.strategy: Two distractors change the regimen or the responsibility. Ask what changed in his life.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A new school, not his condition.

elimination.verdict: That leaves age-specific developmental needs.

questions.stem: A nursing student discusses chronic illness with her preceptor. Which statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "Chronic disease is the clinical process; chronic illness is how the person lives with it."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her central distinction.

options.text: "Two patients with the same diagnosis and the same test results will have similar limitations."
options.rationale: Physical effects and functional limitations vary between patients with the same condition, which is why individual assessment is essential.

options.text: "Family caregivers should be assessed as part of my care planning."
options.rationale: Accurate. They are at risk for poor health themselves.

options.text: "Invisible symptoms like fatigue are part of the illness experience."
options.rationale: Accurate, and named alongside mental health impacts and social change.

questions.takeaway: No two patients with the same condition are the same. Individual assessment is essential and care must be patient-centered.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth predicts one patient's life from another's test results.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Disease and illness, caregivers, invisible symptoms.
Assuming similar limitations from similar results.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement predicting limitations.

questions.scenario: A 67-year-old with heart failure has been admitted twice in four months. His wife, 69, has provided all his personal care at home for two years since his mobility declined. During the admission she tells the nurse she has not seen her own doctor in over a year, has stopped attending her church group, and sleeps in a chair beside him. She says she manages fine. His medications have been taken correctly throughout.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem they address, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Assess the wife's own health and current health care access
options.rationale: She meets four of the five caregiver risk factors, and she has not seen a clinician in a year. Caregivers belong in the assessment.

options.text: Explore what respite or community support could be arranged
options.rationale: Community is a Chronic Care Model component, and it is where sustainable relief for a caregiver comes from.

options.text: Re-teach the medication regimen before discharge
options.rationale: Correct teaching aimed at something that is working. The stem states the medications have been taken correctly.

options.text: Document that the wife reports coping well with caregiving
options.rationale: Records what she said and ignores everything she described. She manages fine is not an assessment finding.

options.text: Caregiver health risk from sustained, unsupported caregiving
options.rationale: More than one year, over 65, a family member with significant needs, and living with the care recipient. Four of the five risk factors.

options.text: Nonadherence contributing to repeated admissions
options.rationale: The stem tells you the medications have been taken correctly. Adherence is not the failure here.

options.text: Knowledge deficit about heart failure management
options.rationale: Nothing suggests either of them misunderstands the regimen.

options.text: The wife's denial about her husband's prognosis
options.rationale: Reads her I manage fine as psychological denial, when it is what exhausted caregivers routinely say.

options.text: Whether the wife has arranged and attended her own health appointment
options.rationale: Measures whether the assessment of her health led anywhere.

options.text: Whether any respite or support has actually started
options.rationale: Arranging a referral is not the same as support arriving, and the difference is what changes her situation.

options.text: Whether the patient's weight remains stable
options.rationale: A real heart failure parameter, and it evaluates his disease rather than anything the actions changed.

options.text: Whether the wife reports feeling less overwhelmed
options.rationale: She already reports managing fine. Asking a caregiver who minimizes how she feels will not measure whether anything changed.

questions.takeaway: Family caregivers are at risk for poor health and belong in the assessment. I manage fine is what caregivers say, not what you record.
questions.strategy: The stem rules out adherence explicitly. Two evaluation options measure his disease or her self-report, neither of which tests what you changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Duration, age, significant needs, shared home.

elimination.verdict: Assess her and arrange support, for caregiver risk, evaluated by her appointment and by support starting.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what makes the Chronic Care Model different from an acute care approach. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: It replaces the physician's role with a nurse-led model of care
options.rationale: It reorganizes how a team works and does not replace anyone.

options.text: It treats the community and the health system as part of the care, not just the clinic encounter
options.rationale: Two of the six components sit outside the consultation entirely, and most chronic disease is managed between visits rather than during them.

options.text: It applies only to patients with more than one chronic condition
options.rationale: It applies to chronic disease management generally.

options.text: It shifts responsibility for outcomes onto the patient
options.rationale: Self-management support builds capability with the patient. That is not the same as transferring responsibility.

questions.takeaway: Six components, and two of them sit outside the clinic: community and health system. Most chronic disease is managed between visits.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns self-management support into offloading responsibility, which is the misreading worth avoiding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Count what is outside the clinic

elimination.verdict: That leaves community and health system as part of the care.

questions.stem: A patient with a chronic condition tells the nurse she read online that her medication causes permanent kidney damage and has stopped taking it. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Find out what she read, and work through reputable sources with her
options.rationale: Using reputable information sources is a named part of the nursing role. Working through it with her treats her as someone trying to make a good decision.

options.text: Tell her not to trust health information found on the internet
options.rationale: Dismisses how most people now look things up, and it does not tell her what to trust instead.

options.text: Notify the provider that the patient has stopped her medication
options.rationale: Necessary, and on its own it reports the behavior without addressing why it happened.

options.text: Explain the consequences of stopping the medication
options.rationale: Correct information delivered over the top of a belief she already holds. She is unlikely to hear it while the original claim stands.

questions.takeaway: Provide health education using reputable information sources. Work through what a patient has read rather than dismissing it.
questions.strategy: One option is genuinely necessary and incomplete on its own. Ask what changes her decision.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what is driving the decision

steps.detail: Tells her nothing to use instead.

steps.action: Cut notifying alone and explaining over the top
steps.detail: One reports, one talks past her.

elimination.verdict: That leaves working through the source with her.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes asks the nurse whether the diagnosis means she has failed to look after herself. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Diabetes is primarily determined by genetics, so the diagnosis was not preventable
options.rationale: Overstates genetics and removes the lifestyle factors she may be able to influence.

options.text: Lifestyle is the main factor, so changes now can reverse the condition
options.rationale: Overstates lifestyle in the other direction, and it implies the diagnosis was her doing.

options.text: Chronic disease develops from genetic, environmental and lifestyle factors interacting, not from one cause
options.rationale: The multifactorial nature is the honest answer, and it neither blames her nor dismisses the part she can change.

options.text: The cause matters less than the management from this point forward
options.rationale: Kindly meant and it sidesteps the question she asked. She is asking whether this is her fault.

questions.takeaway: Chronic disease is multifactorial: genetic, environmental, lifestyle, physical and psychosocial factors interacting.
questions.strategy: Two distractors pick one factor and make it the cause. One avoids the question she actually asked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the multifactorial explanation.

questions.nursesNote: 0800: Patient is 27, diagnosed with type 2 diabetes two years ago and now requires insulin. Admitted with a blood glucose of 322 mg/dL; her target range is 80 to 130. HbA1c 11%, target 7% or less. Became unhoused after losing her job and health insurance. Currently living in shelter-provided housing. Third emergency department visit for the same reason in six months. Previous providers documented that she verbalized understanding of her diabetes management but has difficulty following her treatment plan. Alert and oriented. Answers questions readily.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that represent social determinants affecting her ability to manage her diabetes.

segments.text: Became unhoused after losing her job
segments.rationale: Economic stability, and it is the event that set the rest in motion.

segments.text: Lost her health insurance
segments.rationale: Health care access. Insulin and supplies both depend on it.

segments.text: Living in shelter-provided housing
segments.rationale: Neighborhood and built environment. Shelter living affects refrigeration for insulin, meal timing, and where syringes can be kept safely.

segments.text: Third emergency department visit for the same reason in six months
segments.rationale: The pattern that says the plan is failing repeatedly, and repeated presentation is how a determinant shows up clinically.

segments.text: Blood glucose 322 mg/dL
segments.rationale: A clinical value describing the disease. It is the consequence of the determinants rather than one of them.

segments.text: HbA1c 11%
segments.rationale: Also a clinical measure, and it tells you the problem has been sustained for months rather than naming its cause.

segments.text: Verbalized understanding of her diabetes management
segments.rationale: Documented knowledge. It is the finding that rules out a knowledge deficit, which makes it important and not a determinant.

segments.text: Alert and oriented, answers questions readily
segments.rationale: A normal finding, and it removes cognition as an explanation.

questions.takeaway: Social determinants are the non-medical conditions where a person lives, learns, works and ages. The glucose is what they produce, not what they are.
questions.strategy: Two findings are laboratory values and two rule out the easy explanations. If she understands and is oriented, the barrier is elsewhere.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: s1 through s4: the four conditions surrounding her care.

questions.stem: A nursing student caring for the patient above teaches her the importance of taking insulin as prescribed and how to make healthy food choices. The patient nods and says she has no questions. Which assessment should the student have made first?

options.text: Her level of health literacy before beginning the teaching
options.rationale: A reasonable step in general, and the record already documents verbalized understanding. Literacy is not what is unexplained here.

options.text: What gets in the way of following the plan where she currently lives
options.rationale: Previous providers documented that she understands the management. Teaching again addresses a gap that has already been ruled out; the barrier is in her circumstances.

options.text: Whether she has been storing her insulin correctly
options.rationale: A specific and useful question, and it is one of several barriers rather than the assessment that would find them.

options.text: Her readiness to learn about diabetes management
options.rationale: Readiness matters before teaching, and the deeper problem is that teaching is the wrong intervention for this patient today.

questions.takeaway: When the record says a patient understands and still cannot follow the plan, the barrier is not knowledge. Ask what is in the way.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real barrier rather than the assessment that uncovers barriers. Ask which question would find whatever is actually stopping her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Literacy and readiness both precede teaching.
Insulin storage is one of several.

elimination.verdict: That leaves asking what gets in the way.

questions.stem: The nurse asks the same patient how she stores her insulin. She explains the shelter has one shared refrigerator that is often full, meals are served at fixed times she cannot always attend, and she keeps her supplies in a locker. Which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: Her housing situation directly affects insulin storage, meal timing, and medication access
options.rationale: Every element of her regimen depends on conditions she does not control. Neighborhood and built environment is a determinant with concrete clinical consequences.

options.text: She is nonadherent with the prescribed diabetes regimen
options.rationale: Describes the outcome and blames her for it. The stem has just explained what stands in the way.

options.text: She requires more intensive education about insulin storage requirements
options.rationale: She has just described the problem accurately, which means she understands the requirement and cannot meet it.

options.text: A referral to a diabetes specialist is the priority
options.rationale: Specialist input may help eventually, and it does not change a shared refrigerator or fixed mealtimes.

questions.takeaway: Housing instability affects insulin storage, meal timing, and medication adherence directly. The regimen assumes conditions she does not have.
questions.strategy: One distractor labels her. One sends her to a specialist for a problem the specialist cannot change.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shared fridge, fixed meals, a locker.

steps.action: Cut the label and the referral
steps.detail: One blames her, one misses the cause.

elimination.verdict: That leaves housing affecting storage, timing and access.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse prepares for a difficult conversation with a patient whose beliefs about his treatment differ from her own.

Saying "tell me more about what you think is causing this" is the [[1]] step of LEARN.

Pointing out that they both want him to avoid another admission is the [[2]] step.

Agreeing a plan that keeps his traditional remedies alongside the prescribed treatment is the [[3]] step.

A nurse who examines her own assumptions before entering the room is demonstrating [[4]].

options.text: Listen
options.rationale: Listen to the patient's perception of the problem, nonjudgmentally, using encouraging comments such as tell me more.

options.text: Explain
options.rationale: Explain is where you give your own perception, and it comes after listening.

options.text: Acknowledge
options.rationale: Acknowledge compares the two perceptions once both are on the table.

options.text: Negotiate
options.rationale: Negotiate is the final step, agreeing the plan.

options.text: Acknowledge
options.rationale: Recognize the differences and build on the similarities. Naming a shared goal is exactly that.

options.text: Recommend
options.rationale: Recommend offers options, and it must involve the patient.

options.text: Listen
options.rationale: Listening has already happened by this point.

options.text: Explain
options.rationale: Explaining is giving your view, not comparing the two.

options.text: Negotiate
options.rationale: Negotiate a treatment plan, incorporating selected aspects of the patient's culture into it.

options.text: Recommend
options.rationale: The near-miss. Recommending offers the options; negotiating settles on one both accept.

options.text: Acknowledge
options.rationale: Comparing perceptions rather than building a plan.

options.text: Explain
options.rationale: Giving your perception of the problem.

options.text: cultural awareness
options.rationale: The first Campinha-Bacote construct, and it is self-examination before anything else.

options.text: cultural knowledge
options.rationale: Knowledge is what you learn about other groups, which is outward rather than inward.

options.text: cultural skill
options.rationale: Skill is the doing: history taking, assessment, working with interpreters.

options.text: cultural desire
options.rationale: Desire is the genuine wish to engage rather than the act of self-examination.

questions.takeaway: LEARN: Listen, Explain, Acknowledge, Recommend, Negotiate. Campinha-Bacote: awareness, knowledge, skill, encounters, desire.
questions.strategy: Recommend and Negotiate are the pair that gets confused. Recommending offers options; negotiating lands on a plan the patient accepts.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Listen, Acknowledge, Negotiate, cultural awareness.

questions.stem: A nurse notices she assumed a patient would decline a blood transfusion because of his surname. She stops and asks him directly. Which describes what she recognized in herself?

options.text: Stereotyping, an assumed belief about a group of people
options.rationale: Close, and stereotyping is the assumed belief itself. What she caught was the unconscious process that produced it before she was aware of it.

options.text: Cultural knowledge applied to an individual patient
options.rationale: Knowledge about a group applied without checking becomes the problem rather than the solution.

options.text: A failure of cultural desire
options.rationale: Desire is the genuine wish to engage. Hers is evident in stopping to ask.

options.text: Implicit bias, which is unconscious and shaped by her background
options.rationale: Unconscious, outside our control, and it drives quick judgments. She is responsible for recognizing and managing it, which is what she did.

questions.takeaway: Implicit bias is unconscious and outside our control. Recognizing and managing it is the part we are responsible for.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is stereotyping. One names the unconscious process, the other names the belief it produces.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An automatic assumption, before conscious thought.
That is the belief, not the process.

elimination.verdict: That leaves implicit bias.

questions.stem: A nurse reads that a particular cultural group commonly involves family elders in medical decisions. She assumes her patient from that background will want his father present and arranges it without asking. What error has she made?

options.text: She applied group knowledge to an individual without checking
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge is a genuine construct and becomes stereotyping the moment it is applied without asking. Culturally congruent care is based on the individual's beliefs, practices and values.

options.text: She should not have read about cultural practices at all
options.rationale: Cultural knowledge is part of competence. The problem is applying it without verifying it.

options.text: She demonstrated a lack of cultural awareness
options.rationale: Awareness is self-examination. She may lack it, and what the stem shows is misapplied knowledge.

options.text: She failed to obtain the patient's consent for the arrangement
options.rationale: Consent is a real issue here, and it is a consequence of the underlying error rather than the error itself.

questions.takeaway: Culturally congruent care is based on the individual's beliefs, practices and values. Group knowledge tells you what to ask about, not what to assume.
questions.strategy: One distractor concludes that learning about cultures is itself the mistake. Ask what turned useful knowledge into an error.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what she did with the knowledge

elimination.verdict: That leaves applying group knowledge without checking.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the five social determinants of health domains from Healthy People 2030. Which are included? Select all that apply.

options.text: Economic stability
options.rationale: Income, employment and the ability to meet basic needs.

options.text: Education access and quality
options.rationale: Named, and it connects to health literacy and to lifetime earning.

options.text: Health care access and quality
options.rationale: Named, and it covers insurance, transport and having a usual provider.

options.text: Neighborhood and built environment
options.rationale: Named, and it covers housing, food access and safety.

options.text: Social and community context
options.rationale: Named, and it covers support networks, discrimination and civic participation.

options.text: Genetic predisposition to disease
options.rationale: A genuine influence on health, and it is a biological factor rather than a social determinant. Determinants are non-medical conditions.

questions.takeaway: Five domains: economic stability, education, health care access, neighborhood and built environment, social and community context.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real health influence that is biological rather than social. Determinants are non-medical by definition.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Non-medical conditions where people live, learn, work and age.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.scenario: Four patients attend the same clinic, all with type 2 diabetes diagnosed within the past year.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate the barrier most likely to affect their diabetes management.

rows.text: A 25-year-old who is unhoused and uses a shelter
rows.rationale: Housing and income shape everything else, including whether insulin can be stored and meals eaten on time.

rows.text: An 85-year-old retired nurse in rural Alabama, 50 miles from the nearest endocrinologist
rows.rationale: She has the knowledge and the means. What she lacks is a service she can physically reach.

rows.text: A 32-year-old executive whose church community treats illness as a private matter she does not discuss
rows.rationale: Resources and access are not the problem. Her support network is a place she cannot bring this.

rows.text: An undocumented mother who avoids clinics for fear of immigration consequences
rows.rationale: The service exists and she cannot safely use it. Fear functions as an access barrier.

questions.takeaway: The same diagnosis meets four different lives. Intersectionality is why identical treatment plans produce different outcomes.
questions.strategy: Two patients share a domain for opposite reasons: one cannot reach the service, the other cannot safely use it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Money, distance, safety, or someone to tell.
Distance and fear both block use.
The executive lacks a place to be open.

elimination.verdict: Economic, access, community, access.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked what intersectionality adds to understanding a patient's health. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Identities accumulate, so more marginalized identities produce proportionally worse outcomes
options.rationale: Treats them as additive. The framework describes interlocking systems rather than a running total.

options.text: Overlapping identities interact, so privilege and oppression work as interlocking systems
options.rationale: The identities do not simply add up. A person can hold advantage in one dimension and disadvantage in another, and the combination shapes the outcome.

options.text: The most significant identity should be identified and addressed first
options.rationale: Ranking identities misses the point that they operate together and cannot be separated.

options.text: Patients with shared identities will have comparable health experiences
options.rationale: Contradicts the framework, and it is the assumption that produces stereotyping.

questions.takeaway: Intersectionality: social identities overlap, and privilege and oppression interlock rather than adding up.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns it into arithmetic. One turns it into a ranking. Both simplify what the framework exists to describe.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves interlocking systems.

questions.stem: A nurse works with a patient whose first language is not English. She speaks slowly, uses simple words, and asks the patient's adult son to interpret the consent discussion. Which action requires correction?

options.text: Speaking slowly during the conversation
options.rationale: Reasonable, and it helps when someone is working in a second language.

options.text: Using plain language rather than clinical terms
options.rationale: A named cultural skill, and it applies regardless of language.

options.text: Continuing the conversation in English with support
options.rationale: Not itself wrong. What is wrong is who was asked to bridge the gap for a consent discussion.

options.text: Using the patient's son as the interpreter for the consent discussion
