elimination.verdict: That leaves achievable.

questions.stem: A nurse begins a planned bed bath and the patient becomes short of breath and asks to sit forward. He was assessed as stable at the start of the shift. Which action is most appropriate?

options.text: Continue with the head of the bed raised and monitor him
options.rationale: Better, and it still continues a non-urgent task through an unexplained change in breathing.

options.text: Stop, reassess, and act on the new finding before continuing
options.rationale: Implementation requires ongoing reassessment while performing care. A plan made an hour ago does not override what is happening now.

options.text: Complete the bath quickly so he can rest afterwards
options.rationale: Prioritizes finishing the task over a change in his condition.

options.text: Document that the bath was not tolerated and reschedule it
options.rationale: Records the event and leaves the breathlessness unassessed.

questions.takeaway: Implementation requires ongoing reassessment during care. A change mid-task sends you back to assessment.
questions.strategy: Two distractors continue the task in some form. Ask what has changed since the plan was made.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: New breathlessness in a stable patient.
The task is not urgent; the change is.

elimination.verdict: That leaves stopping and reassessing.

questions.stem: A nurse gathers her equipment, reviews the steps, and confirms the patient's identity and allergies before starting a procedure she has performed many times. Which principle does this reflect?

options.text: Individualization takes precedence over standardization
options.rationale: A real tension in implementation, and nothing here is being individualized.

options.text: Standard interventions ensure evidence-based care
options.rationale: Standard interventions concern what the care is, not how she readies herself to give it.

options.text: Preparation reduces adverse events
options.rationale: Named directly. Familiarity with a procedure is not a substitute for preparing for this instance of it.

options.text: Care coordination requires appropriate use of resources
options.rationale: Coordination concerns communication, time management and resources across the whole assignment.

questions.takeaway: Preparation reduces adverse events. Care coordination skills are communication, time management, and appropriate use of resources.
questions.strategy: Three distractors name real implementation principles that describe something other than what she did.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves preparation reducing adverse events.

questions.nursesNote: 1015: Nurse enters to perform a scheduled dressing change on a 66-year-old, second day after bowel surgery. Supplies gathered and identity confirmed. Patient states the pain is 8 of 10 and he has not had analgesia since 0400. He is diaphoretic. Respiratory rate 24, up from 16 at 0800. Wound edges approximated, no drainage. Temperature 36.9 C. He says he would rather wait. Blood pressure 138/84.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that should stop the nurse proceeding with the dressing change now.

segments.text: Pain 8 of 10 with no analgesia since 0400
segments.rationale: Six hours without analgesia at 8 of 10. Performing a painful procedure on top of uncontrolled pain is avoidable harm.

segments.text: Diaphoretic
segments.rationale: A finding with several possible causes, none of which should be worked through during a dressing change.

segments.text: Respiratory rate 24, up from 16 at 0800
segments.rationale: A change from his own baseline within two hours. It may be pain, and it may not.

segments.text: He says he would rather wait
segments.rationale: The patient declining is sufficient on its own, and here he is also telling you something the numbers support.

segments.text: Wound edges approximated, no drainage
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding, and it is why this dressing change is not urgent.

segments.text: Temperature 36.9 C
segments.rationale: Normal, and it makes infection less likely as the cause of the other findings.

segments.text: Blood pressure 138/84
segments.rationale: Acceptable, and it does not by itself require action.

segments.text: Supplies gathered and identity confirmed
segments.rationale: Correct preparation. Preparing well does not oblige you to proceed.

questions.takeaway: Ongoing reassessment during implementation means the plan can be stopped. A prepared nurse is still allowed to change her mind.
questions.strategy: One finding tells you the task is not urgent. Another shows the preparation was correct, which is a reason to feel committed and not a reason to proceed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether the task is urgent

steps.detail: Pain, sweating, rate up from baseline.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s4: pain, diaphoresis, rising rate, and his own request.

questions.stem: A nurse follows a standard turning schedule but adapts it for a patient who cannot lie on his left side after surgery. Which implementation principle does this show?

options.text: Standard interventions provide evidence-based care and must still be individualized
options.rationale: Both halves are named on her slide. The standard gives the evidence base; the individual gives the constraints.

options.text: Nurses should develop an original plan for every patient
options.rationale: Discards the evidence base that standard interventions carry.

options.text: Deviation from a standard requires a provider order
options.rationale: Adapting how nursing care is delivered sits within nursing judgment.

options.text: Standard interventions should be followed exactly to ensure consistency
options.rationale: Removes individualization, which her slide names explicitly as a requirement.

questions.takeaway: Standard interventions help nurses provide evidence-based care, and care should be individualized. Both are required.
questions.strategy: Two distractors take one half of the principle and discard the other.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves standards individualized.

questions.stem: A nurse hands over a patient whose condition changed during the shift. Which activities are part of implementation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Communicating the change at handoff
options.rationale: Care coordination skills include communication, and handoff is where it matters most.

options.text: Documenting the findings and the care given
options.rationale: Part of carrying out the plan, and it is how the next nurse can act on what happened.

options.text: Beginning patient and family teaching
options.rationale: Teaching is an intervention delivered rather than a separate activity.

options.text: Performing the wound care per protocol
options.rationale: The most visible form of taking action.

options.text: Reassessing the patient while performing the care
options.rationale: Named directly. Implementation requires ongoing reassessment.

options.text: Writing the expected outcome the care is aimed at
options.rationale: Outcomes are written during planning, before implementation begins.

questions.takeaway: Implementation: carry out the plan, individualize it, reassess while performing care, prepare properly, and coordinate through communication, time management and resources.
questions.strategy: One distractor belongs to the step before. Ask when the outcome was written.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: An outcome states that a patient will walk 100 feet twice daily by day four. On day four he walks 60 feet once, having managed 20 feet on day one. Which evaluation is accurate?

options.text: Met, because he has made significant progress
options.rationale: The outcome named 100 feet twice daily. Progress is not the same as achievement.

options.text: Partially met, because he improved substantially without reaching the stated target
options.rationale: Three verdicts exist: met, partially met, not met. Real progress that falls short of the target is what partially met describes.

options.text: Cannot be evaluated until he reaches his baseline
options.rationale: The outcome had a deadline, and day four has arrived.

options.text: Not met, because he did not reach 100 feet twice daily
options.rationale: Technically accurate about the target and it discards a tripling of his distance, which the plan revision needs to know.

questions.takeaway: Evaluation asks whether the goal was met, partially met, or not met, and what data supports that conclusion.
questions.strategy: The middle verdict exists precisely for this situation. Two options collapse it into all or nothing.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One ignores the target, one ignores the progress.

elimination.verdict: That leaves partially met.

questions.stem: A patient's mobility outcome was not met. Which actions does the nurse take when revising the plan? Select all that apply.

options.text: Reassess the patient for new or overlooked data
options.rationale: Named first. Something may have been missed, or may have changed since the plan was written.

options.text: Reconsider whether the nursing diagnosis is still the priority
options.rationale: Named, and it is the step students skip. The plan may be failing because the problem was named wrongly.

options.text: Adjust the goal, the outcome, or the target timeframe
options.rationale: Named, and sometimes only the deadline was wrong.

options.text: Select new or additional interventions
options.rationale: Named, and it is what most people think of first.

options.text: Document that the patient was nonadherent with the mobility plan
options.rationale: Attributes the failure to the patient and closes the revision before it starts.

options.text: Continue the current plan for a further 48 hours before changing anything
options.rationale: Delays a revision the evaluation has already shown is needed.

questions.takeaway: When an outcome is not met: reassess for new data, reconsider the diagnosis, adjust goals or timeframes, and select new interventions.
questions.strategy: One distractor blames the patient. One waits. Neither is among the four named steps.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The evaluation already answered the question.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.scenario: A 72-year-old was admitted with pneumonia. An outcome stated he would maintain an oxygen saturation above 92% on room air by day three. On day three his saturation is 89% on room air and 94% on 2 L by nasal cannula. He is completing his antibiotics, his temperature is normal, and his chest sounds have improved. He has been on bed rest since admission and has not mobilized.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 conclusion she reaches, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Reassess for factors the original plan did not account for
options.rationale: The first step when an outcome is not met. His infection is resolving, so something else is keeping his saturation down.

options.text: Add mobilization and deep breathing to the plan of care
options.rationale: Selecting new or additional interventions. Three days of bed rest is the factor the original plan missed.

options.text: Document that the outcome was not met and continue the current plan
options.rationale: Records the verdict and changes nothing, which is the one thing evaluation is meant to prevent.

options.text: Extend the target date by a further three days
options.rationale: Adjusting the timeframe is a legitimate revision, and doing it alone assumes the plan would work given longer. Nothing suggests it would.

options.text: The outcome was not met, and the plan omitted a contributing factor
options.rationale: He needs oxygen to reach 94%, so the outcome as written was not achieved. The infection is treated and the immobility is not.

options.text: The outcome was met, since his saturation is 94%
options.rationale: The outcome specified room air. Meeting it with supplemental oxygen is not meeting it.

options.text: The outcome was partially met and the plan should continue unchanged
options.rationale: Partially met is defensible as a verdict, and continuing unchanged is not, since the evaluation has revealed something.

options.text: The antibiotic regimen has failed and should be reviewed
options.rationale: His temperature is normal and his chest sounds have improved. The infection is responding.

options.text: Oxygen saturation on room air after mobilization begins
options.rationale: The original outcome, remeasured under the same conditions, after the new intervention.

options.text: Distance mobilized and frequency of deep breathing exercises
options.rationale: Measures whether the added intervention is actually happening, which has to be true before it can work.

options.text: White cell count at the next blood test
options.rationale: Tracks the infection, which is already resolving and is not what the actions changed.

options.text: Whether he can describe the purpose of deep breathing
options.rationale: Tests knowledge. The outcome concerns his saturation, not his understanding.

questions.takeaway: An unmet outcome is information. Reassess for what the plan missed before assuming the plan needs longer.
questions.strategy: The outcome specified room air, which is what makes 94% on oxygen a non-achievement. Two distractors track the infection, which is already resolving.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Reassess and add mobilization, outcome not met with a missed factor, evaluated by room-air saturation and by uptake.

questions.stem: After an outcome is not met, a nurse reconsiders whether the nursing diagnosis she wrote is still accurate. Which step of the clinical judgment model has she returned to?

options.text: Generating solutions
options.rationale: Choosing new interventions is generating solutions. She is questioning the problem, not the plan.

options.text: Prioritizing hypotheses
options.rationale: Ranking competing explanations. She is asking whether the one she chose was right at all.

options.text: Analyzing cues
options.rationale: Questioning whether the problem was named correctly is a return to interpretation, one step further back than revising the plan.

options.text: Evaluating outcomes
options.rationale: That step produced the verdict. Acting on it is what comes next.

questions.takeaway: Revising the plan can send you back to different steps. New data goes to recognizing cues; a wrong diagnosis goes to analyzing cues; a wrong intervention goes to generating solutions.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are also steps you can return to. Ask which part of the plan she is questioning.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That would be doubting the intervention.
One just finished, one ranks rather than names.

elimination.verdict: That leaves analyzing cues.

questions.stem: A nurse evaluates whether a patient met the outcome of demonstrating correct inhaler technique. Which method is appropriate?

options.text: Observe him use the inhaler and compare against the correct steps
options.rationale: A psychomotor outcome is evaluated by watching it performed. Asking whether he understands does not show that he can.

options.text: Ask him to describe the steps in the correct order
options.rationale: The near-miss. Describing shows knowledge; the outcome required performance.

options.text: Confirm that the teaching session was completed and documented
options.rationale: Records what the nurse did. It says nothing about what the patient achieved.

options.text: Ask him whether he feels confident using the inhaler
options.rationale: Confidence is not competence, and the outcome specified demonstration.

questions.takeaway: Evaluate an outcome by the method the outcome specified. Demonstration is evaluated by watching.
questions.strategy: One distractor offers what the nurse did as evidence of what the patient achieved. The near-miss tests knowledge instead of performance.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves observing him use it.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse plans the assignment for a shift with one registered nurse, one licensed practical nurse, and one assistive personnel.
questions.stem: For each task, indicate whether it may be delegated to assistive personnel or must be retained by a licensed nurse.
columns: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

rows.text: Recording intake and output for a stable patient
rows.rationale: A routine measurement task on a stable patient, and it requires no clinical judgment to perform.

rows.text: Teaching a newly diagnosed patient how to inject insulin
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
rows.rationale: Patient education requires assessment of readiness and understanding, and it cannot be delegated.

rows.text: Taking vital signs on a patient whose condition has not changed
rows.rationale: Right circumstance is satisfied: the patient is stable. The nurse still interprets what comes back.

rows.text: Assessing a patient who has become newly short of breath
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
rows.rationale: Assessment of an unstable patient. Neither the task nor the circumstance permits delegation.

rows.text: Assisting a patient who ambulates independently to the bathroom
rows.rationale: Routine assistance for a patient whose mobility status is known and stable.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a patient met his mobility outcome
rows.answer: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
rows.rationale: Evaluation is a step of the nursing process and stays with the nurse, even when the walking itself was assisted by someone else.

answer.r2: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
answer.r4: Must be retained by a licensed nurse
answer.r6: Must be retained by a licensed nurse

questions.takeaway: Assessment, teaching, evaluation, and unstable patients stay with the nurse. Routine tasks on stable patients may be delegated.
questions.strategy: Two things decide it: what the task requires, and how stable the patient is. A delegable task on an unstable patient is no longer delegable.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask how stable the patient is

steps.detail: The walking can be delegated; the verdict cannot.

elimination.verdict: Three delegable, three retained.

questions.stem: A nurse tells assistive personnel to get the vital signs on the patient in room 12 and walks away. The readings are taken an hour later and the patient's blood pressure has fallen to 86/50 without anyone reporting it. Which right of delegation was not met?

options.text: Right task
options.rationale: Vital signs on a stable patient are appropriate to delegate. The task itself was fine.

options.text: Right directions and communication
options.rationale: Clear instructions, expectations, and when to report back. She gave a task and no parameters, so nobody knew 86/50 needed reporting.

options.text: Right person
options.rationale: Nothing suggests the assistive personnel were unqualified to take a blood pressure.

options.text: Right circumstance
options.rationale: The patient was stable when the task was assigned. What followed came from the missing instructions, not from the circumstance.

questions.takeaway: Five rights: right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, right supervision and evaluation.
questions.strategy: Three of the five were satisfied. Ask what the assistive personnel would have needed to know to act differently.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Get the vital signs. Nothing else.
When to report, and what would count as abnormal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves right directions and communication.

questions.stem: A nurse delegates a bed bath to assistive personnel. During the bath the patient's oxygen tubing is dislodged and not replaced, and his saturation falls. Who is accountable?

options.text: The assistive personnel, because the omission occurred during their care
options.rationale: They answer for their own performance. That does not remove the nurse's accountability for the outcome.

options.text: Both equally, since the task was shared
options.rationale: Accountability is not divided into halves. Each answers fully for their own part, and the nurse answers for the outcome.

options.text: The charge nurse, who made the assignment
options.rationale: The charge nurse answers for the assignment. The nurse who delegated this task answers for this outcome.

options.text: The nurse, because accountability for the outcome remains with her even when she delegates
options.rationale: Her slide states this directly. The task moves; the accountability does not.

questions.takeaway: Accountability means you own the outcome of what you do, even if you delegate it. The task transfers; the accountability does not.
questions.strategy: Two distractors move accountability elsewhere. One splits it. Ask what delegation actually transfers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the nurse who delegated.

questions.stem: A charge nurse considers delegating a task to assistive personnel. Which questions must she answer before doing so? Select all that apply.

options.text: Is this task appropriate to delegate
options.rationale: Right task, and it is the first question because nothing else matters if the answer is no.

options.text: Is the patient's condition stable and appropriate for delegation
options.rationale: Right circumstance. A delegable task on an unstable patient is not delegable.

options.text: Is this person competent and qualified to perform it
options.rationale: Right person, and qualified and competent are two separate checks.

options.text: Have I given clear instructions, expectations, and when to report back
options.rationale: Right directions and communication.

options.text: Will I monitor the outcome and follow up
options.rationale: Right supervision and evaluation, which is the one people treat as optional.

options.text: Does the patient agree to the task being performed by assistive personnel
options.rationale: Consent concerns whether care happens, not who may lawfully perform it. It is not among the five rights.

questions.takeaway: Five rights of delegation: right task, right circumstance, right person, right directions and communication, right supervision and evaluation.
questions.strategy: One distractor names something reasonable that is not one of the five.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse is worried about a patient whose condition is changing.

Reporting the situation, background, assessment and recommendation to the provider uses [[1]].

Saying "I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue" uses [[2]].

Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support are the pillars of [[3]].

Her legal power to call the provider and question an order is [[4]].

options.text: SBAR
options.rationale: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. A structure for handing over information.

options.text: CUS
options.rationale: CUS escalates a concern when reporting has not produced a response.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: A framework with four pillars, not a report structure.

options.text: the five rights
options.rationale: A delegation checklist.

options.text: CUS
options.rationale: Concerned, Uncomfortable, Safety issue. Graded language for escalating when the first report did not work.

options.text: SBAR
options.rationale: The near-miss. SBAR reports; CUS escalates after reporting has failed.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: The wider framework these tools sit inside.

options.text: shared governance
options.rationale: A structure for staff involvement in decisions, not a communication tool.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS
options.rationale: Its four pillars: communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, mutual support.

options.text: the interprofessional competencies
options.rationale: The near-miss. Those four are values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork.

options.text: the Magnet standards
options.rationale: Shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, professional development.

options.text: the decision-making framework
options.rationale: Responsibility, autonomy, authority, accountability.

options.text: authority
options.rationale: The legal power to act, including calling a provider and questioning an order.

options.text: autonomy
options.rationale: The near-miss. Autonomy is freedom to choose within scope; authority is the power to act on it.

options.text: responsibility
options.rationale: What you are supposed to do, your job duties.

options.text: accountability
options.rationale: Owning the outcome of what you do.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports. CUS escalates. TeamSTEPPS has four pillars. Authority is the legal power to act; autonomy is the freedom to choose.
questions.strategy: Two pairs of four get confused: TeamSTEPPS pillars against the interprofessional competencies, and authority against autonomy.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the two sets of four

elimination.verdict: SBAR, CUS, TeamSTEPPS, authority.

questions.stem: A nurse reports a patient's falling blood pressure and rising pulse to the provider using a structured format. He says to continue monitoring. Two hours later the pressure has fallen further and she calls again. Which tool should she use now?

options.text: SBAR, to repeat the report in a clearer structure
options.rationale: She already reported it using a structure. Repeating the same tool that did not work is unlikely to change the outcome.

options.text: TeamSTEPPS situation monitoring, to continue observing the patient
options.rationale: Situation monitoring is what produced her concern. It does not communicate it to anyone.

options.text: CUS, stating that she is concerned, uncomfortable, and that this is a safety issue
options.rationale: CUS exists for the moment when reporting has not produced a response. The graded language makes the concern impossible to file away.

options.text: The chain of command, going directly to the nursing supervisor
options.rationale: Appropriate if CUS fails, and escalating past the provider before using the graded language skips a step that often works.

questions.takeaway: SBAR hands over information. CUS escalates when the handover has not produced a response.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is repeating SBAR. Ask what changed between the first call and the second.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reported it in a structured format.
It did not work the first time.
One does not communicate, one skips a step.

elimination.verdict: That leaves CUS.

questions.stem: A nurse notices a colleague about to give a medication to the wrong patient and says nothing, assuming the colleague has checked. Which TeamSTEPPS pillar was not applied?

options.text: Communication
options.rationale: Involved in the sense that she said nothing, and the pillar that names watching out for a colleague is mutual support.

options.text: Mutual support
options.rationale: Mutual support means team members watch out for each other and speak up. Assuming someone else has checked is how errors reach patients.

options.text: Situation monitoring
options.rationale: She did monitor the situation. She saw it. What failed was acting on what she saw.

options.text: Team leadership
options.rationale: Concerns how the team is directed and coordinated, rather than one member covering another.

questions.takeaway: TeamSTEPPS pillars: communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, mutual support.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is situation monitoring, and the stem tells you she noticed. Noticing was not the failure.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves mutual support.

questions.stem: A nurse decides that a patient's scheduled bath can wait because he is exhausted after physiotherapy. She makes the decision herself without consulting anyone. Which element of the decision-making framework is she exercising?

options.text: Authority, her legal power to act
options.rationale: The near-miss. Authority is the power to act, such as calling a provider and questioning an order. Autonomy is choosing what to do within scope.

options.text: Responsibility, her assigned job duties
options.rationale: Responsibility is what she is supposed to do. The bath is one of those duties; deciding when is autonomy.

options.text: Accountability, owning the outcome
options.rationale: She will own this decision, and accountability describes answering for it rather than making it.

options.text: Autonomy, her freedom to make independent choices within her scope
options.rationale: Timing routine care is squarely within nursing judgment, and she made the call herself.

questions.takeaway: Responsibility is what you are supposed to do. Autonomy is your freedom to choose within scope. Authority is your legal power to act. Accountability is owning the outcome.
questions.strategy: All four elements are present in any nursing decision. Ask which one names the act of deciding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Chose, within her scope, without asking.
Power to act, not freedom to choose.
One is the duty, one is the aftermath.

elimination.verdict: That leaves autonomy.

questions.stem: A nurse questions an order for a dose she believes is unsafe, contacts the prescriber, and documents the conversation. Which elements of the decision-making framework does this demonstrate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Authority, the legal power to call a provider and question an order
options.rationale: Her slide gives this as the example of authority, almost word for word.

options.text: Autonomy, the freedom to make an independent judgment within her scope
options.rationale: Deciding the dose looked wrong and acting on that judgment is autonomy.

options.text: Accountability, owning the outcome of what she does
options.rationale: She answers for the decision to question it, and she would have answered for giving it.

options.text: Responsibility, carrying out her job duties
options.rationale: Safe medication administration is among her duties, and questioning an unsafe order is part of performing it.

options.text: Delegation, transferring the task to someone more senior
options.rationale: She did not hand the problem to anyone. She acted on it herself.

questions.takeaway: The four elements are not alternatives. A single nursing action usually involves all of them at once.
questions.strategy: The distractor describes handing the problem on. Ask whether she transferred anything.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what she did with the problem

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A new graduate says she does not see herself as a leader because she manages no one. Which response is most accurate?

options.text: Leading her own patient care requires clinical judgment, priority setting, time management, delegation, and team communication
options.rationale: Her slide lists these as ground-level skills every nurse needs. Leadership is framed as practical rather than positional.

options.text: Leadership skills develop naturally with clinical experience
options.rationale: They are described as learnable and practical, which implies they are taught and practised rather than absorbed.

options.text: Leadership becomes relevant once she moves into a management role
options.rationale: The slide states the opposite: this is not just a management-track skill.

options.text: Her focus should remain on clinical skills until she is more experienced
options.rationale: Separates clinical work from leading it, when prioritizing and delegating are part of the clinical work itself.

questions.takeaway: Leadership skills are learnable and practical: clinical judgment, priority setting, time management, delegation, and team communication.
questions.strategy: Three distractors defer leadership to later, to a role, or to experience. Ask what she does on her own assignment today.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the ground-level skills.

questions.stem: A patient is discharged from hospital to a rehabilitation facility and then home, with one person coordinating across all three settings. Which nursing care delivery model is in use?

options.text: Case management
options.rationale: Someone coordinates care across multiple settings, which is her definition of the model.

options.text: Primary nursing
options.rationale: One registered nurse follows a patient throughout, and it operates within a setting rather than across several. Her slide notes it is rare today because it is expensive.

options.text: Team nursing
options.rationale: A group led by a registered nurse working together on one unit.

options.text: Patient- and family-centered care
options.rationale: Treats the patient and family as partners. It describes the relationship rather than how care is organized across settings.

questions.takeaway: Team nursing is a group led by an RN. Primary nursing is one RN following a patient through. Case management coordinates across settings. Patient- and family-centered care treats them as partners.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is primary nursing, which also involves one person following a patient. The difference is whether it crosses settings.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut team nursing and the partnership model
steps.detail: One is a unit group, one is a relationship.

elimination.verdict: That leaves case management.

questions.stem: A hospital applies for Magnet recognition. Which standards must it demonstrate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Shared decision-making
options.rationale: Named first, and it connects to shared governance and decentralization.

options.text: Leadership
options.rationale: Named, and it reflects how a unit is led affecting outcomes and burnout.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Named among the six standards.

options.text: Quality
options.rationale: Named, and it is measured through nursing-sensitive outcomes.

options.text: Well-being
options.rationale: Named, and it reflects nurse satisfaction and moral distress.

options.text: Cost containment per patient day
options.rationale: A real organizational concern and not among the Magnet standards. The standards concern how nursing is practised and supported.

questions.takeaway: Magnet standards: shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, and professional development.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a legitimate hospital priority that is not one of the six.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Shared decision-making, leadership, safety, quality, well-being, professional development.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A unit adopts a Professional Practice Model built around patient- and family-centered care. Which set of elements defines it?

options.text: Communication, team leadership, situation monitoring, and mutual support
options.rationale: The TeamSTEPPS pillars, which concern how the team works rather than how patients are engaged.

options.text: Respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, and collaboration
options.rationale: Her four core elements of patient- and family-centered care within the practice model.

options.text: Values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teamwork
options.rationale: The four interprofessional competencies.

options.text: Responsibility, autonomy, authority, and accountability
options.rationale: The decision-making framework.

questions.takeaway: Patient- and family-centered care: respect and dignity, information sharing, participation, collaboration. The practice model drives the nursing care delivery model.
questions.strategy: All four options are real sets of four from this chapter. Ask which set is about patients rather than about staff.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves respect, information sharing, participation, collaboration.

questions.stem: A nurse executive introduces a program inviting staff nurses to propose and trial changes to unit practice, with protected time to do so. Which characteristic of an empowered nursing team does this support?

options.text: Compliance with regulatory standards for nursing practice
options.rationale: Regulation sets a floor. Empowerment is about what happens above it.

options.text: Standardization of nursing care across the organization
options.rationale: The opposite direction. This program invites variation in order to test improvements.

options.text: Clear separation between management and clinical decision-making
options.rationale: Decentralization and shared governance blur that line deliberately.

options.text: An environment that supports risk-taking, innovation, and professional growth
options.rationale: Named directly as what empowering environments do, and protected time is what turns the invitation into something real.

questions.takeaway: Empowering environments support risk-taking, innovation, and professional growth. A culture of autonomy, quality and collaboration raises satisfaction and lowers moral distress.
questions.strategy: Two distractors describe control rather than empowerment. Ask what protected time to trial a change actually enables.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Trying something that might not work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves risk-taking and innovation.

questions.stem: A nurse asks what shared governance means in practice on her unit. Which example fits?

options.text: The nurse manager consults staff before announcing a decision
options.rationale: Consultation is better than none and it keeps the decision in one place. Governance means staff hold part of it.

options.text: Staff nurses are surveyed annually about their satisfaction
options.rationale: Collects views without giving anyone a decision to make.

options.text: Staff nurses sit on a council that decides how care is delivered on the unit
options.rationale: Decentralization and shared governance mean decisions move toward the people doing the work.

options.text: Policies are written by a central committee and applied to every unit
options.rationale: Centralization, which is what shared governance moves away from.

questions.takeaway: Decentralization and shared governance move decision-making toward the staff who deliver the care.
questions.strategy: Two distractors gather opinions without transferring any decision. Ask who actually decides in each.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both inform a decision held elsewhere.

elimination.verdict: That leaves staff sitting on the deciding council.

questions.stem: A nurse participates in interprofessional rounds with a physician, a pharmacist, a physical therapist and a social worker. Which interprofessional competencies are being exercised? Select all that apply.

options.text: Values and ethics for interprofessional practice
options.rationale: Named, and it underlies mutual respect between disciplines.

options.text: Roles and responsibilities
options.rationale: Named, and rounds only work if everyone knows what each discipline contributes.

options.text: Interprofessional communication
options.rationale: Named, and it is the visible activity of a round.

options.text: Teams and teamwork
options.rationale: Named, and it is what turns four disciplines into one plan.

options.text: Delegation of tasks across disciplines
options.rationale: Delegation operates within nursing to appropriate personnel. Coordinating with other disciplines is collaboration rather than delegation.

questions.takeaway: Four interprofessional competencies: values and ethics, roles and responsibilities, communication, and teams and teamwork.
questions.strategy: One distractor applies a nursing-specific concept to interdisciplinary work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Values and ethics, roles, communication, teamwork.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.nursesNote: 0730: Charge nurse reviewing the shift. Unit has four registered nurses, one licensed practical nurse, and two assistive personnel for 28 patients. One registered nurse is orienting on her second shift. Three patients are scheduled for transfer to a step-down unit today. A patient in room 14 was admitted overnight with chest pain and has not yet been assessed this shift. The assistive personnel were told to 'do the vitals' with no reporting parameters given. A newly admitted patient in room 22 needs discharge teaching for a new insulin regimen, and this has been assigned to an assistive personnel. Two patients are stable and awaiting routine morning care.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that the charge nurse must address before the shift proceeds.

segments.text: A registered nurse orienting on her second shift
segments.rationale: Right person applies to assignments as well as to delegation. A nurse two shifts in needs an assignment matched to her competence and support.

segments.text: A patient admitted overnight with chest pain, not yet assessed this shift
segments.rationale: An unassessed patient with a cardiac presentation. Nobody currently knows his status.

segments.text: Assistive personnel told to 'do the vitals' with no reporting parameters
segments.rationale: Right directions and communication. Without parameters, an abnormal reading may sit unreported.

segments.text: Discharge teaching for a new insulin regimen assigned to assistive personnel
segments.rationale: Patient education cannot be delegated. This fails right task before any other consideration.

segments.text: Four registered nurses, one licensed practical nurse and two assistive personnel for 28 patients
segments.rationale: The staffing she has. It shapes every decision she makes and is not itself a finding she can correct this morning.

segments.text: Three patients scheduled for transfer to a step-down unit
segments.rationale: Planned work requiring coordination. Expected, and not a safety problem.

segments.text: Two stable patients awaiting routine morning care
segments.rationale: Routine care on stable patients. This is the work the shift exists to do.

questions.takeaway: Delegation errors and unassessed patients come first. Staffing constraints shape the plan rather than being a correctable finding.
questions.strategy: One finding is the constraint she is working inside rather than a problem to solve. Two describe expected work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The staffing number is the constraint.
No parameters, and teaching assigned to AP.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s4: the orientee, the unassessed patient, and two delegation errors.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate describe her understanding of delegation. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "Once I delegate a task, the person performing it becomes accountable for the outcome."
options.rationale: Accountability stays with the delegating nurse. The task transfers and the answerability does not.

options.text: "A task that is usually delegable may not be, if the patient is unstable."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is right circumstance.

options.text: "I need to tell them what to report back and when."
options.rationale: Accurate. Right directions and communication.

options.text: "I cannot delegate assessment, teaching or evaluation."
options.rationale: Accurate. Those require nursing judgment and remain with the nurse.

questions.takeaway: Delegation transfers the task. Accountability for the outcome stays with the nurse who delegated it.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the rights correctly. The fourth moves accountability with the task.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the statement transferring accountability.

questions.stem: A unit reports rising nurse turnover, frequent reports of moral distress, and falling patient satisfaction. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Recruitment should be the priority before addressing culture
options.rationale: Recruiting into a unit people are leaving addresses the symptom and refills a leaking bucket.

options.text: The findings reflect individual nurses' resilience and coping skills
options.rationale: Locates a unit-level pattern in individual character, which is the misreading that leaves the culture unchanged.

options.text: How a unit is led affects patient outcomes, nurse satisfaction and burnout together
options.rationale: Her first key takeaway. These are not three separate problems, and leadership is the common factor.

options.text: Turnover and satisfaction are unrelated to clinical quality measures
options.rationale: They move together, which is why Magnet treats well-being as a standard alongside quality.

questions.takeaway: Leadership shapes care quality. Patient outcomes, nurse satisfaction and burnout move together rather than separately.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns a unit pattern into a personal shortcoming. Ask what the three findings have in common.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All three sit on one unit.

steps.action: Cut the unrelated and recruitment options
steps.detail: One denies the link, one treats the symptom.

elimination.verdict: That leaves leadership affecting all three.

questions.scenario: A nurse reports to the provider that her patient's blood pressure has fallen from 132/78 to 94/56 over three hours, his pulse has risen from 78 to 118, and his urine output has been 15 mL/hr for two hours. She uses a structured report. The provider says to continue monitoring and recheck in two hours. She remains concerned.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Escalate using graded language: concerned, uncomfortable, this is a safety issue
options.rationale: CUS exists for exactly this moment. She reported once and the response did not match the findings, so the next step is language that cannot be filed away.

options.text: Notify the charge nurse and prepare to move up the chain of command
options.rationale: Her authority includes questioning an order and escalating. Preparing the next step is not going over anyone's head prematurely.

options.text: Recheck in two hours as instructed and document the conversation
options.rationale: Following an instruction that does not match the findings, and documenting it does not make two hours safe.

options.text: Repeat the same structured report to the same provider
options.rationale: The report was already given clearly. Repeating the tool that did not work is unlikely to change the response.

options.text: A deteriorating patient whose concern has not been acted on
options.rationale: Three parameters moving together in one direction, and a response that does not match them. Both halves are the problem.

options.text: A communication failure requiring a clearer handover
options.rationale: She communicated clearly using a structure. The failure is in the response, not in the report.

options.text: A conflict between the nurse and the provider
options.rationale: Frames a patient safety issue as an interpersonal one, which is how escalation gets delayed.

options.text: An expected postoperative variation in vital signs
options.rationale: Falling pressure with rising pulse and oliguria is not expected variation in any context.

options.text: Blood pressure, pulse and urine output at short intervals
options.rationale: The three parameters that defined the deterioration, measured frequently enough to catch the next change.

options.text: Whether a provider has assessed the patient in person
options.rationale: Measures whether the escalation worked. A verbal instruction is not an assessment.

options.text: Whether the incident report has been completed
options.rationale: Administrative follow-up. It records what happened and does not evaluate whether he is safe now.

options.text: The provider's response to being escalated
options.rationale: Concerns the relationship rather than the patient, and escalation is judged by whether the patient was assessed.

questions.takeaway: SBAR reports and CUS escalates. When the response does not match the findings, the graded language is the next tool, and the chain of command is behind it.
questions.strategy: Two distractors frame this as a communication or relationship problem. Three numbers are moving together, which makes it a patient problem.

strategies: Match each part to what the stem gives

steps.detail: Pressure down, pulse up, output 15 mL/hr.
Not a handover failure, not a conflict.

elimination.verdict: Escalate with CUS and prepare the chain of command, for a deteriorating patient, evaluated by the trends and by an in-person assessment.

questions.scenario: A nurse works on a unit where several difficult situations arise during one week.
questions.stem: For each situation, indicate which ethical principle is most directly at stake.

rows.text: A competent patient refuses a recommended amputation
rows.rationale: His right to decide for himself, even when the team disagrees with the decision.

rows.text: A nurse withholds a medication because the dose would harm the patient
rows.rationale: Do no harm. The action is defined by what she is preventing.

rows.text: A nurse promised to return after her break and does
rows.rationale: Keeping the promises you make, which is what builds trust across a shift.

rows.text: A unit reviews whether two patients with equal need receive equal access to a scarce bed
rows.rationale: Fairness in distributing care and resources between people.

rows.text: A nurse arranges additional analgesia so a patient can tolerate physiotherapy
rows.rationale: Acting to do good, not merely to avoid harm.

rows.text: A nurse tells a patient she will pass his question to the provider today, and does
rows.rationale: Another promise kept. Fidelity appears twice because it is the principle that runs through ordinary shifts.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy is the patient deciding. Beneficence is doing good. Nonmaleficence is avoiding harm. Justice is fairness between people. Fidelity is keeping promises.
questions.strategy: Beneficence and nonmaleficence are the pair that gets confused. One adds a benefit; the other prevents a harm.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate doing good from avoiding harm
steps.detail: Adding analgesia, or withholding a dose.

steps.action: Watch for more than one person

elimination.verdict: Autonomy, nonmaleficence, fidelity, justice, beneficence, fidelity.

questions.stem: A nurse is caring for a patient whose family insists that aggressive treatment continue while the patient has a valid advance directive declining it. The team is divided. Which type of ethical problem is this?

options.text: Moral distress, because the nurse knows the right action but cannot take it
options.rationale: The near-miss. Moral distress is knowing what is right and being unable to do it. Here the right course is genuinely contested.

options.text: A legal problem requiring the risk management department
options.rationale: Legal input may follow, and the situation is first an ethical one about whose wishes govern.

options.text: A communication failure between the team and the family
options.rationale: Communication is involved and the conflict would remain even if everyone understood each other perfectly.

options.text: An ethical dilemma, because two defensible courses of action conflict
options.rationale: A dilemma exists when there are competing legitimate claims and no option satisfies everyone. Both positions have an ethical basis.

questions.takeaway: An ethical dilemma has competing defensible options. Moral distress is knowing the right action and being prevented from taking it.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is moral distress. Ask whether the right course is unclear, or clear and blocked.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask whether the right action is known

steps.detail: That requires a known right action.

steps.action: Cut the legal and communication framings
steps.detail: Both would leave the conflict intact.

elimination.verdict: That leaves an ethical dilemma.

questions.stem: A nurse is repeatedly assigned to give treatments she believes are prolonging suffering in a dying patient. She has raised it twice and nothing has changed. She dreads her shifts. Which is she experiencing?

options.text: An ethical dilemma
options.rationale: A dilemma is uncertainty between two defensible options. She is not uncertain; she is blocked.

options.text: Moral distress
options.rationale: She knows what she believes is right and is constrained from acting on it. The repetition and the dread are characteristic.

options.text: Compassion fatigue
options.rationale: Exhaustion from prolonged exposure to suffering. Related, and it does not name the constraint she is describing.

options.text: Burnout from workload
options.rationale: Workload is not what she describes. The distress is about what she is being asked to do, not how much.

questions.takeaway: Moral distress is knowing the ethically right action and being unable to take it. An ethical dilemma is not knowing which action is right.
questions.strategy: The pair worth separating is dilemma and distress. Uncertainty against constraint.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She is clear about what she believes is right.

elimination.verdict: That leaves moral distress.

questions.stem: A nurse encounters a situation involving a disagreement about a patient's care. Place the steps of processing an ethical problem in the correct order.

options.text: Ask whether this is an ethical problem
options.rationale: First. Not every difficult situation is an ethical one, and some are clinical or communication problems.

options.text: Gather information relevant to the case
options.rationale: Second. Patient, family, agency and social perspectives are all relevant sources.

options.text: Identify the ethical elements and examine your own values
options.rationale: Third. Clarify values, recognize the principles involved, and distinguish facts from opinions from values.

options.text: Name the problem in a clear, simple statement
options.rationale: Fourth. Difficult to do well, and it is what makes the final plan effective and the discussion possible.

options.text: Identify possible courses of action
options.rationale: Fifth. Seek others' input and be creative about the options.

options.text: Create and implement an action plan
options.rationale: Sixth. Gather support, and identify an alternative if the chosen action does not resolve it.

options.text: Evaluate the action plan
options.rationale: Seventh. Decide whether further action is needed, and what transfers to the next situation.

questions.takeaway: Seven steps: is it ethical, gather information, identify elements and examine values, name the problem, identify options, create and implement a plan, evaluate.
questions.strategy: The step people invert is naming the problem. It comes after examining values, not before, because your values shape how you name it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Is this even an ethical problem?
A clear problem statement makes the options possible.

elimination.verdict: Ask, gather, identify, name, options, implement, evaluate.

questions.stem: A nurse working through an ethical problem has gathered information from the patient, the family and the agency. Which step comes next?

options.text: Name the problem in a clear statement
options.rationale: Step four, and it comes after the elements have been identified. Naming it first risks naming it wrongly.

options.text: Identify possible courses of action
options.rationale: Step five. Options generated before the problem is named tend to answer the wrong question.

options.text: Identify the ethical elements and examine her own values
options.rationale: Step three. Clarify values, recognize the principles involved, and distinguish facts from opinion from values.

options.text: Convene the ethics committee
options.rationale: Committees support the process rather than replacing its steps, and this stage is still hers to work through.

questions.takeaway: The seven steps run in order: ask, gather, identify elements and examine values, name, options, implement, evaluate.
questions.strategy: Two distractors are later steps in the same sequence. Ask what has to happen before you can name a problem accurately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Naming and options both come after.

elimination.verdict: That leaves identifying elements and examining values.

questions.stem: A nursing student asks which principles the profession's code of ethics identifies as key. Which are included? Select all that apply.

options.text: Advocacy
options.rationale: Named, and it places the nurse between the patient and everyone else.

options.text: Responsibility
options.rationale: Named, and it concerns what the nurse is obliged to do.

options.text: Accountability
options.rationale: Named, and it concerns answering for what was done.

options.text: Confidentiality
options.rationale: Named, and it underlies every documentation and disclosure decision.

options.text: Efficiency in the use of resources
options.rationale: A legitimate organizational value and not among the code's key principles.

options.text: Loyalty to the employing institution
options.rationale: The code binds the nurse to the patient. Institutional loyalty is not a principle of it, and it can conflict with advocacy.

questions.takeaway: A code of ethics is a set of guiding principles all members of a profession accept. Its key principles are advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality.
questions.strategy: One distractor would put the institution where the patient belongs. That substitution is the reason advocacy is first on the list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse posts on social media that she had 'a rough shift with a difficult 40-year-old motorcycle crash patient' without naming anyone. Which problem does this create?

options.text: It should have been posted to a private group of nurses instead
options.rationale: A private audience is still an audience, and the information is still disclosed.

options.text: None, because no name or medical record number was used
options.rationale: Identifiability is not limited to names. This is the misunderstanding that produces most social media breaches.

options.text: It reflects poorly on the profession but breaches no principle
options.rationale: Professional image is a real concern and the confidentiality breach is the specific problem here.

options.text: The detail may identify the patient, which breaches confidentiality
options.rationale: A specific age, mechanism and timeframe can identify someone in a small community. Removing the name does not anonymize a case.

questions.takeaway: Social media is a named contemporary ethical issue. Confidentiality is breached by identifiable detail, not only by names.
questions.strategy: One distractor states the exact reasoning that causes these breaches. Ask whether a reader could work out who this is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a reader could piece together

elimination.verdict: That leaves potential identification.

questions.stem: A nurse strongly disagrees with a competent patient's decision to decline dialysis. Which action reflects her professional obligation?

options.text: Ensure he has the information he needs, then support the decision he makes
options.rationale: Autonomy means the competent patient decides. Her role is making sure the decision is informed, not making sure it is the one she would choose.

options.text: Arrange for the provider to explain the consequences again
options.rationale: Reasonable once, and repeated explanation after a settled decision becomes pressure rather than information.

options.text: Document that the patient is refusing recommended treatment
options.rationale: Necessary, and documenting alone does nothing about whether the decision was informed.

options.text: Request an ethics committee consultation
options.rationale: Committees are for genuine dilemmas. A competent patient declining treatment is not one.

questions.takeaway: Autonomy governs when a competent patient has made an informed decision. The nurse's disagreement is not an ethical problem.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats a settled competent decision as a dilemma. Ask whether anything here is actually contested.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves informing and supporting.

questions.stem: A nurse says she thinks it is wrong to lie, and her colleague says the hospital policy requires honest disclosure of errors. Which distinction do these two statements illustrate?

options.text: Ethics are individual and morals are institutional
options.rationale: Reverses both terms.

options.text: Values are personal and morals are professional
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship. Values are what a person holds important; morals are personal beliefs about right and wrong.

options.text: Morals are personal beliefs; ethics are the shared standards of a group or profession
options.rationale: Her first belief is a moral position she holds. The policy expresses an ethical standard the profession and institution accept.

options.text: Both statements describe bioethics applied to nursing
options.rationale: Bioethics concerns ethical questions arising in health care and the life sciences. Neither statement is specifically bioethical.

questions.takeaway: Morals are personal beliefs about right and wrong. Ethics are the standards a group or profession accepts. Values are what a person holds important.
questions.strategy: Two distractors swap the two terms. Fix which one is personal before reading the options.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves morals personal, ethics shared.

questions.stem: A unit convenes an ethics committee for a contested end-of-life decision. Which statement describes its role?

options.text: It provides a structured forum for discussion and recommendation
options.rationale: Committees support the resolution process, bringing perspectives together and helping the team work through the steps.

options.text: It determines whether the nurse acted within her legal scope
options.rationale: That is a regulatory and legal question, not an ethics committee function.

options.text: It replaces the need to work through the ethical steps
options.rationale: The steps are how the case is prepared for and used in the discussion.

options.text: It makes the final decision when the team cannot agree
options.rationale: Committees advise. The decision remains with the patient, the surrogate and the treating team.

questions.takeaway: Ethics committees support the process of resolving ethical problems. They advise rather than decide.
questions.strategy: One distractor makes the committee the decision-maker. Ask who is left holding the decision afterwards.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the scope and replacement options
steps.detail: One is regulatory, one skips the work.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a structured forum and recommendation.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate describe an ethical problem. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "Naming the problem clearly makes the final plan more effective."
options.rationale: Accurate, and her slide says so directly.

options.text: "If I feel strongly enough about it, my personal beliefs should guide the plan."
options.rationale: Examining your values is step three, and examining them means recognizing their influence rather than letting them determine the outcome.

options.text: "If the first action does not resolve it, I should have an alternative identified."
options.rationale: Accurate. Step six includes identifying an alternative action.

options.text: "I should distinguish among facts, opinions and values when I look at the situation."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is part of step three.

questions.takeaway: Examine your own values so you know what is influencing you. That is not the same as letting them decide the outcome.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the steps correctly. The fourth turns self-examination into justification.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Personal belief as the deciding factor.

elimination.verdict: That leaves personal beliefs guiding the plan.

questions.stem: A patient in skeletal traction develops pale, cold toes with reduced sensation. The nurse becomes occupied elsewhere and neither documents nor reports it. Two days later the leg requires amputation. Which term describes the nurse's conduct?

options.text: Negligence, which does not apply to licensed professionals
options.rationale: Malpractice is a type of negligence. The distinction is that the person held liable is a professional, not that negligence stops applying.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: Quasi-intentional torts involve no intent to harm and include breaches such as confidentiality. This is a failure to meet a standard of care.

options.text: Malpractice, which is negligence committed by a professional
options.rationale: Conduct falling below the standard of a reasonably prudent nurse, by someone acting in a professional role, causing harm.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Intentional torts require intent. Nothing suggests she meant harm.

questions.takeaway: Negligence is conduct falling below the standard of a reasonably prudent person. Malpractice is negligence by a professional.
questions.strategy: One distractor says negligence does not apply to professionals. It does; malpractice is a subtype of it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A licensed nurse in her professional role.
Malpractice is a type of negligence.

elimination.verdict: That leaves malpractice.

questions.stem: A nursing expert is asked to testify in a case about a patient harmed on a medical unit. Against what standard will the nurse's conduct be judged?

options.text: What a reasonably prudent nurse would do in similar circumstances in that geographical area
options.rationale: The standard of proof, almost word for word. It is not the best possible nurse and it is not this nurse's own opinion.

options.text: What the most experienced nurse on the unit would have done
options.rationale: The standard is reasonably prudent, not exemplary. Holding everyone to the best performer would make the standard unreachable.

options.text: What the hospital's policy manual required at the time
options.rationale: Policy is evidence of the standard and does not define it. A policy can itself fall below the standard.

options.text: What the nurse herself believed was appropriate at the time
options.rationale: The standard is external. Personal belief does not set it.

questions.takeaway: Standard of proof: what a reasonably prudent nurse would do under similar circumstances in the geographical area where the alleged breach occurred.
questions.strategy: Two distractors set the bar too high or too low. One substitutes policy for the standard itself.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reasonably prudent, similar circumstances, same area.
One is evidence, one is internal.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the reasonably prudent nurse standard.

questions.scenario: A charge nurse assigns work among a registered nurse, a licensed vocational nurse, and a certified nursing assistant.
questions.stem: For each task, indicate the least qualified person who may appropriately perform it.

rows.text: Recording intake and output
rows.rationale: Named on her Delegation 411 slide among the assistant's tasks, alongside vitals, ambulation, position changes, bathing and eating.

rows.text: Initial admission assessment of a newly admitted patient
rows.rationale: Assessment belongs to the registered nurse. The licensed vocational nurse may perform secondary assessment and reinforcement.

rows.text: Reinforcing teaching the registered nurse has already provided to a stable patient
rows.rationale: Her slide gives the vocational nurse secondary and reinforcing roles: assess, teach, monitor, stable patients and discharge.

rows.text: Evaluating whether a patient met an outcome
rows.rationale: Evaluation is named on her slide as a registered nurse function.

rows.text: Assisting a stable patient with ambulation
rows.rationale: Ambulation is named among the assistant's tasks, and the patient is stable.

rows.text: Caring for a patient whose condition is unstable
rows.rationale: Unstable patients are named as a registered nurse responsibility.

questions.takeaway: RN: unstable patients, assessment, evaluation, teaching. LVN: secondary and reinforcing, stable patients, discharge. CNA: vitals, ambulation, positioning, bathing, eating, intake and output.
questions.strategy: Two rows are about teaching and assessment at different depths. First contact belongs to the registered nurse; reinforcement can go to the vocational nurse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask how stable the patient is
Ask whether it is initial or reinforcing

elimination.verdict: Two CNA, one LVN, three RN.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews what a patient must receive for informed consent to be valid. Which elements are required? Select all that apply.

options.text: An explanation of the procedure
options.rationale: Named first. He must know what is proposed.

options.text: The names and qualifications of those performing and assisting
options.rationale: Named, and it is the element most often omitted in practice.

options.text: A description of serious harm including death, and anticipated pain or discomfort
options.rationale: Named, and it must include death where that is a possibility.

options.text: An explanation of alternative therapies and the risks of doing nothing
options.rationale: Named, and doing nothing is itself an alternative with consequences.

options.text: Knowledge that he may refuse without losing other supportive care
options.rationale: Named, and it removes the fear that refusing one thing costs him everything else.

options.text: A guarantee that the procedure will achieve the intended result
options.rationale: No procedure can be guaranteed, and promising an outcome would invalidate rather than strengthen the consent.

questions.takeaway: Informed consent requires explanation of the procedure, who is performing it, serious harm including death, alternatives and the risks of doing nothing, the right to refuse without losing other care, and the right to withdraw even after the procedure has begun.
questions.strategy: One distractor offers a guarantee. Consent describes risk honestly; it never promises a result.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Procedure, people, risks, alternatives, right to refuse.
He may refuse even after it has begun.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse stops at the scene of a road collision and provides care within her competence until paramedics arrive. Which law addresses her legal position?

options.text: The Emergency Medical Treatment and Active Labor Act
options.rationale: EMTALA governs how hospitals must treat people presenting for emergency care. It does not apply at a roadside.

options.text: Good Samaritan laws, which limit liability and offer legal immunity
options.rationale: Named directly. They protect a nurse who helps at the scene of an accident.

options.text: Her state nurse practice act, which permits emergency care
options.rationale: The practice act defines her scope. Good Samaritan laws address liability for helping outside employment.

options.text: Her employer's malpractice insurance
options.rationale: Employer coverage concerns care given in the course of employment.

questions.takeaway: Good Samaritan laws limit liability and offer legal immunity to a nurse who helps at the scene of an accident.
questions.strategy: One distractor is a real emergency statute that governs hospitals rather than roadsides.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: At a roadside, not at work.

steps.action: Cut the practice act and insurance
steps.detail: One is scope, one is employment coverage.

elimination.verdict: That leaves Good Samaritan laws.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews the federal statutes affecting her practice.

The law requiring institutions to give patients written information about their right to refuse treatment and to formulate an advance directive is the [[1]].

The law giving patients rights over their health information and protecting employees is [[2]].

The law requiring insurers to cover mental health and substance use treatment is the [[3]].

The act prohibiting the purchase or sale of organs is the [[4]].

options.text: Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: Requires written information about the right to make decisions, refuse treatment, and formulate an advance directive such as a power of attorney or living will.

options.text: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
options.rationale: Concerns consumer rights and protections, affordable coverage, access, and quality.

options.text: Americans with Disabilities Act
options.rationale: Protects the rights of people with physical or mental disabilities.

options.text: Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act
options.rationale: Altered the way health care is provided to older adults.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: Provides rights to patients over their health information and protects employees.

options.text: HITECH
options.rationale: The near-miss. HITECH concerns health information technology and requires nurses to ensure protected health information is secured.

options.text: EMTALA
options.rationale: Governs emergency treatment and active labor.

options.text: the Mental Health Parity Act
options.rationale: Concerns insurance coverage for mental health and substance use.

options.text: Mental Health Parity and Addiction Equity Act
options.rationale: Requires insurers to provide coverage for mental health and substance use disorder treatment.

options.text: Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act
options.rationale: Broader coverage and access legislation.

options.text: Americans with Disabilities Act
options.rationale: Concerns discrimination and access, not insurance coverage.

options.text: HIPAA
options.rationale: Concerns health information.

options.text: National Organ Transplant Act
options.rationale: Prohibits the purchase or sale of organs.

options.text: Uniform Anatomical Gift Act
options.rationale: The near-miss. It provides the foundation for the national organ donation system; the Transplant Act is what prohibits sale.

options.text: Uniform Determination of Death Act
options.rationale: Determines actual death, cardiopulmonary or irreversible cessation of the entire brain and brain stem.

options.text: Patient Self-Determination Act
options.rationale: Concerns advance directives and the right to refuse treatment.

questions.takeaway: Self-Determination is advance directives. HIPAA is information rights. Parity is insurance coverage. Anatomical Gift builds the donation system; Transplant Act prohibits sale.
questions.strategy: Two near-miss pairs: HIPAA against HITECH, and the two organ acts. One builds the system, the other prohibits the market.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Self-Determination, HIPAA, Parity, Transplant Act.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares a medication and the vial does not look like the one she usually uses. She is behind on her round. Which action reflects the lessons drawn from the RaDonda Vaught case?

options.text: Give it and document that the appearance was unfamiliar
options.rationale: Documenting a concern is not resolving it, and the patient receives the drug either way.

options.text: Stop, verify with a drug guide or the pharmacist before proceeding
options.rationale: Pause and verify when something does not look right, particularly with high-alert medications, and use resources when in doubt.

options.text: Proceed, since she selected it from the automated cabinet under the correct name
options.rationale: An override and a confirmation error were central to that case. The cabinet is not the verification.

options.text: Ask another nurse to check it while she moves to her next patient
options.rationale: The check belongs to the person giving it. Delegating the verification does not transfer the accountability.

questions.takeaway: Follow all the rights, pause and verify when something looks wrong, use resources, avoid workarounds, and report system failures.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats the automated cabinet as the verification step. That was central to what went wrong.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An override and confirmation error caused the harm.

steps.action: Cut delegating the check and documenting
steps.detail: Neither resolves the doubt before administration.

elimination.verdict: That leaves stopping to verify.

questions.stem: A nurse discusses a patient's diagnosis in a hospital lift where visitors can hear. No harm was intended. Which category does this fall into?

options.text: An unintentional tort
options.rationale: The near-miss. Unintentional torts arise when someone is harmed and the person knew or should have known their actions fell below the standard of practice, which describes negligence.

options.text: An intentional tort
options.rationale: Requires intent to cause the harm. She intended to speak, not to harm.

options.text: A quasi-intentional tort
options.rationale: Acts where the person does not intend harm but causes it. Breach of confidentiality is the classic example.

options.text: A criminal offense under state law
options.rationale: Torts are civil wrongs. Criminal law concerns felonies and misdemeanors.
