steps.action: Ask what a data set is
steps.detail: A structured format for recording assessment.
Neither is a home health data set.

elimination.verdict: That leaves OASIS and the Omaha system.

questions.stem: A preceptor reviews a new graduate's documentation practice. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "Findings within the defined norm are not separately recorded on this unit."
options.rationale: Accurate for charting by exception, which is what her unit uses.

options.text: "I document what I observed and what I did, not what I assumed."
options.rationale: Accurate. Factual is the first guideline.

options.text: "If I am busy, I can chart the whole shift at the end while it is still fresh."
options.rationale: Documentation must be current. Charting hours later loses accuracy and creates a record that is difficult to defend.

options.text: "I use only the abbreviations approved by the organization."
options.rationale: Accurate. Appropriate use of abbreviations is a named guideline.

questions.takeaway: Current is one of the six documentation guidelines. Charting at the end of a shift risks both accuracy and credibility.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate the guidelines correctly. The fourth trades one guideline for convenience.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Factual, accurate, abbreviations, current, organized, complete.

elimination.verdict: That leaves charting the whole shift at the end.

questions.nursesNote: 1120: Nurse reviews an entry made by a colleague earlier in the shift. Entry reads: 'Patient seemed anxious and was probably worried about the surgery. Appeared uncomfortable but refused to say much. Family member was rude to staff. Gave pain medication PRN. Will continue to monitor. BP 118/72, HR 84. Patient ambulated in corridor with assistance x1. Dressing dry and intact.'
questions.stem: Highlight the parts of this entry that do not meet the guidelines for quality documentation.

segments.text: Patient seemed anxious and was probably worried about the surgery
segments.rationale: Not factual. Seemed and probably are the nurse's inference. Record what he said or what she observed.

segments.text: Appeared uncomfortable but refused to say much
segments.rationale: Appeared is an impression, and refused characterizes him. Record the observed behavior and his actual words.

segments.text: Family member was rude to staff
segments.rationale: A judgment about a person rather than a record of what occurred, and it has no place in a patient's record.

segments.text: Gave pain medication PRN
segments.rationale: Not accurate or complete. No drug, dose, route, time, or response to it.

segments.text: Will continue to monitor
segments.rationale: A phrase that commits to nothing measurable and documents no action taken.
Factual and accurate. Measured values recorded as measured.

segments.text: Patient ambulated in corridor with assistance x1
segments.rationale: Factual, specific about the level of assistance, and useful to the next nurse.

segments.text: Dressing dry and intact
segments.rationale: An observed finding stated plainly.

questions.takeaway: Factual means observed and done, not inferred. Accurate and complete means the drug, dose, route, time and response.
questions.strategy: Three parts of this entry are exactly right, which is what makes the rest visible. Watch for seemed, probably, appeared, and judgments about people.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No drug, dose, route or response.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s5: inference, impression, judgment, incomplete medication, empty commitment.

questions.scenario: A nurse assesses four patients experiencing stress.
questions.stem: For each set of findings, indicate which stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome it represents.

rows.text: Pulse 118, respirations 26, diaphoretic and restless five minutes after being told his biopsy was positive
rows.rationale: Sympathetic activation within minutes of a perceived threat. Fight or flight.

rows.text: Six weeks into caring for her husband, she says she is managing and her blood pressure has risen from 118/74 to 146/88
rows.rationale: Functioning is maintained while stress hormones stay elevated. Patients may appear fine while carrying high stress.

rows.text: After eight months of financial strain: fatigue, irritability, poor sleep, and three chest infections
rows.rationale: Resources depleted, with frequent illness reflecting the immune suppression chronic stress produces.

rows.text: Pupils dilated, blood glucose 148, muscle tension, moments after a near-miss in traffic
rows.rationale: The full sympathetic picture, including the rise in glucose, immediately after the threat.

rows.text: Three months after a job loss she has stopped seeing friends, cannot concentrate, and has begun drinking daily
rows.rationale: Coping resources overwhelmed, with maladaptive coping and social withdrawal appearing together.

questions.takeaway: Alarm is the immediate fight-or-flight response. Resistance is adapting while hormones stay elevated. Exhaustion is depletion, with illness and maladaptive coping.
questions.strategy: Resistance is the stage people miss, because the patient looks well. Rising blood pressure with I am managing is the picture.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Two alarm, one resistance, two exhaustion.

questions.stem: A patient has been caring for a disabled child for eleven years. Her blood pressure is now 152/94, she sleeps poorly, and she has developed reflux. Which concept explains the link between her circumstances and these findings?

options.text: The alarm stage, because her sympathetic nervous system is activated
options.rationale: Alarm is the immediate response to a threat. Eleven years is not an alarm response.

options.text: An adventitious crisis arising from an unplanned event
options.rationale: Adventitious crises are rare catastrophic events. This is sustained rather than sudden.

options.text: Allostatic load, the cumulative wear and tear of repeated or chronic stress
options.rationale: Long-term stress produces hypertension, sleep problems, digestive problems and raised glucose. The load accumulates rather than resolving between episodes.

options.text: Secondary traumatic stress from exposure to another person's suffering
options.rationale: Secondary traumatic stress comes from repeated exposure to others' trauma. Hers is the ongoing demand of caregiving.

questions.takeaway: Allostatic load is the cumulative physiologic wear and tear caused by repeated or chronic stress. It produces hypertension, heart disease, sleep problems, digestive problems and raised glucose.
questions.strategy: Two distractors name real concepts that describe short or sudden stress. The stem gives you eleven years.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: That is exposure to others' trauma.

elimination.verdict: That leaves allostatic load.

questions.stem: A patient whose home was destroyed in a wildfire three weeks ago tells the nurse her usual ways of coping are no longer working and she does not know what to do next. Which does this describe?

options.text: Exhaustion, the third stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome
options.rationale: Exhaustion describes physiologic depletion over prolonged stress. Crisis names the failure of coping specifically.

options.text: Post-traumatic stress disorder following a traumatic event
options.rationale: PTSD involves flashbacks, nightmares, avoidance and hypervigilance. Nothing in the stem describes those.

options.text: A crisis, a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work
options.rationale: Her definition. A crisis is defined by coping failing, not by the size of the event.

options.text: Maladaptive coping, because her strategies are ineffective
options.rationale: Maladaptive coping means using strategies that harm, such as substance use or withdrawal. Hers have stopped working rather than become harmful.

questions.takeaway: A crisis is a turning point where previous coping methods no longer work. Developmental, situational and adventitious are the three types.
questions.strategy: One distractor requires symptoms the stem does not give. One confuses coping failing with coping harming.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Her usual coping no longer works.
No flashbacks, avoidance or hypervigilance described.
Failed is not the same as harmful.

elimination.verdict: That leaves a crisis.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse works with several patients in crisis.

A first-time mother overwhelmed by the transition to parenthood is experiencing a [[1]] crisis.

A man whose business closed last month is experiencing a [[2]] crisis.

A family displaced by an earthquake is experiencing an [[3]] crisis.

A nurse who feels guilt and loss of confidence after a medication error caused harm is experiencing [[4]].

options.text: developmental
options.rationale: Triggered by a normal life transition. Becoming a parent is expected and can still overwhelm coping.

options.text: situational
options.rationale: The near-miss. Situational crises come from external events rather than from expected life stages.

options.text: adventitious
options.rationale: Unplanned, rare and catastrophic.

options.text: traumatic
options.rationale: Not one of the three named crisis types.

options.text: situational
options.rationale: Provoked by an external event such as job loss, a crash or serious illness.

options.text: developmental
options.rationale: Developmental crises arise from normal life transitions.

options.text: adventitious
options.rationale: Reserved for rare catastrophic events.

options.text: chronic
options.rationale: A type of stress rather than a type of crisis.

options.text: adventitious
options.rationale: Unplanned, rare and catastrophic. A natural disaster is the standard example.

options.text: situational
options.rationale: The near-miss. Both are externally provoked; adventitious is reserved for the rare and catastrophic.

options.text: developmental
options.rationale: Nothing about an earthquake is a life stage.

options.text: secondary
options.rationale: Not a crisis type.

options.text: second victim syndrome
options.rationale: Emotional and psychological trauma after involvement in an unexpected adverse event, error or injury. Guilt, shame, anxiety, fear and decreased confidence.

options.text: compassion fatigue
options.rationale: The near-miss. Compassion fatigue comes from repeated exposure to others' suffering; second victim syndrome follows a specific adverse event she was involved in.

options.text: secondary traumatic stress
options.rationale: Stress from repeated exposure to others' trauma.

options.text: moral distress
options.rationale: Knowing the right action and being constrained from taking it.

questions.takeaway: Developmental crises come from life transitions, situational from external events, adventitious from rare catastrophes. Second victim syndrome follows an adverse event you were involved in.
questions.strategy: Situational and adventitious both come from outside. Adventitious is reserved for the rare and catastrophic.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A life stage, an event, or a catastrophe.
Cumulative exposure, or one specific event.

elimination.verdict: Developmental, situational, adventitious, second victim syndrome.

questions.stem: A patient tells the nurse her diagnosis must be a laboratory error and that she feels completely well. Which defense mechanism is she using?

options.text: Compensation, making up for a weakness by excelling elsewhere
options.rationale: Compensation involves building up one area to offset another. Nothing here describes that.

options.text: Denial, refusing to accept that something is real
options.rationale: She is rejecting the reality of the diagnosis rather than reinterpreting it.

options.text: Projection, attributing her own feelings to someone else
options.rationale: Projection means putting your own feeling onto another person. She is not describing anyone else's feelings.

options.text: Dissociation, detaching from thoughts, feelings or surroundings
options.rationale: Dissociation involves separating from your own experience. She is present and arguing.

questions.takeaway: Five defense mechanisms: denial, projection, dissociation, regression, compensation.
questions.strategy: Ask what she is doing with the information. Rejecting it outright is different from reinterpreting it or detaching from it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She is present, and nothing is being offset.

elimination.verdict: That leaves denial.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old who has been toilet trained for four years begins wetting the bed after his parents separate. Which defense mechanism does this represent?

options.text: Compensation, offsetting a loss in one area with achievement in another
options.rationale: Nothing here describes achievement elsewhere.

options.text: Dissociation, detaching from the situation
options.rationale: Dissociation involves separation from one's own thoughts, feelings or surroundings.

options.text: Denial, refusing to accept the separation is real
options.rationale: Denial rejects the reality. The bedwetting is a return to earlier functioning rather than a rejection of facts.

options.text: Regression, returning to an earlier stage of functioning under stress
options.rationale: A behavior appropriate to a younger age reappearing when coping is overwhelmed.

questions.takeaway: Regression is a return to an earlier stage of functioning under stress. It is common in children and it occurs in adults too.
questions.strategy: The signal is a skill that was established being lost. Ask what direction the behavior moved.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A skill held for four years.

elimination.verdict: That leaves regression.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient who has just learned of a terminal diagnosis. Which findings represent the alarm stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heart rate increased from 78 to 116
options.rationale: Sympathetic activation raises heart rate.

options.text: Respirations increased and shallow
options.rationale: Named among the alarm findings.

options.text: Pupils dilated
options.rationale: A classic sympathetic sign.

options.text: Blood glucose rising
options.rationale: Named, and it is how the body mobilizes fuel for fight or flight.

options.text: Restless and fearful
options.rationale: Alertness, restlessness and fear are all named alarm findings.

options.text: Increased bowel sounds and hunger
options.rationale: Digestion decreases during alarm rather than increasing. The body diverts resources away from it.

questions.takeaway: Alarm: raised heart rate, respirations, blood pressure, glucose, muscle tension, sweating, dilated pupils, increased alertness, restlessness, fear, and decreased digestion.
questions.strategy: One distractor reverses a real alarm finding. Digestion goes down, not up.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A patient facing surgery organizes her questions, researches the procedure, and arranges childcare for the recovery period. Which type of coping is she using?

options.text: Emotion-focused coping, managing feelings related to the stressor
options.rationale: Emotion-focused coping addresses the feelings. Hers addresses the circumstances.

options.text: Problem-focused coping, taking action to change or solve the stressor
options.rationale: Every action she has taken alters the situation itself rather than her feelings about it.

options.text: Maladaptive coping, because she is avoiding her feelings
options.rationale: Nothing suggests avoidance, and problem-focused coping is not maladaptive.

options.text: Defense mechanisms operating unconsciously
options.rationale: Defense mechanisms are unconscious. Her actions are deliberate.

questions.takeaway: Problem-focused coping acts on the stressor. Emotion-focused coping manages the feelings about it. Neither is inherently better; effectiveness depends on the situation.
questions.strategy: One distractor reads deliberate practical action as avoidance. Ask what her actions changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: She did not address her feelings.

elimination.verdict: That leaves problem-focused coping.

questions.stem: A patient facing a diagnosis she cannot change spends time with family, prays, and uses a breathing exercise when she feels overwhelmed. A student asks whether this is less effective than problem solving. Which response is accurate?

options.text: Problem-focused coping is more effective in most situations
options.rationale: Neither type is inherently superior. The fit with the situation is what matters.

options.text: She should be encouraged to use both types equally
options.rationale: Balance sounds sensible and it ignores that some stressors offer nothing to solve.

options.text: Emotion-focused coping is a form of avoidance
options.rationale: Avoidance is maladaptive. Managing feelings deliberately is not the same thing.

options.text: Effectiveness depends on the person and the situation, and some stressors cannot be changed
options.rationale: Coping effectiveness depends on the person, the situation, culture, past experiences, resources and support. Where the stressor is fixed, emotion-focused coping is the appropriate strategy.

questions.takeaway: Coping effectiveness depends on the person, situation, culture, past experiences, resources and support systems.
questions.strategy: One distractor ranks the two types. Ask what problem-focused coping could do about a diagnosis that cannot be changed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut avoidance and the equal-use option
steps.detail: One mislabels it, one ignores the situation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves effectiveness depending on the fit.

questions.stem: A nurse identifies maladaptive coping in a patient under prolonged stress. Which behaviors are examples? Select all that apply.

options.text: Avoiding or denying the problem
options.rationale: Named first, and it provides short-term relief while the problem grows.

options.text: Substance use
options.rationale: Named, and it is the one most likely to produce a second problem.

options.text: Overeating or undereating
options.rationale: Named, and either direction counts.

options.text: Excessive sleeping
options.rationale: Named, and it is distinct from the sleep disturbance stress also causes.

options.text: Social withdrawal
options.rationale: Named, and it removes the support system that would otherwise help.

options.text: Talking through the problem with a trusted friend
options.rationale: An adaptive strategy using the support system. Maladaptive coping gives short-term relief at a longer-term cost.

questions.takeaway: Maladaptive coping provides short-term relief and is harmful or ineffective over time: avoidance, substance use, disordered eating, excessive sleeping, withdrawal, aggression.
questions.strategy: One distractor uses the support system rather than retreating from it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Uses support rather than avoiding it.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.nursesNote: 1530: Patient is 34, admitted following a house fire two days ago in which her partner died. Sitting upright, staring at the door. Has not slept since admission. Startles when the door opens. Says she cannot stop seeing it. Has not eaten. States she does not see the point of any of this and that everyone would manage without her. Declines to contact her sister. Vital signs stable. No injuries requiring treatment. Chart notes she has a supportive sister two hours away.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings that require immediate nursing action.

segments.text: States she does not see the point of any of this and that everyone would manage without her
segments.rationale: A statement suggesting suicidal ideation. Stay with the patient, complete screening per policy, ensure immediate safety, and notify the team. This is the finding that outranks everything else here.

segments.text: Has not slept since admission
segments.rationale: Two days without sleep worsens every other finding and is itself a safety issue.

segments.text: Has not eaten
segments.rationale: An immediate need. Identifying pain, food, rest, privacy and support is part of acute crisis care.

segments.text: Startles when the door opens and says she cannot stop seeing it
segments.rationale: Hypervigilance and intrusive images. Trauma responses are not overreactions and they need recognizing.

segments.text: Declines to contact her sister
segments.rationale: Withdrawal from an available support, and support systems are one of the factors that determine coping.

segments.text: Vital signs stable
segments.rationale: A reassuring finding, and it is what tells you the problem is not physiological.

segments.text: No injuries requiring treatment
segments.rationale: Also reassuring. She survived the fire physically intact, which is not the same as intact.

segments.text: Has a supportive sister two hours away
segments.rationale: A resource rather than a finding. It is what makes the declining to contact her actionable.

questions.takeaway: In acute crisis: ensure safety first, screen for self-harm when it is mentioned or suspected, then identify immediate needs of pain, food, rest, privacy, information and support.
questions.strategy: One finding outranks all the others and it is easy to read past because it is phrased indirectly. Everyone would manage without her is not a throwaway line.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: s1 through s5, with the safety statement taking priority.

questions.stem: A patient in the emergency department after an assault says she does not want to talk about it and asks whether she can keep her coat on. Which response reflects trauma-informed care?

options.text: Tell her she can keep the coat on and ask what would make her more comfortable
options.rationale: Choice and safety are two of the elements. Offering options wherever possible restores control to someone who has just had it taken.

options.text: Encourage her to talk, since expressing what happened will help
options.rationale: Overrides her stated preference. Listening without minimizing does not mean requiring disclosure.

options.text: Arrange for a family member to stay with her to provide support
options.rationale: Well intentioned, and it decides for her who should be present.

options.text: Explain that the coat must be removed for the examination
options.rationale: May be true eventually, and stated as an instruction it removes the choice she has just asked for.

questions.takeaway: Trauma-informed care: safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, respect.
questions.strategy: Three distractors decide something on her behalf. Ask which option returns a decision to her.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: To keep her coat, and not to talk.

steps.action: Cut the instruction and the encouragement

elimination.verdict: That leaves offering choice.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a patient's stress and coping. Which questions belong in that assessment? Select all that apply.

options.text: Whether the patient is currently safe
options.rationale: Named first, and safety is prioritized before anything else.

options.text: How the patient perceives the stressor
options.rationale: Named, and appraisal determines the impact more than the event does.

options.text: What coping resources are available
options.rationale: Named, and it covers support, finances and problem-solving skills.

options.text: Whether maladaptive coping is being used
options.rationale: Named, and it changes both the risk and the plan.

options.text: Adherence to healthy practices
options.rationale: Named, and it covers sleep, eating and activity.

options.text: Which defense mechanism the patient is using
options.rationale: Defense mechanisms are useful to recognize and are not among the named assessment questions. They operate unconsciously and labelling them is not the assessment.

questions.takeaway: Assessment questions: patient safety, perception of the stressor, available coping resources, maladaptive coping used, and adherence to healthy practices.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a real concept from the chapter that is not one of the five assessment questions.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Safety, perception, resources, maladaptive coping, healthy practices.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse on an oncology unit reports feeling emotionally drained and numb, irritable with colleagues, and less affected by patients' distress than she used to be. She has made no errors. Which does this describe?

options.text: A situational crisis provoked by an external event
options.rationale: No single external event is described. This is cumulative.

options.text: Compassion fatigue from repeated exposure to others' suffering
options.rationale: Emotional and physical exhaustion from repeated exposure. Irritability, numbness, decreased empathy and reduced job satisfaction.

options.text: Second victim syndrome following an adverse patient event
options.rationale: Second victim syndrome follows involvement in a specific adverse event, error or injury. The stem states she has made no errors.

options.text: The alarm stage of the General Adaptation Syndrome
options.rationale: Alarm is the acute sympathetic response to an immediate threat.

questions.takeaway: Compassion fatigue: irritability, trouble sleeping, emotional numbness, decreased empathy, feeling overwhelmed or detached, reduced job satisfaction.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is second victim syndrome, and the stem rules it out by stating she has made no errors.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: No errors, so no adverse event.

elimination.verdict: That leaves compassion fatigue.

questions.stem: A nurse involved in a medication error that harmed a patient reports guilt, shame and loss of confidence in her practice. Which support is most appropriate?

options.text: Reassure her that errors happen to everyone
options.rationale: False reassurance. It minimizes what she is carrying and closes the conversation.

options.text: Recommend she take time away from clinical practice
options.rationale: May be appropriate and it is a decision, not a support. Offered first it can read as removal.

options.text: Recognize this as second victim syndrome and connect her with peer support
options.rationale: Emotional and psychological trauma after involvement in an adverse event. Naming it is what allows support to be offered rather than endured privately.

options.text: Advise her to focus on the system factors rather than her own role
options.rationale: System analysis is necessary and it does not address what she is feeling.

questions.takeaway: Second victim syndrome: guilt, shame, anxiety, fear and decreased confidence after involvement in an unexpected adverse event, error or injury.
questions.strategy: Two distractors redirect her away from the feeling. Ask what she has actually described.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut time away as the first move

elimination.verdict: That leaves naming it and connecting her with peer support.

questions.stem: A nurse plans care for a patient experiencing severe stress after a serious diagnosis. Which is the first priority in the plan?

options.text: Realistic, patient-centered outcomes
options.rationale: Named second. Outcomes matter once safety is established.

options.text: Including the patient in defining what better coping looks like
options.rationale: Named, and it follows safety rather than preceding it.

options.text: Collaborating with the health care team and support system
options.rationale: Named, and it is part of the plan rather than its first priority.

options.text: Safety
options.rationale: Prioritize safety first. Everything else in the plan depends on the patient being safe while it happens.

questions.takeaway: Planning for stress management: prioritize safety first, then realistic patient-centered outcomes, include the patient in defining better coping, collaborate, and set time frames that match the setting.
questions.strategy: All four appear on her planning slide. The question asks which comes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what everything else depends on

elimination.verdict: That leaves safety.

questions.stem: A nurse implements health promotion interventions for a patient with high stress. Which are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Teaching deep breathing and progressive muscle relaxation
options.rationale: Named relaxation techniques, alongside guided imagery.

options.text: Educating about stress triggers and self-management strategies
options.rationale: Named, and it lets the patient recognize the pattern rather than only the episode.

options.text: Referring to counseling, therapy or a peer support group
options.rationale: Named, and it extends support beyond the admission.

options.text: Arranging a quiet space with reduced stimuli
options.rationale: Environmental modification, named directly.

options.text: Scheduling rest breaks
options.rationale: Named alongside environmental modification.

options.text: Advising the patient to avoid thinking about the stressor
options.rationale: Avoidance is named as maladaptive coping. It provides short-term relief and does not help over time.

questions.takeaway: Health promotion interventions: relaxation techniques, education on triggers and self-management, referral, and environmental modification. Tailor them to the patient.
questions.strategy: One distractor recommends the first item on the maladaptive coping list.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old living alone tells the nurse she has stopped going out since her husband died, cannot get to the shops, and is worried about money. Which additional assessments does her age make important?

options.text: Depression, loneliness, safety and suicidal thoughts
options.rationale: Named specifically for older adults, and each of her stated concerns raises the likelihood of all four.

options.text: Cognitive function and memory
options.rationale: Relevant generally and not what her slide names for stress and coping in older adults.

options.text: Medication adherence and polypharmacy
options.rationale: Important in older adults generally and not what this chapter names for stress and coping.

options.text: Nutritional intake and weight
options.rationale: Worth assessing given she cannot reach the shops, and it is not among the four named.

questions.takeaway: In older adults, assess depression, loneliness, safety and suicidal thoughts when indicated. Daily stressors include health changes, transportation, finances, loss and home maintenance.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuinely important in older adults. The question asks what this chapter names for stress and coping.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves depression, loneliness, safety and suicidal thoughts.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss stress and coping. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "A patient in the resistance stage is coping well and needs no intervention."
options.rationale: Patients may appear fine while carrying high stress, and stress hormones remain elevated. Looking well is not the same as being well.

options.text: "A crisis is defined by coping failing, not by how large the event was."
options.rationale: Accurate. That is what makes a developmental crisis possible.

options.text: "Trauma responses are responses to remembered threat, not overreactions."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her wording.

options.text: "Allostatic load is the cumulative wear and tear of chronic stress."
options.rationale: Accurate.

questions.takeaway: In the resistance stage the patient may appear fine while stress hormones stay elevated. Functioning is not the same as recovery.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth reads a stage as a resolution.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Appearing fine read as coping well.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the resistance statement.

questions.scenario: A 45-year-old is admitted for observation after a collapse at work. Tests show no physical cause. She tells the nurse she has been working double shifts for seven months since her divorce, sleeps about four hours a night, has lost 9 kg, and has had three chest infections this year. She says she is coping and does not want to worry anyone. She has stopped seeing the friends she used to see weekly.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Assess her safety, her perception of the stressor, and what support is available
options.rationale: The named assessment questions, and safety comes first. Withdrawal plus exhaustion plus I do not want to worry anyone warrants direct enquiry.

options.text: Explore with her what reconnecting with her support system could look like
options.rationale: Support systems are one of the factors determining coping, and she has withdrawn from one she had.

options.text: Reassure her that many people go through difficult periods after a divorce
options.rationale: False reassurance, and it normalizes seven months of physiological depletion.

options.text: Recommend she reduce her shifts and take time off work
options.rationale: Sensible advice offered before understanding why she is working doubles. The finances may be the reason.

options.text: Exhaustion stage with maladaptive coping and depleted resources
options.rationale: Seven months of sustained stress with fatigue, poor sleep, weight loss, frequent infection and social withdrawal. That is depletion, not adaptation.

options.text: Alarm stage with sympathetic activation
options.rationale: Alarm is the immediate response to a threat, measured in minutes.

options.text: An adventitious crisis following a catastrophic event
options.rationale: Adventitious crises are rare catastrophes. A divorce is a situational stressor, and this has been building for months.

options.text: An expected adjustment reaction following divorce
options.rationale: Three infections, 9 kg lost and four hours of sleep is not an expected adjustment. It is the physiology of exhaustion.

options.text: Whether she reports her stress feels more manageable
options.rationale: Asking the patient directly is the first evaluation step named on her slide.

options.text: Sleep, appetite and concentration at follow-up
options.rationale: The symptoms that defined the exhaustion, reassessed. Named among the evaluation measures.

options.text: Whether she can name three relaxation techniques
options.rationale: Tests recall of teaching. It does not measure whether her coping improved.

options.text: Whether her employer reduces her shift allocation
options.rationale: Evaluates the employer rather than the patient, and it may not be within anyone's control.

questions.takeaway: Exhaustion presents physically: fatigue, poor sleep, impaired concentration and frequent illness. I am coping is what people say while depleted.
questions.strategy: Two condition distractors describe short-term responses. The timeframe of seven months and the three infections are what rule them out.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: Assess safety and support, explore reconnection, for exhaustion with maladaptive coping, evaluated by her report and her symptoms.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old takes his furosemide at 6 pm because that is when he remembers it with his evening meal. He wakes three or four times each night to void and struggles to fall back asleep. He is drowsy during the day and has stumbled twice on the way to the bathroom. Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.text: Restrict his fluid intake after the early evening
options.rationale: Commonly suggested, and it risks dehydration in an older adult while the 6 pm dose keeps working. The fluid he passes at night is drug-driven.

options.text: Review his sleep hygiene and evening routine
options.rationale: The right approach when habits are the problem. No bedtime routine will outlast a diuretic taken at 6 pm.

options.text: Discuss moving the diuretic to the morning with the provider
options.rationale: A diuretic peaks two to six hours after the dose. At 6 pm that peak lands overnight; in the morning it is finished before bedtime. Changing the timing removes the cause.

options.text: Provide a bedside commode to shorten the walk
options.rationale: Reduces the immediate fall risk and is worth doing alongside the timing change, and on its own it accepts three or four awakenings as unchangeable.

questions.takeaway: Diuretic timing affects nocturia and nighttime awakenings. Medication reconciliation and timing review are part of the sleep assessment.
questions.strategy: Three options manage the consequences of the awakenings. Ask what is producing them, and check the time the drug is given.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A diuretic at 6 pm peaks overnight.
The fluid is drug-driven and restriction risks dehydration.
Both work around a cause that can be removed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves moving the dose to the morning.

questions.stem: A 59-year-old admitted for elective surgery is accompanied by his wife, who reports that he snores loudly and that she has watched him stop breathing for several seconds at a time most nights. He falls asleep during meetings and once while stopped in traffic, though he believes he sleeps enough. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Advise him to sleep alone so his wife is not disturbed
options.rationale: Solves her problem, not his, and it removes the only person who has witnessed the pauses.

options.text: Report the findings and discuss evaluation for obstructive sleep apnea
options.rationale: Snoring with witnessed pauses plus daytime sleepiness is the classic picture, and it matters now because anesthesia and opioids relax the airway further.

options.text: Teach sleep hygiene and reassess in one month
options.rationale: Hygiene does not open an obstructed airway, and a month's delay means his surgery happens first.

options.text: Reassure him that snoring is common and not concerning
options.rationale: Snoring alone is common. Snoring with witnessed apnea and falling asleep in traffic is not, and reassurance sends him to theatre with an unassessed airway.

questions.takeaway: Obstructive sleep apnea: loud snoring, witnessed pauses, and daytime sleepiness. Before surgery it is urgent, because anesthesia and opioids worsen airway collapse.
questions.strategy: The surgery in the stem is doing work. Ask what changes about the risk once he is anesthetized.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Snoring, witnessed pauses, asleep in traffic.
Both send him to theatre unassessed.

elimination.verdict: That leaves reporting it for evaluation.

questions.scenario: A nurse reviews the sleep patterns of patients across different age groups.
questions.stem: For each patient, indicate whether the reported sleep duration is expected or requires further assessment.

rows.text: A 2-month-old sleeping 15 to 16 hours a day
rows.rationale: Neonates and infants sleep 15 to 16 hours a day, with a high proportion of REM.

rows.text: A 15-year-old sleeping 5 hours on school nights
rows.rationale: Children and adolescents need 9 to 12 hours. Five is well short and affects mood, learning and safety.

rows.text: A 34-year-old sleeping 8 hours
rows.rationale: Adults need 7 to 9 hours.

rows.text: An 80-year-old sleeping about 6 hours with two brief awakenings
rows.rationale: Older adults sleep under 7 hours and their sleep is fragmented. This is the expected pattern rather than a problem.

rows.text: An 80-year-old who falls asleep during conversations and has fallen twice
rows.rationale: Excessive daytime sleepiness significantly increases fall risk, and two falls makes it urgent rather than expected.

questions.takeaway: Neonates 15 to 16 hours, children and adolescents 9 to 12, adults 7 to 9, older adults under 7 and fragmented.
questions.strategy: Two rows describe 80-year-olds and they fall on opposite sides. Fragmented nighttime sleep is expected; falling asleep in the daytime is not.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match each to the age band

steps.detail: One sleeps short at night, one sleeps by day.
Daytime sleepiness plus falls is never expected.

elimination.verdict: Three expected, two requiring assessment.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a 79-year-old who reports poor sleep. Which risk factors for sleep problems in older adults should she assess? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nocturia
options.rationale: Named first, and it is the most common cause of fragmented sleep in this group.

options.text: Polypharmacy
options.rationale: Named, and the timing of several drugs may matter as much as the number.

options.text: Pain
options.rationale: Named, and untreated pain both delays sleep onset and causes awakenings.

options.text: Comorbidities
options.rationale: Named, and respiratory, cardiac and gastrointestinal conditions each disrupt sleep in their own way.

options.text: Sensory impairments
options.rationale: Named, and they affect orientation at night as well as comfort.

options.text: Reduced need for sleep with age
options.rationale: Older adults sleep less and their need is not reduced. Assuming a reduced need is how poor sleep goes unassessed.

questions.takeaway: Risk factors in older adults: nocturia, polypharmacy, pain, comorbidities, and sensory impairments. Around 30 to 40% report sleep problems.
questions.strategy: One distractor turns a change in pattern into a change in need. Less sleep is not the same as needing less.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A patient recovering from abdominal surgery has slept poorly for three nights because of noise and frequent checks. Which consequence should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: Slower wound healing and reduced pain tolerance
options.rationale: Growth hormone released during sleep drives tissue repair. Poor sleep impairs immune function, wound healing and pain tolerance.

options.text: Improved memory consolidation as the body compensates
options.rationale: REM supports memory consolidation, and losing sleep reduces it rather than triggering compensation.

options.text: No measurable effect, since the surgery itself drives recovery
options.rationale: Sleep plays a critical role in physical healing and clinical outcomes. It is not incidental to recovery.

options.text: A reduced requirement for analgesia over the next few days
options.rationale: The opposite. Reduced pain tolerance means he is likely to need more, not less.

questions.takeaway: Growth hormone released during sleep drives tissue repair and wound healing. Poor sleep impairs immunity, healing and pain tolerance.
questions.strategy: One distractor reverses the effect on analgesia. Ask what happens to a wound when growth hormone release is interrupted.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut the compensation and no-effect options

elimination.verdict: That leaves slower healing and reduced pain tolerance.

questions.stem: Complete each sentence by selecting from the choices below.
questions.sentence:
A nurse reviews sleep physiology with a student.

The internal clock governing the 24-hour sleep-wake cycle is the [[1]].

The stage that supports memory consolidation and emotional processing is [[2]].

The chemicals promoting wakefulness and REM are [[3]].

The tool that measures daytime sleepiness specifically is the [[4]].

options.text: circadian rhythm
options.rationale: Governs the 24-hour sleep-wake cycle.

options.text: sleep latency
options.rationale: The time taken to fall asleep, which is assessed rather than a regulating mechanism.

options.text: the sleep cycle
options.rationale: The near-miss. The sleep cycle is the NREM and REM sequence within a night; the circadian rhythm sets the 24-hour pattern.

options.text: the hypothalamus
options.rationale: The structure involved in regulation, not the rhythm itself.

options.text: REM sleep
options.rationale: Supports memory consolidation and emotional processing.

options.text: NREM sleep
options.rationale: The near-miss. NREM is where growth hormone release and physical restoration predominate.

options.text: sleep latency
options.rationale: The time to fall asleep.

options.text: a parasomnia
options.rationale: A category of sleep disorder involving abnormal behaviors during sleep.

options.text: hypocretins, also called orexins
options.rationale: Named on her slide for wakefulness and REM.

options.text: melatonin
options.rationale: Promotes sleep onset and is released as light falls.

options.text: L-tryptophan
options.rationale: Named among the sleep regulators and it is a precursor rather than a wakefulness promoter.

options.text: prostaglandin
options.rationale: Also named among the regulators, with a different role.

options.text: Epworth Sleepiness Scale
options.rationale: Measures daytime sleepiness.

options.text: Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index
options.rationale: The near-miss. Pittsburgh assesses overall sleep quality and patterns; Epworth measures daytime sleepiness.

options.text: Holmes-Rahe Life Stress Inventory
options.rationale: Measures recent life events contributing to stress.

options.text: Geriatric Depression Scale
options.rationale: Screens for depression in older adults.

questions.takeaway: Circadian rhythm sets the 24-hour cycle. REM supports memory and emotion; NREM supports physical repair. Epworth measures daytime sleepiness; Pittsburgh measures overall quality.
questions.strategy: Three near-miss pairs: circadian against the sleep cycle, REM against NREM, and Epworth against Pittsburgh. Each turns on what is being measured or restored.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the day from the night
steps.detail: Circadian is 24 hours; the cycle is within a night.
REM for memory, NREM for repair.

elimination.verdict: Circadian rhythm, REM, hypocretins, Epworth.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old with heart failure tells the nurse he wakes most nights with chest discomfort that eases when he sits up. Which does this most likely represent?

options.text: Nocturnal angina related to his cardiac disease
options.rationale: Named under cardiac disease. Lying flat increases venous return and cardiac workload, which is what brings it on and why sitting up relieves it.

options.text: Gastroesophageal reflux causing nocturnal symptoms
options.rationale: Reflux does wake people and is worse lying flat, which makes it a real possibility. Chest discomfort relieved specifically by sitting up in a patient with heart failure points to the heart.

options.text: A parasomnia occurring during the night
options.rationale: Parasomnias are abnormal behaviors during sleep, such as sleepwalking. Chest discomfort is not a behavior.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea causing the awakenings
options.rationale: Apnea wakes people through obstruction rather than pain, and his wife would describe snoring and pauses.

questions.takeaway: Cardiac disease disrupts sleep through nocturnal angina and heart failure-related apnea. Lying flat raises venous return.
questions.strategy: The near-miss is reflux, which is genuinely worse lying flat. His diagnosis and the relief on sitting up are what separate them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Sitting up, which reduces venous return.
One is a behavior, one wakes through obstruction.

elimination.verdict: That leaves nocturnal angina.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches sleep hygiene to a patient with insomnia. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep a consistent bedtime and wake time, including weekends
options.rationale: Named first, and consistency is what stabilizes the circadian rhythm.

options.text: Avoid caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals close to bedtime
options.rationale: All three named, and alcohol is the one patients least expect.

options.text: Limit screen time for 30 minutes before bed and reserve the bed for sleep
options.rationale: Named, and both halves matter.

options.text: Exercise during the day but not within one to two hours of bedtime
options.rationale: Named, with the timing specified.

options.text: Use relaxation techniques such as deep breathing, guided imagery or a warm bath
options.rationale: Named, and the bath is best taken with time to spare before bed so core temperature can fall.

options.text: Stay in bed when unable to sleep, to maximize rest
options.rationale: Reserve the bed for sleep. Lying awake in bed trains the association between the bed and wakefulness.

questions.takeaway: Sleep hygiene: consistent times including weekends, avoid caffeine, alcohol and heavy meals near bedtime, limit screens and reserve the bed for sleep, daytime exercise not within 1 to 2 hours of bed, relaxation techniques.
questions.strategy: One distractor sounds restful and contradicts reserving the bed for sleep.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Contradicts reserving the bed for sleep.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse wants to improve sleep for patients on a busy medical unit. Which intervention addresses the most common modifiable cause of nighttime awakening in hospital?

options.text: Dim the lights during evening hours
options.rationale: Named and useful, supporting melatonin release. It does not stop anyone entering the room.

options.text: Close doors and lower alarm volumes
options.rationale: Named under noise control and it addresses a different disruption.

options.text: Position patients for comfort and airway safety
options.rationale: Named, and it addresses comfort rather than the number of awakenings.

options.text: Cluster nursing care to reduce the number of nighttime interruptions
options.rationale: Named first among hospital environment interventions, and interruptions are the cause nursing most directly controls.

questions.takeaway: Hospital sleep interventions: cluster care, dim lights in the evening, control noise, and position for comfort and airway safety.
questions.strategy: All four are on her slide. The question asks which addresses the most common modifiable cause.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Both real and neither stops entries.

elimination.verdict: That leaves clustering care.

questions.stem: A 74-year-old in intensive care has been sleeping poorly and is becoming confused at night. Which evidence-based intervention should the nurse consider?

options.text: A benzodiazepine at bedtime to establish a sleep pattern
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines carry a risk of falls and confusion in older adults, and confusion is already present.

options.text: Moving him to a single room away from the nursing station
options.rationale: May reduce noise and it distances him from observation in a unit where he needs it, and it is not the intervention with the evidence behind it.

options.text: A sleep bundle including earplugs, eye masks and lavender aromatherapy
options.rationale: Sleep bundles have shown measurable benefit in intensive care, reducing delirium and improving perceived sleep quality.

options.text: Allowing him to sleep during the day to make up the deficit
options.rationale: Daytime sleep reduces the drive to sleep at night and worsens the circadian disruption.

questions.takeaway: Sleep bundles in intensive care use earplugs, eye masks and aromatherapy. They reduce delirium and improve perceived sleep quality.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats confusion with a drug that causes confusion. Ask what the evidence supports in this setting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Causes the problem it is meant to treat.

steps.action: Cut daytime sleep and the room move
steps.detail: One worsens the rhythm, one reduces observation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the sleep bundle.

questions.nursesNote: 0800: Patient is 71, admitted three days ago with a chest infection. Reports sleeping poorly since admission. Furosemide scheduled at 2000. Chest discomfort rated 6 of 10 overnight, no analgesia given since 2200. Overhead light switched on each time staff enter. Vital signs taken separately by three different staff members between 2300 and 0500. Drinks one cup of coffee at breakfast. Has a history of hypertension managed with medication. Slept well at home before admission. Room is shared with one other patient.
questions.stem: Highlight the findings contributing to his poor sleep that nursing can modify.

segments.text: Furosemide scheduled at 2000
segments.rationale: Diuretic timing affects nocturia. The nurse cannot change the order alone and raising it with the provider is squarely nursing work.

segments.text: Chest discomfort 6 of 10 overnight with no analgesia since 2200
segments.rationale: Pain is a named cause of disrupted sleep in older adults, and this is uncontrolled and within nursing control.

segments.text: Overhead light switched on each time staff enter
segments.rationale: Dimming lights during evening hours supports melatonin release. Using a task light is a nursing decision.

segments.text: Vital signs taken separately by three staff members between 2300 and 0500
segments.rationale: Clustering care is the first named hospital intervention, and three separate entries is the clearest example of what it prevents.

segments.text: Drinks one cup of coffee at breakfast
segments.rationale: Caffeine matters close to bedtime. One cup at breakfast is not what is waking him at 0300.

segments.text: History of hypertension managed with medication
segments.rationale: A stable condition, and nothing about it is contributing to the awakenings.

segments.text: Slept well at home before admission
segments.rationale: The finding that tells you this is situational rather than a chronic sleep disorder. Useful, and not a modifiable cause.

segments.text: Room is shared with one other patient
segments.rationale: A real source of disruption and not something nursing can modify on a full unit. Noise control is addressed differently.

questions.takeaway: Cluster care, control light and noise, treat pain, and review medication timing. Those are the four levers nursing actually holds.
questions.strategy: One finding tells you the problem is situational rather than chronic, which is why it is there. One is real and outside nursing's control.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One cup at breakfast is not the cause.

elimination.verdict: s1 through s4: the four modifiable causes.

questions.stem: A nurse takes a sleep history. Which source of information is primary?

options.text: The overnight nurse's observations of when he appeared asleep
options.rationale: Useful supporting data, and appearing asleep is not the same as sleeping. Only he knows what the night was like.

options.text: The number of hours recorded on the flow sheet
options.rationale: A count of observed time, which misses awakenings and quality entirely.

options.text: His partner's account of his sleep pattern
options.rationale: Valuable for witnessed events such as apnea or movement, and it is a supplementary source rather than the primary one.

options.text: The patient's own report of his sleep
options.rationale: Sleep is subjective and the patient is the primary source. Perceived quality matters as much as the hours.

questions.takeaway: Sleep is subjective. The patient is the primary source: bedtime routine, sleep latency, nighttime awakenings, wake time, and perceived quality.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuinely useful supporting sources. The question asks which is primary.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Supplementary, and essential for witnessed apnea.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the patient's own report.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with insomnia asks for something to help her sleep. She has already tried a consistent bedtime and reducing evening caffeine. Which is the most appropriate first pharmacological option to discuss?

options.text: Trazodone as a safer alternative
options.rationale: Named as a safer alternative for older or depressed patients, and it sits behind melatonin rather than ahead of it.

options.text: Melatonin, which is generally safe, particularly in older adults with low endogenous levels
options.rationale: Named as generally safe and specifically useful in older adults whose own melatonin production has fallen.

options.text: A benzodiazepine for short-term use
options.rationale: Short-term use only, with risk of falls, confusion and respiratory depression in older adults. Not the first option.

options.text: Diphenhydramine, available without prescription
options.rationale: Anticholinergic, and it causes confusion and falls in older adults. Availability is not safety.

questions.takeaway: Non-drug strategies come first. Melatonin is generally safe, benzodiazepines are short-term only, and trazodone is a safer alternative for older or depressed patients.
questions.strategy: The stem tells you non-drug strategies have been tried, which is what makes this a pharmacological question at all. Rank the options by risk in an older adult.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Anticholinergic, and dangerous in older adults.

elimination.verdict: That leaves melatonin.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a patient's medications as part of a sleep assessment. Which are recognized as affecting sleep? Select all that apply.

options.text: Caffeine, nicotine and alcohol
options.rationale: Named as common but underreported sleep disruptors.

options.text: Benzodiazepines
options.rationale: Named, with risk of falls and confusion in older adults and short-term use only.

options.text: Antidepressants
options.rationale: Named among the agents that suppress REM and cause daytime drowsiness.

options.text: Opiates
options.rationale: Named alongside antidepressants and anticonvulsants.

options.text: Anticonvulsants
options.rationale: Named, and the daytime drowsiness is often mistaken for poor night sleep.

options.text: Inhaled bronchodilators taken in the morning
options.rationale: Not among the named agents, and morning dosing does not disrupt sleep. Her slide names diuretic timing specifically, not bronchodilators.

questions.takeaway: Medications and sleep: caffeine, nicotine and alcohol; benzodiazepines; antidepressants, opiates and anticonvulsants suppressing REM; diuretic timing.
questions.strategy: One distractor names a drug class not on her list, taken at a time that would not affect sleep anyway.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Substances, benzodiazepines, REM suppressors, diuretic timing.
Not named, and timed away from sleep.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A patient's family says they co-sleep with their toddler and asks whether the nurse disapproves. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Explain that co-sleeping is unsafe and should be discontinued
options.rationale: Delivers a verdict rather than a conversation, and it is likely to end the discussion of safety entirely.

options.text: Acknowledge the practice and discuss safety considerations without judgment
options.rationale: Her slide names respecting cultural sleep practices such as co-sleeping, and discussing safety without judgment.

options.text: Tell them the practice is entirely a family matter
options.rationale: Avoids the safety discussion the nurse is placed to have.

options.text: Refer them to the pediatrician for advice about sleeping arrangements
options.rationale: Passes on a conversation within nursing scope, and it implies the topic is too difficult to discuss.

questions.takeaway: Respect cultural sleep practices such as co-sleeping, and discuss safety without judgment.
questions.strategy: One distractor avoids the safety topic and one delivers it as a verdict. The instruction is to do both things at once.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves acknowledging it and discussing safety.

questions.stem: A patient has been taking a benzodiazepine nightly for three weeks. His nurse stops it abruptly at discharge on the patient's request. Which does the nurse monitor for?

options.text: Increased REM sleep resolving his daytime drowsiness
options.rationale: REM does rebound, and the presentation is disrupted sleep rather than resolution of drowsiness.

options.text: Immediate improvement in sleep quality
options.rationale: Not what follows abrupt withdrawal after regular use.

options.text: Rebound insomnia, with sleep worse than before the drug was started
options.rationale: Named under the nursing role: monitor response, advocate for the lowest effective dose, and watch for rebound insomnia.

options.text: No change, since three weeks is too short for dependence
options.rationale: Three weeks of nightly use is enough for rebound to occur, which is why short-term use is specified.

questions.takeaway: Nursing role with sleep medications: monitor response, advocate for the lowest effective dose, and watch for rebound insomnia.
questions.strategy: One distractor treats three weeks as too brief to matter. Short-term use is specified precisely because this happens.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves rebound insomnia.

questions.stem: A nurse explains why rest is not the same as sleep. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Rest is a state of mental, physical and spiritual calm, and does not require inactivity
options.rationale: Her wording. Rest is not the absence of activity, and it is not a substitute for sleep.

options.text: Rest is any period during which the patient is not moving
options.rationale: Equates rest with inactivity, which her slide explicitly separates.

options.text: Rest is only achievable once a patient is free of pain
options.rationale: Pain makes rest harder and does not make it impossible.

options.text: Rest and sleep are interchangeable in meeting the body's needs
options.rationale: Both are basic needs and they are not the same. Sleep does things rest cannot.

questions.takeaway: Sleep and rest are as essential as nutrition and exercise. Rest is a state of mental, physical and spiritual calm rather than inactivity.
questions.strategy: One distractor collapses rest and sleep into the same thing. Her slide separates them deliberately.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Cut interchangeable and the pain condition

elimination.verdict: That leaves rest as a state of calm.

questions.stem: A hospitalized 82-year-old has slept four hours a night for three nights. Which safety concern should the nurse prioritize?

options.text: Delayed wound healing from reduced growth hormone
options.rationale: A genuine consequence of poor sleep and it is not the immediate safety concern.

options.text: Impaired immune function raising infection risk
options.rationale: Also genuine, and it develops over a longer period than the next few hours.

options.text: Reduced pain tolerance requiring more analgesia
options.rationale: Real, and it concerns comfort and management rather than immediate safety.

options.text: Increased fall risk from confusion and slowed reflexes
options.rationale: Sleep deprivation produces confusion, slowed reflexes and higher fall risk, and excessive daytime sleepiness raises it further in older adults.

questions.takeaway: Sleep deprivation causes confusion, slowed reflexes and higher fall risk. Sleep disturbances affect patient safety directly.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuine consequences of poor sleep. The question asks specifically about safety.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves fall risk.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss sleep. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "Older adults need less sleep, so fragmented sleep is not a concern."
options.rationale: Their pattern changes and their need does not. Around 30 to 40% report sleep problems, and treating fragmentation as expected means it goes unassessed.

options.text: "The patient is the primary source of information about his own sleep."
options.rationale: Accurate, because sleep is subjective.

options.text: "Non-drug strategies come first and sedatives are a last resort."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her stated order.

options.text: "Sleep deprivation raises fall risk through confusion and slowed reflexes."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is why sleep is a safety issue.

questions.takeaway: Older adults sleep less and their sleep is fragmented. That is a change in pattern, not a reduced need, and problems still require assessment.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth uses an expected pattern to dismiss a problem.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Drug order, primary source, fall risk.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the reduced-need statement.

questions.scenario: A 66-year-old with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has slept in a chair for four nights because lying flat leaves him breathless. He asks the nurse to get him something to help him sleep. He is using his inhalers correctly, his oxygen saturation is 93% on room air, and his pain is 1 of 10. He says he is exhausted and cannot think straight.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Raise the head of the bed and support him with pillows so he can sleep in bed
options.rationale: Positioning for comfort and airway safety is a named hospital intervention. A chair gives him neither proper rest nor proper positioning.

options.text: Cluster overnight care and reduce light and noise during the night
options.rationale: The environmental interventions named first for the hospital setting, and four nights of poor sleep needs every lever pulled.

options.text: Request an order for a sedative so he can settle
options.rationale: Sedatives depress respiration, which is the opposite of what a patient breathless on lying flat can afford. Non-drug strategies come first.

options.text: Reassure him that sleeping in a chair is adequate rest
options.rationale: A chair rarely allows the deep sleep that repairs tissue, and four nights of it is already showing in his thinking.

options.text: Sleep disrupted by a positioning need arising from his respiratory disease
options.rationale: Respiratory disease disrupts sleep through positioning needs and breathlessness. The cause is mechanical and it is solvable.

options.text: Insomnia requiring pharmacological management
options.rationale: Names the symptom and reaches for a drug. He is not failing to fall asleep; he cannot lie down.

options.text: Obstructive sleep apnea causing fragmented sleep
options.rationale: No snoring or witnessed pauses are described, and his difficulty is with lying flat rather than with obstruction during sleep.

options.text: Uncontrolled pain preventing sleep
options.rationale: Pain is 1 of 10. The stem rules this out directly.

options.text: Whether he is able to sleep in bed rather than the chair
options.rationale: Measures whether the positioning change solved the mechanical problem.

options.text: His own report of sleep quality the following morning
options.rationale: Sleep is subjective, so the patient's perception is the measure. Compare it with his report from the previous nights.

options.text: The number of hours recorded as asleep on the flow sheet
options.rationale: Records observed time rather than experienced sleep, and it misses awakenings entirely.

options.text: Whether his oxygen saturation remains above 92%
options.rationale: A real respiratory parameter, and it was already 93% before anything changed.

questions.takeaway: Respiratory disease disrupts sleep through positioning and breathlessness. Fix the position before reaching for a drug, and evaluate sleep by what the patient reports.
questions.strategy: He asks for a sedative, which is the pull. His pain and saturation are given to rule out the two obvious alternatives.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Depresses respiration in a patient who cannot spare it.

elimination.verdict: Reposition and cluster care, for a positioning problem, evaluated by where he sleeps and what he reports.

chapters.title: Concepts of Care for LGBTQ+ Patients

questions.stem: A teenage boy hands his intake form to the receptionist, who says the mother's and father's names are required and offers to fill them in. He looks away and says quietly that he has two dads. The receptionist becomes flustered and says loudly that he does not have a mother. Heads turn in the waiting area and he starts for the door. What would have prevented this?

options.text: An intake form that asks for parent or guardian names rather than mother and father
options.rationale: The form created the problem before anyone spoke. Updating policies and forms is one of the five ways to build a safe space, and it removes the assumption at the point it is made.

options.text: Displaying symbols of inclusivity in the waiting area
options.rationale: Part of an inclusive environment, and a rainbow sticker does not change what the form demands.

options.text: Training the receptionist to respond calmly when a patient discloses family structure
options.rationale: Worth doing, and it addresses the reaction rather than the assumption. He still has to correct a form that assumed his family wrong.

options.text: Having him complete the form privately with a nurse instead of at the desk
options.rationale: Reduces the audience for the exchange. The form still asks the wrong question.

questions.takeaway: Foster an inclusive environment: update policies and forms, display symbols of inclusivity, and build sexual orientation and gender identity into records.
questions.strategy: Three options improve what happens after the assumption is made. Only one removes the assumption.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The form asked for a mother and a father.
Both improve the response to a problem still built in.
Moves the exchange, not the question.

elimination.verdict: That leaves changing the form.

questions.stem: During the exchange above, the receptionist realizes what she has said. Which response is most appropriate at that moment?

options.text: Briefly say sorry, correct the record, and continue with the check-in
options.rationale: A short correction keeps the attention on him and signals that the mistake is routine rather than a crisis he has to manage.

options.text: Offer to move him to a private room to finish the conversation
options.rationale: Well meant, and it makes the moment larger and marks him out further in front of the people already looking.

options.text: Say nothing further and complete the form as he has described it
options.rationale: Reads as not having noticed, or as not caring. Acknowledgment matters; length is what does not.

options.text: Apologize at length and explain that she did not mean anything by it
options.rationale: Makes him manage her distress. A long apology asks a patient in a waiting room to reassure the person who upset him.

questions.takeaway: Acknowledge briefly, correct, move on. The repair should cost the nurse something, not the patient.
questions.strategy: Every option except one enlarges the moment. Ask who ends up doing the emotional work.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A long apology puts him in charge of her feelings.
Makes a small moment into a scene.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the brief correction.

questions.stem: A clinician asks a patient whether she is sexually active with men, women, or both. She answers that she is sexually active with one woman. He skips the questions about condom use. Her partner is a transgender woman. Which error has he made?

options.text: He used outdated terminology in the question itself
options.rationale: The question was reasonably framed. What went wrong came after her answer.

options.text: He should not have asked about sexual activity at all
options.rationale: The sexual history is appropriate care. The failure is in the reasoning that followed her answer.

options.text: He failed to ask about the number of partners
options.rationale: She told him there is one. The omission is about what happens, not how many.

options.text: He inferred the anatomy involved from the gender of the partner
options.rationale: Sexual health risk follows anatomy and practices, not the gender of either person. Assuming from the label is what skipped a question she needed.

questions.takeaway: Assess anatomy and practices rather than inferring them from gender or orientation. Avoid assumptions.
questions.strategy: Three options criticize the question. The stem tells you the question was answered, then something was skipped.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He assumed what her partner's body was.

steps.action: Cut the options about the question
steps.detail: The question was asked and answered.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the inference from gender to anatomy.

questions.stem: The clinician in that encounter is openly gay and had recently skipped his center's training on LGBTQ+ care, saying he already knew the subject. What does this illustrate?

options.text: The training should have been mandatory rather than optional
options.rationale: A reasonable policy conclusion, and it names an administrative fix rather than what the case shows.

options.text: Belonging to a community does not substitute for training in its health care needs
options.rationale: Personal identity gives lived experience, not clinical knowledge of every population under an umbrella. Ongoing training is the first of the five safe-space practices.

options.text: His error was one of attitude rather than knowledge
options.rationale: His attitude let him skip the training, and what harmed the patient was a specific knowledge gap.

options.text: Clinicians who are themselves LGBTQ+ should not care for LGBTQ+ patients
options.rationale: Nothing suggests he should be excluded. The point is that identity did not supply what training would have.

questions.takeaway: Educate yourself: learn the terminology, know the specific health issues, and take part in ongoing training. Every team member needs it.
questions.strategy: Two options draw policy or personnel conclusions. Ask what the missing training would actually have given him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He did not know to assess anatomy over label.

steps.action: Cut the policy and attitude options

elimination.verdict: That leaves identity not substituting for training.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to admit a patient whose chart lists a legal name different from the one on the referral letter. Which actions create a safe space? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ask what name and pronouns the patient uses and record them where staff will see
options.rationale: Affirming language starts with asking rather than guessing, and recording it means every subsequent staff member gets it right.

options.text: Keep the legal name in the record for billing and identification
options.rationale: Both names belong in the record. The legal name is needed for insurance and identification; the used name is needed for care.

options.text: Use the name the patient gives from that point on, in every interaction
options.rationale: Consistency is what makes it affirming. Asking and then not using it is worse than not asking.

options.text: Explain to colleagues why the patient's name differs from the chart
options.rationale: Discloses information that is the patient's to share. Respect privacy is part of affirming communication.

options.text: Ask which surgeries the patient has had, to know how to refer to them
options.rationale: Surgical history is relevant when it bears on the care being given. Asking to satisfy curiosity about someone's body is not assessment.

options.text: Wait for the patient to raise the difference before mentioning names
options.rationale: Leaves the patient to correct staff repeatedly, which is the burden the practice exists to remove.

questions.takeaway: Affirming communication: use preferred names and pronouns, avoid assumptions, be mindful of nonverbal cues, and respect privacy.
questions.strategy: Two distractors involve telling someone else, or asking about a body without a clinical reason.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Staff need the name, not the explanation.
Privacy is part of affirming care.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.scenario: A clinic manager reviews practice after two patients did not return following a first visit.
questions.stem: For each action, indicate which of the five safe-space practices it represents.

rows.text: Adds a field for gender identity and pronouns to the electronic record
rows.rationale: Building identity into records and forms is part of the environment, not of any single conversation.

rows.text: A nurse notices she assumed a patient's partner was a man and examines why
rows.rationale: Examining your own assumptions and holding yourself accountable for them.

rows.text: Sends a survey asking patients what would make the clinic feel safer
rows.rationale: Seeking patient feedback rather than deciding for them what would help.

rows.text: Schedules quarterly training on terminology and population-specific health issues
rows.rationale: Ongoing training, terminology, and awareness of specific health issues.

rows.text: Introduces herself with her own pronouns before asking the patient's
rows.rationale: Makes the question routine rather than singling anyone out, and it avoids the assumption.

rows.text: Displays a visible inclusivity symbol at the reception desk
rows.rationale: A signal built into the space, which is what the environment practice covers.

questions.takeaway: Five safe-space practices: educate yourself, self-reflection, affirming communication, inclusive environment, prioritize patient needs.
