questions.stem: Highlight the findings that indicate diabetes complications or gaps in self-management.

segments.text: Leg feels numb and he did not notice the original wound
segments.rationale: Peripheral neuropathy. Decreased sensation means injuries go unnoticed, which is exactly how this admission started.

segments.text: Blood glucose 268 mg/dL
segments.rationale: Persistent hyperglycemia, which is what drives every complication on this list and impairs healing now.

segments.text: Checks his feet when he remembers
segments.rationale: Daily inspection is the teaching priority, and in a patient with reduced sensation it is the only way an injury is found.

segments.text: Wears open sandals on the unit
segments.rationale: Protective footwear at all times is a named teaching point, and open sandals on an insensate foot invite the next wound.

segments.text: Blurred vision worsening over six months, no optometrist in four years
segments.rationale: Possible retinopathy going unmonitored. Eyes are one of the named sites of microvascular damage.

segments.text: Blood pressure 148/88
segments.rationale: Raised blood pressure compounds the cardiovascular and kidney risk that diabetes already carries.

segments.text: Takes metformin as prescribed
segments.rationale: Adherence to his medication. A strength rather than a gap.

segments.text: Ate 100% of breakfast
segments.rationale: Adequate intake, and it is reassuring in a patient at risk of hypoglycemia.

segments.text: Temperature 37.2 C
segments.rationale: Within normal limits, which is reassuring given the cellulitis.

questions.takeaway: Long-term complications affect eyes, kidneys, nerves, cardiovascular system, skin and feet. Decreased sensation plus unprotected feet is how ulcers begin.
questions.strategy: Three findings are strengths or normal values. One of them, taking metformin as prescribed, is there to stop you assuming the whole picture is nonadherence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: s1 through s6: nerves, glucose, feet, footwear, eyes and pressure.

questions.stem: A nurse teaches foot care to a patient with diabetic neuropathy. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Inspect the feet daily for wounds, redness or swelling
options.rationale: The first teaching priority, and the only way an injury is found on an insensate foot.

options.text: Wear proper footwear at all times
options.rationale: Named, and at all times includes indoors.

options.text: Report any sores, cuts or changes promptly
options.rationale: Named, and delayed healing means a small break becomes an infection quickly.

options.text: Attend regular follow-up appointments
options.rationale: Named, and it is how changes are caught before he can feel them.

options.text: Test water temperature with the hand before bathing the feet
options.rationale: Follows directly from decreased sensation. A foot that cannot feel heat cannot warn him.

options.text: Use a heating pad on the feet to improve circulation
options.rationale: Dangerous on an insensate foot. He will not feel a burn, and poor circulation impairs healing of one.

questions.takeaway: Foot care matters because decreased sensation means injuries go unnoticed, healing is delayed, circulation is poor, and ulcers lead to serious complications.
questions.strategy: One distractor applies heat to a foot that cannot feel it. Every foot care rule follows from the lost sensation.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: He cannot feel injury or heat.
He would not feel a burn.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, D, and E are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares to administer insulin. Which step reflects its status as a high-alert medication?

options.text: Confirm the patient's identity using one identifier
options.rationale: Two identifiers are standard, and identity verification is not what makes insulin high-alert specifically.

options.text: Document the dose immediately after administration
options.rationale: Necessary, and it happens after the dose is already in.

options.text: Complete an independent double-check of the type, dose and timing before giving it
options.rationale: High-alert medications require strict safety practices, and the double-check is the one never to skip.

options.text: Administer it promptly so the dose is not delayed
options.rationale: Timing matters and speed is not the safety practice. Rushing is how the wrong type gets drawn.

questions.takeaway: Insulin is a high-alert medication. Verify patient identity, insulin type, dose and timing. Never skip double-checks, and consider meal timing.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are reasonable practice that happen at the wrong moment or apply to every medication.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves the independent double-check.

questions.stem: A nursing student says a patient must have type 1 diabetes because he uses insulin. Which response is accurate?

options.text: The distinction between the two types is determined by the patient's age
options.rationale: Type 2 onset is gradual and not determined by age or weight alone.

options.text: Some patients with type 2 diabetes require insulin, and it does not indicate poor control
options.rationale: Her slide states this directly. Type 2 may require lifestyle change, oral medication, insulin, or a combination.

options.text: Insulin use always indicates that oral medications have failed
options.rationale: Framing it as failure is what makes patients resist it. Insulin may be needed as the pancreas becomes unable to keep up.

options.text: Type 2 diabetes is managed with oral medication and lifestyle change only
options.rationale: Contradicts her slide, which names insulin therapy among the options for type 2.

questions.takeaway: Type 1 always requires insulin. Type 2 may require it over time, and using insulin does not mean poor control or a failure.
questions.strategy: Two distractors treat insulin in type 2 as a failure or exclude it entirely. One falls back on age.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Lifestyle, oral agents, insulin, or a combination.
Onset is not determined by age alone.

elimination.verdict: That leaves insulin being appropriate in type 2.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing to administer a diabetes medication to a newly admitted patient. Which assessment should be completed first?

options.text: The patient's understanding of the medication
options.rationale: Essential for discharge teaching and not the safety check before administration.

options.text: The patient's most recent A1C
options.rationale: Useful for evaluating control over time and it does not determine whether this dose is safe now.

options.text: Renal and hepatic function
options.rationale: Always assess renal and hepatic function before administering diabetes medications. Some agents require dose adjustment or are contraindicated in organ impairment.

options.text: The patient's usual home dose
options.rationale: Part of medication reconciliation and it does not establish whether the drug is safe with his current organ function.

questions.takeaway: Assess renal and hepatic function before administering diabetes medications. Some require dose adjustment or are contraindicated in organ impairment.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are genuinely useful. The question asks what must be established before the dose goes in.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Whether the organs can handle it.

steps.action: Cut the A1C and home dose
steps.detail: Both inform management rather than safety.

elimination.verdict: That leaves renal and hepatic function.

questions.stem: A patient with diabetes is found confused and irritable, with a heart rate of 112. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Check the blood glucose
options.rationale: Always check blood glucose when neurological changes occur. Mental status changes may indicate hypoglycemia, which progresses rapidly.

options.text: Review his medication record for recent doses
options.rationale: Informative once you know what you are dealing with. The glucose reading takes seconds.

options.text: Reorient the patient and ensure the environment is safe
options.rationale: Worth doing alongside, and it manages the confusion without finding out what is causing it.

options.text: Assess for signs of infection as a cause of the confusion
options.rationale: Infection is a real cause of both confusion and hyperglycemia. It takes longer to establish and hypoglycemia can seize within minutes.

questions.takeaway: Always check blood glucose when neurological changes occur in a patient with diabetes. Confusion, irritability or unresponsiveness may be hypoglycemia.
questions.strategy: Three options are reasonable and slower. Ask which possible cause could kill him in the next fifteen minutes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: All take longer than a glucose check.

elimination.verdict: That leaves checking the glucose.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes who normally walks 20 minutes daily plans to hike for four hours at the weekend. Which teaching is most important?

options.text: Exercise has no predictable effect on blood glucose
options.rationale: It has a substantial and fairly predictable lowering effect, which is why it appears on the hypoglycemia causes list.

options.text: She should avoid prolonged exercise because of her diabetes
options.rationale: Activity is part of management. The answer is adjustment rather than avoidance.

options.text: She should increase her insulin to cover the extra exertion
options.rationale: Backwards. Exercise lowers glucose, so more insulin compounds the risk.

options.text: The increased activity raises the risk of hypoglycemia and the plan needs adjusting
options.rationale: Increased physical activity without adjustment is a named cause of hypoglycemia. Exercise increases glucose uptake independently of insulin.

questions.takeaway: Increased physical activity without adjustment causes hypoglycemia. Exercise increases glucose uptake, so the plan is adjusted rather than the activity avoided.
questions.strategy: One distractor increases insulin before exercise, which is the dangerous inversion. Ask which direction exercise moves the glucose.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what exercise does to glucose

steps.detail: One restricts, one denies the effect.

elimination.verdict: That leaves adjusting for the hypoglycemia risk.

questions.stem: A preceptor listens to a new graduate discuss diabetes. Which statement requires correction?

options.text: "Insulin is a high-alert medication and I never skip the double-check."
options.rationale: Accurate.

options.text: "DKA involves ketones and acidosis; HHS has severe hyperglycemia without significant ketones."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is the distinction her slide draws.

options.text: "I check the glucose whenever a patient with diabetes becomes confused."
options.rationale: Accurate, and it is her stated nursing point.

options.text: "A patient with type 2 diabetes who needs insulin has failed to manage his condition."
options.rationale: Some type 2 patients require insulin as the pancreas becomes unable to keep up. It does not indicate poor control.

questions.takeaway: Type 2 may require insulin over time. Needing insulin is not evidence of failure.
questions.strategy: Three statements restate her slides correctly. The fourth attaches a judgment to a treatment.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what insulin in type 2 means
steps.detail: The pancreas can no longer keep up.

elimination.verdict: That leaves the failure statement.

questions.scenario: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes is admitted with influenza. She tells the nurse she stopped taking her insulin two days ago because she has not been able to keep food down and thought insulin without food would be dangerous. Her blood glucose is 412 mg/dL, urinary ketones are moderate, and her respirations are deep and rapid at 28. Her blood pressure is 96/58 and her mucous membranes are dry.
questions.stem: Select 2 actions the nurse takes, the 1 problem this represents, and 2 parameters to evaluate.

options.text: Administer intravenous fluids and insulin per protocol
options.rationale: Both are needed. The fluids address the dehydration from osmotic diuresis and the insulin stops the fat breakdown producing the ketones.

options.text: Monitor blood glucose, ketones, pH and electrolytes closely
options.rationale: Named among DKA nursing priorities, and the treatment response has to be tracked rather than assumed.

options.text: Withhold insulin until she is able to tolerate food
options.rationale: The belief that brought her in. Insulin need usually rises during illness, and stopping it is what produced the ketones.

options.text: Encourage oral fluids and reassess in two hours
options.rationale: She cannot keep anything down, and a two-hour delay in a patient with moderate ketones and Kussmaul respirations is not safe.

options.text: Diabetic ketoacidosis from insulin omission during illness
options.rationale: Ketones, Kussmaul respirations, hyperglycemia and dehydration, with a clear precipitant she has told you herself.

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
options.rationale: HHS has no significant ketones and develops over days in type 2. She has moderate ketones and type 1.

options.text: Dehydration from influenza and poor oral intake
options.rationale: The dehydration is real and it is a component rather than the diagnosis. It does not explain the ketones.

options.text: Hypoglycemia from inadequate food intake
options.rationale: Her glucose is 412. The absence of food did not produce a low because there was no insulin either.

options.text: Blood glucose trend and clearance of ketones
options.rationale: The two findings that defined the emergency, measured as the treatment takes effect.

options.text: Respiratory rate and level of consciousness
options.rationale: Kussmaul respirations should settle as the acidosis corrects, and mental status is the fastest bedside indicator of the response.

options.text: Whether she can state the sick-day rules
options.rationale: Essential teaching before discharge, and it evaluates knowledge rather than whether she is recovering now.

options.text: Her temperature over the next 24 hours
options.rationale: Tracks the influenza rather than the ketoacidosis the actions targeted.

questions.takeaway: Insulin need rises during illness. Stopping it because food is not being kept down is the most dangerous sick-day error and it is what produces DKA.
questions.strategy: She tells you the precipitant herself. One action distractor repeats the belief that caused the admission.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Read the ketones and the breathing

elimination.verdict: Fluids and insulin with close monitoring, for DKA from insulin omission, evaluated by glucose, ketones, respirations and consciousness.

skills.title: Administering Nonparenteral Medications
skills.subtitle: Oral, enteral tube, topical, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled routes

questions.stem: A 74-year-old being discharged on six medications explains his plan to the nurse, including an enteric-coated tablet, a topical ointment, and eye drops. He lives alone and will manage the regimen himself. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will keep the head of my bed raised for an hour after my tube feed medication."
options.rationale: Accurate. A minimum of 30 degrees for one hour reduces aspiration risk.

options.text: "I will clean the skin before applying the next dose of my ointment."
options.rationale: Accurate. New medication is never applied over a previous application.

options.text: "If a tablet is hard to swallow I will crush it and mix it with applesauce."
options.rationale: An enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split, because the coating protects the stomach lining from the medication. A different form is requested from the prescriber or pharmacist instead.

options.text: "Temporary blurring after my eye drops is expected rather than a reaction."
options.rationale: Accurate. Temporary burning or blurring may follow ophthalmic medication.

questions.takeaway: Never crush or split an enteric-coated tablet. Change the form, not the technique.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is what a patient with swallowing difficulty would reasonably do. It destroys the coating that protects the stomach.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Topical, tube feed positioning, and eye drops are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: request a different form rather than crushing.

questions.stem: A nurse is working with assistive personnel and reviews which parts of medication administration may be assigned and what the AP must be told. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Administering oral medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel
options.rationale: The skill itself stays with the nurse.

options.text: Administering medications through an enteral feeding tube cannot be delegated
options.rationale: And the aspiration risk is why.

options.text: Assistive personnel may give oral medications if the nurse observes
options.rationale: Observation does not change scope. Administration remains with the nurse.

options.text: The AP reports coughing, choking, gagging, or drooling of liquid to the nurse immediately
options.rationale: The AP is told what to watch for and what to report, which is what makes the instruction complete.

options.text: Assistive personnel may crush tablets if the nurse has checked they are crushable
options.rationale: Preparing a medication is part of administration and remains with the nurse.

options.text: Ophthalmic and otic medications may be delegated if the AP has been shown the technique
options.rationale: Neither may be delegated. Being shown a technique does not change the scope.

questions.takeaway: The administration itself stays with the nurse. What is delegated is observation, positioning, and reporting. The administration of oral, enteral, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel. Some agencies permit specially trained AP to apply certain topical agents, so agency policy is checked.
questions.strategy: Topical is the single exception where agency policy may allow trained AP, and being shown a technique never expands scope on its own.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Separate the skill from the support
steps.detail: Administration stays; positioning and reporting go.
Some topical agents, by agency policy.
Technique training does not change scope.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: The administration of oral, enteral, ophthalmic, otic, nasal, and inhaled medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel. Some agencies permit specially trained AP to apply certain topical agents, so agency policy is checked.

questions.stem: A patient with asthma has been prescribed a pressurized metered-dose inhaler but cannot reliably coordinate pressing the canister with inhaling. His technique has been assessed twice with the same result. Which options should the nurse discuss with the provider?

options.text: A spacer device or a breath-actuated inhaler
options.rationale: Both remove the need to coordinate actuation with the breathing cycle, which is the specific problem.

options.text: Having the AP administer the inhaler for him
options.rationale: Administering inhaled medication cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.

options.text: Increasing the number of puffs to compensate for poor delivery
options.rationale: Delivers more of a dose that is not reaching the airways, and it risks adverse effects.

options.text: Switching to an oral tablet because inhalers are unsuitable
options.rationale: Abandons the inhaled route without trying the adaptations that exist for this problem.

questions.takeaway: A pMDI requires coordination during the breathing cycle. Poor coordination calls for a spacer or a breath-actuated inhaler. A pressurized metered-dose inhaler uses a propellant and requires coordination during the breathing cycle. A breath-actuated inhaler triggers on inhalation. A dry powder inhaler has no propellant, needs no spacer, and depends on the patient's inspiratory effort.
questions.strategy: The three inhaler types differ in what they ask of the patient: a pMDI needs coordination, a BAI triggers on inhalation, and a DPI needs inspiratory effort but no propellant and no spacer.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: More puffs of an undelivered dose.
One abandons the route, one exceeds AP scope.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: remove the coordination requirement.

questions.concept: A pressurized metered-dose inhaler uses a propellant and requires coordination during the breathing cycle. A breath-actuated inhaler triggers on inhalation. A dry powder inhaler has no propellant, needs no spacer, and depends on the patient's inspiratory effort.

questions.stem: A newly prescribed oral medication is due for a patient admitted this morning. She wants to be sure she has gathered what safe administration requires before she goes into the room. Which actions are part of safe medication preparation? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess the patient for drug allergies
options.rationale: Always assessed before administration, and a documented allergy changes whether the drug is given at all.

options.text: Determine the purpose, usual dose and route, common side effects, onset and peak, and contraindications
options.rationale: The information gathered about any ordered drug before it is given.

options.text: Confirm the patient has not eaten within the past hour
options.rationale: Food timing matters for specific medications rather than as a universal preparation step.

options.text: Check the expiration date
options.rationale: An expired medication may have lost potency or changed chemically, and that applies to every route.

options.text: Administer the dose if the calculation looks approximately correct
options.rationale: Calculations are double-checked, and a dose that appears incorrect is not given.

options.text: Check that a second nurse is available to witness
options.rationale: A second check applies to high-alert medications rather than to every oral dose.

questions.takeaway: Allergies, drug information, interactions, expiry, and the patient's sensory and physical capacity.
questions.strategy: The wrong option lowers the standard on a calculation. If a dose appears incorrect it is not given, and approximately correct is not a standard.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Five actions occur before the drug reaches the patient.
Approximately correct is not a safety standard.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.stem: The next scheduled dose of a prescribed ointment is due for a patient's forearm. The previous application from twelve hours ago is still visible on the skin, and the area is intact with no redness. Which action is correct?

options.text: Apply the new dose over the existing layer to avoid disturbing the skin
options.rationale: Layering doses makes the amount absorbed unpredictable.

options.text: Apply the new dose to an adjacent area of skin instead
options.rationale: Changes the prescribed site rather than preparing it.

options.text: Withhold the dose until the previous application has worn off
options.rationale: Delays a prescribed dose when cleaning the site resolves the problem.

options.text: Clean the skin thoroughly to remove the previous application, then apply the new dose
options.rationale: New medication is never applied over a previous application, and the skin or wound is cleaned before each new dose.

questions.takeaway: Never apply new medication over a previous application. Clean the skin or wound thoroughly before each new dose. Topical medications are applied to skin, mucous membranes, or tissues. Lotions, patches, pastes, and ointments produce local effects and can produce systemic effects if absorbed through the skin.
questions.strategy: Topical doses look forgiving and are not. Lotions, patches, pastes, and ointments produce local effects and can produce systemic effects if absorbed through the skin, so the amount matters.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One moves the site, one delays the dose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: clean first, then apply.

questions.concept: Topical medications are applied to skin, mucous membranes, or tissues. Lotions, patches, pastes, and ointments produce local effects and can produce systemic effects if absorbed through the skin.

questions.stem: Medications are due through a newly inserted small-bore nasogastric tube. The medications are in liquid form and the correct connector is attached. The tube was placed 20 minutes ago. Which action must she take before administering?

options.text: Flush the tube with 200 mL of water to confirm patency
options.rationale: A large flush before confirming placement risks delivering fluid into the lungs.

options.text: Verify correct placement of the tube
options.rationale: Placement is verified before medications are given, because a displaced tube delivers the dose into the airway.

options.text: Position the patient flat to ease instillation
options.rationale: The head of the bed is elevated, not lowered, and flat positioning increases aspiration risk.

options.text: Crush the medications finely before mixing
options.rationale: They are already in liquid form, and crushing requires pharmacist consultation in any case.

questions.takeaway: Verify tube placement before giving anything through it. A newly inserted tube requires x-ray confirmation. Medications given through a feeding tube should be in liquid form, and a pharmacist is consulted before crushing or dissolving any tablet. The correct enteral access connector is used and tube placement is verified before administration.
questions.strategy: Every wrong option here delivers something into a tube whose position has not been confirmed. Placement comes before patency, positioning, and preparation.

strategies: Assessment before intervention
elimination.verdict: That leaves B: confirm placement first.

questions.concept: Medications given through a feeding tube should be in liquid form, and a pharmacist is consulted before crushing or dissolving any tablet. The correct enteral access connector is used and tube placement is verified before administration.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the precautions for administering eye and ear medications with a student before a shift on a unit where two patients receive both. The student asks what differs between the two routes. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Ear medications are administered at room temperature
options.rationale: Cold solution instilled into the ear canal causes dizziness and discomfort.

options.text: Sterile drops and solutions are used in case the eardrum is ruptured
options.rationale: A ruptured drum means the solution reaches the middle ear.

options.text: Warm ear drops in hot water immediately before instillation
options.rationale: Drops are at room temperature. Hot water risks burning the canal.

options.text: Temporary burning or blurring of vision may follow eye medication
options.rationale: Expected, and the AP is told about it so it is not mistaken for an adverse reaction.

options.text: Eye ointments are instilled directly onto the cornea
options.rationale: Medication is placed in the conjunctival sac. The cornea is sensitive and direct instillation causes pain and injury.

options.text: Occlude the ear canal with the dropper to prevent leakage
options.rationale: Occluding the canal creates pressure during instillation.

questions.takeaway: Ear drops at room temperature, sterile, without occluding the canal. Eye medication into the conjunctival sac, never onto the cornea. Medications applied to membranes such as the cornea or the rectal mucosa are absorbed quickly because of the vascularity of the membrane and can produce systemic effects.
questions.strategy: The wrong option names an anatomical target that sounds plausible and is wrong. The cornea is highly vascular and highly sensitive, which is why medications applied to membranes absorb quickly and why the cornea is not the target.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The conjunctival sac is the target.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: Medications applied to membranes such as the cornea or the rectal mucosa are absorbed quickly because of the vascularity of the membrane and can produce systemic effects.

questions.stem: During medication administration through a feeding tube the patient begins coughing, his respiratory rate rises from 18 to 30, and his saturation falls from 96% to 89%. Which action does the nurse take first?

options.text: Notify the health care provider
options.rationale: Necessary, and another staff member makes the call while the nurse stays with the patient.

options.text: Stop all medications and fluids going through the tube
options.rationale: Stopping the instillation halts what is entering the airway, and it is the first step before positioning or assessment.

options.text: Continue the medication slowly to avoid wasting the dose
options.rationale: Continues delivering fluid into a patient showing signs of aspiration.

options.text: Assess vital signs and breath sounds
options.rationale: Follows once the instillation has stopped and the head of the bed is elevated.

questions.takeaway: Stop all medications and fluids, elevate the head of the bed, stay with the patient, and assess while another staff member notifies the provider. Signs of aspiration during tube medication include respiratory distress and changes in vital signs or oxygen saturation.
questions.strategy: Two options here are genuinely required and both come after stopping. The key word FIRST separates the correct sequence from the correct list.

strategies: Priority key word
Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Coughing, rising respiratory rate, falling saturation.
Both required, and both follow stopping the instillation.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: stop what is going in before doing anything else.

questions.concept: Signs of aspiration during tube medication include respiratory distress and changes in vital signs or oxygen saturation. Stop all medications and fluids, elevate the head of the bed, stay with the patient, and assess while another staff member notifies the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing scheduled 0800 medications for four patients. Her preceptor asks her to name when each of the three safety checks occurs. At which points does she perform them?

options.text: Once at the cabinet and twice at the bedside
options.rationale: Misplaces the second check, which occurs before entering the room.

options.text: At the order, at transcription, at administration
options.rationale: Describes the order's journey rather than the nurse's own verification points.

options.text: At the cabinet, before entering the room, at the bedside
options.rationale: All three compare the medication against the MAR, and the third happens with the patient present, immediately before administration.

options.text: At the start, midpoint, and end of the shift
options.rationale: Checks are tied to each medication rather than to the clock.

questions.takeaway: Three safety checks, all against the MAR: at the cabinet, before entering the room, and at the bedside before administering. The three safety checks each compare the medication against the MAR: when removing it from the automated dispensing cabinet, before entering the patient's room, and at the bedside before administering.
questions.strategy: The third check is the one students skip because the work feels done. It is the only one performed with the patient in front of you, and it is the last chance to catch a wrong-patient error.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Three, each comparing the medication to the MAR.
Describes the order's journey rather than the nurse's own verification points.
Checks are tied to each medication rather than to the clock.
Misplaces the second check, which occurs before entering the room.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: all three compare the medication against the MAR, and the third happens with the patient present, immediately before administration.

questions.concept: The three safety checks each compare the medication against the MAR: when removing it from the automated dispensing cabinet, before entering the patient's room, and at the bedside before administering.

questions.stem: Twenty minutes after receiving a newly prescribed oral antibiotic, a patient develops a raised itchy rash, reports his nose is running, and has audible wheezing. Which nursing actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Withhold further doses of the medication
options.rationale: Further doses would add to a reaction already in progress.

options.text: Notify the health care provider and pharmacy immediately
options.rationale: Both are notified, and emergency medications may be needed.

options.text: Assess the patient's vital signs
options.rationale: Establishes how far the reaction has progressed and whether the airway is threatened.

options.text: Enter the allergy in the patient's medical record
options.rationale: Prevents the drug being given again by anyone caring for him later.

options.text: Give the next scheduled dose and observe whether the reaction repeats
options.rationale: Deliberately re-exposes a patient to a drug he is reacting to.

options.text: Document the findings and reassess at the end of the shift
options.rationale: Wheezing indicates airway involvement and cannot wait.

questions.takeaway: Urticaria, rash, pruritus, rhinitis, and wheezing may indicate an allergic reaction and the need for emergency medications. Withhold, notify provider and pharmacy, assess vital signs, and record the allergy. Withhold further doses, notify the provider and pharmacy immediately, assess vital signs, and add the allergy to the medical record.
questions.strategy: Wheezing is the finding that raises this from a rash to an airway problem, which is why observing or deferring are both wrong.

strategies: Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Wheezing cannot wait until the end of the shift.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Urticaria, rash, pruritus, rhinitis, and wheezing may indicate an allergic reaction and the need for emergency medications. Withhold further doses, notify the provider and pharmacy immediately, assess vital signs, and add the allergy to the medical record.

questions.stem: A patient with difficulty swallowing is prescribed an enteric-coated tablet. The nurse considers how to give it, since the patient manages liquids and crushed tablets well but gags on whole tablets. Which action is correct?

options.text: Contact the provider or pharmacist to request an alternative form of the medication
options.rationale: An enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split, so the form has to change rather than the technique.

options.text: Have the patient swallow it with a large volume of water
options.rationale: Does not address the gagging and risks aspiration in a patient with swallowing difficulty.

options.text: Crush the tablet and mix it with applesauce
options.rationale: Destroys the coating that protects the stomach lining from irritation by the medication.

options.text: Split the tablet in half so it is easier to swallow
options.rationale: Splitting breaks the coating just as crushing does.

questions.takeaway: Never crush or split an enteric-coated medication. The coating protects the stomach lining from the drug. Enteric coating protects the stomach lining from irritation by the medication, so an enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split. Liquids are absorbed faster than tablets or capsules and are usually absorbed in the stomach.
questions.strategy: When a form cannot be altered and the patient cannot take it as supplied, the answer is always to change the form through the prescriber or pharmacist rather than to work around it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Does not solve the swallowing problem.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: change the form, not the technique.

questions.concept: Enteric coating protects the stomach lining from irritation by the medication, so an enteric-coated tablet is never crushed or split. Liquids are absorbed faster than tablets or capsules and are usually absorbed in the stomach.

skills.title: Blood Glucose Monitoring and Subcutaneous Insulin
skills.subtitle: Interpreting the value, recognizing hypoglycemia, insulin types and timing, and injection technique

questions.stem: A 72-year-old receives 18 units of Humulin N subcutaneously at 0800. He eats breakfast at 0830 and lunch at 1230. The nurse plans when to monitor most closely for hypoglycemia from this dose. Which window is correct?

options.rationale: NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and is barely acting in the first hour.
NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose, so a 0800 dose carries risk across the afternoon into the evening.
Beyond the 14 to 24 hour duration of a morning dose and outside the peak.
Within the onset period rather than the peak, and this window fits regular insulin.

questions.takeaway: NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N): onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. That wide peak is why NPH catches people off guard. The wide peak spreads the hypoglycemia risk across a whole shift.
questions.strategy: The NPH peak is broad rather than sharp, so the risk is spread across a whole shift rather than concentrated in an hour.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH has an onset of 1 to 2 hours and is barely acting in the first hour.
Within the onset period rather than the peak, and this window fits regular insulin.
Beyond the 14 to 24 hour duration of a morning dose and outside the peak.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: NPH peaks 4 to 12 hours after the dose, so a 0800 dose carries risk across the afternoon into the evening.

questions.concept: NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N): onset 1 to 2 hours, peak 4 to 12 hours, duration 14 to 24 hours. The wide peak spreads the hypoglycemia risk across a whole shift.

questions.stem: A nurse is orienting a student who will be checking insulin doses with her. She asks the student to identify each vial by appearance before reading the label, as a first check rather than a substitute for one. Which insulins are clear? Select all that apply.

options.text: Humalog
options.rationale: Lispro is rapid-acting and comes as a clear solution, so cloudiness in this vial would mean something is wrong.

options.text: NovoLog
options.rationale: Aspart is rapid-acting and clear. Clear insulins do not need resuspending before you draw them up.

options.text: Humulin R
options.rationale: Regular insulin, short-acting and clear.

options.text: Novolin R
options.rationale: Regular insulin, short-acting and clear.

options.text: Humulin N
options.rationale: NPH is a suspension, so it is cloudy by design and has to be rolled to mix it evenly before drawing.

options.text: Novolin N
options.rationale: Also NPH, and also cloudy. The cloudiness is the suspension, not spoilage.

questions.takeaway: Rapid-acting and regular insulins are clear. NPH is the cloudy one. Rapid-acting insulins (Humalog, NovoLog) and regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R) are clear. NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N) is cloudy. Long-acting insulins are clear and are never mixed.
questions.strategy: Appearance narrows the field and never replaces reading the label. Two different insulins can look identical and act over completely different time courses.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Humulin N and Novolin N are NPH.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Rapid-acting insulins (Humalog, NovoLog) and regular insulin (Humulin R, Novolin R) are clear. NPH (Humulin N, Novolin N) is cloudy. Long-acting insulins are clear and are never mixed.

questions.stem: A 61-year-old newly started on insulin is preparing for discharge and demonstrates his technique to the nurse while explaining what he plans to do at home. Which patient statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will not inject into my thigh right before I go for a walk."
options.rationale: Accurate. Exercise speeds absorption from the injected limb.

options.text: "I will roll the cloudy vial gently rather than shaking it."
options.rationale: Accurate. NPH is a suspension and shaking froths it.

options.text: "I will rotate between my abdomen, arm, and thigh so I never use the same area twice."
options.rationale: Anatomical site rotation is no longer recommended, because absorption differs by site and rotating between regions makes each dose absorb at a different rate. One anatomical site is selected and rotation occurs within that region.

options.text: "If my glucose is under 70 and I can swallow, I take 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate."
options.rationale: Accurate, and the glucose is rechecked in 15 minutes.

questions.takeaway: One anatomical site, rotate within that region. Between-region rotation varies absorption dose to dose.
questions.strategy: This guidance changed, so the wrong statement is what patients were taught for years.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Rolling, rule of 15, and exercise are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: rotate within one region, not between regions.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a patient's insulin orders before the morning round and must identify which doses are timed to meals and which are not. The patient is prescribed four different insulin products. Which insulins are given in relation to a meal? Select all that apply.

options.text: Humalog, just before or with the meal
options.rationale: Rapid-acting, onset 10 to 30 minutes.

options.text: NovoLog, just before or with the meal
options.rationale: Rapid-acting, onset 10 to 30 minutes.

options.rationale: Lactic acidosis is a metformin concern, not a sulfonylurea one.

options.text: The beta blocker may mask the early warning signs of hypoglycemia
options.rationale: The shakiness, sweating, and racing heart that warn of a low are adrenergic. A beta blocker blunts them, so the first sign may be confusion instead.

questions.takeaway: Beta blockers mask the adrenergic warning signs of hypoglycemia. Sweating usually persists; shakiness and palpitations do not.
questions.strategy: Ask what the patient would normally feel first during a low, and what a beta blocker does to that.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Ask what a beta blocker blocks

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: the warning signs are masked.

questions.stem: A patient who takes acarbose with each meal becomes hypoglycemic. Which does the nurse administer?

options.text: Table sugar dissolved in water
options.rationale: Sucrose has to be split into glucose and fructose first, and acarbose is blocking exactly that step. This is the trap.

options.text: A slice of bread
options.rationale: A complex carbohydrate needing digestion, and slower still.

options.text: A glass of milk
options.rationale: Lactose also requires breakdown, and milk raises glucose too slowly for an acute low.

options.text: Glucose tablets
options.rationale: Acarbose blocks the enzyme that breaks table sugar into absorbable glucose, so sucrose will not work. Glucose tablets need no digestion.

questions.takeaway: On acarbose or miglitol, treat hypoglycemia with glucose specifically. Sucrose and starch will not be absorbed.
questions.strategy: This is the one hypoglycemia scenario where the usual juice-or-sugar answer is wrong. The drug name in the stem is the signal.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Breakdown of complex sugars in the gut.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: glucose tablets.

questions.stem: A patient is starting empagliflozin. Which teaching does the nurse include?

options.text: Expect increased urination, and report burning or genital itching
options.rationale: SGLT-2 inhibitors work by dumping glucose into the urine. Sugar in the urine raises the risk of urinary and genital yeast infections.

options.text: This is a form of insulin taken by mouth
options.rationale: There is no oral insulin. Insulin is destroyed in the stomach.

options.text: Your urine should stay free of glucose on this medication
options.rationale: The opposite. Glucose in the urine is the mechanism, not a complication.

options.text: Take it only when the glucose reads above 200
options.rationale: It is taken on a schedule, not in response to a reading.

questions.takeaway: SGLT-2 inhibitors lower glucose by excreting it in the urine, which brings polyuria and a risk of urinary and yeast infections.
questions.strategy: Work out the mechanism from the drug class and the side effects follow from it.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Glucose is excreted in the urine.
More urine, and sugar feeding organisms.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: more urination, and report infection signs.

questions.stem: A patient on metformin is scheduled for a computed tomography scan with iodinated contrast. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Give half the usual dose
options.rationale: Not a recognized approach. The decision is to hold or not, and it is the provider's.

options.text: Confirm with the provider that the metformin is held around the study
options.rationale: Contrast can impair kidney function, and metformin cleared by the kidneys accumulates. The build-up risks lactic acidosis.

options.text: Give the metformin with a full glass of water before the scan
options.rationale: Water does not protect the kidneys from the contrast or clear the drug faster.

options.text: No action, since metformin does not interact with contrast
options.rationale: It does, and this is one of the most tested medication-procedure interactions.

questions.takeaway: Metformin is held around iodinated contrast because contrast-related kidney impairment lets it accumulate and cause lactic acidosis.
questions.strategy: Ask what clears the drug and what the contrast does to that organ.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves B: confirm the hold with the provider.

questions.stem: Which oral antidiabetic agents carry a meaningful risk of hypoglycemia when taken alone? Select all that apply.

options.text: Glipizide
options.rationale: A sulfonylurea. It pushes the pancreas to release insulin whether or not glucose is high, so a low can follow.

options.text: Glyburide
options.rationale: Also a sulfonylurea, and the same mechanism.

options.text: Glimepiride
options.rationale: The third of the commonly used sulfonylureas.

options.text: Metformin
options.rationale: Reduces liver glucose output and improves sensitivity. It does not force insulin release, so alone it rarely causes a low.

options.text: Sitagliptin
options.rationale: A DPP-4 inhibitor. It acts through incretins, which work only when glucose is rising, so the risk is low.

options.text: Acarbose
options.rationale: Slows carbohydrate absorption rather than adding insulin. Low risk alone, though it changes how a low must be treated.

questions.takeaway: Sulfonylureas cause hypoglycemia because they force insulin release regardless of the glucose level. Metformin, DPP-4 inhibitors and acarbose do not.
questions.strategy: Sort by mechanism. Anything that pushes insulin out regardless of glucose can cause a low; anything that is glucose-dependent cannot.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.detail: Force insulin, or work only when glucose rises.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews a patient's insulin supply. Which observation requires follow-up?

options.text: The regular insulin appears clear
options.rationale: Regular insulin is a clear solution. This is normal.

options.text: The NPH insulin appears cloudy
options.rationale: NPH is a suspension and is cloudy by design. It is rolled to mix it before drawing.

options.text: The insulin lispro appears clear
options.rationale: Rapid-acting insulin is also clear. Normal.

options.text: The insulin glargine appears cloudy
options.rationale: Glargine is a clear solution. Cloudiness means contamination or degradation, and the vial must not be used.

questions.takeaway: Only NPH should look cloudy. Every other insulin is clear, and cloudiness in a clear insulin means discard it.
questions.strategy: One insulin is meant to be cloudy. Any other cloudy vial is the finding.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: NPH cloudy, regular and lispro clear.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: cloudy glargine.

questions.stem: A patient wakes with a glucose of 240 mg/dL. Overnight readings show a fall to 48 mg/dL at 0300 followed by a rise. Which does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Somogyi phenomenon
options.rationale: An overnight low triggers counter-regulatory hormones, which drive the glucose up by morning. The high reading is the rebound from the low.

options.text: Insufficient evening basal insulin
options.rationale: That would produce a steady overnight rise, not a fall to 48 first.

options.text: An inaccurate morning meter reading
options.rationale: The overnight trend explains the morning value. Dismissing it as error loses the pattern.

options.text: Dawn phenomenon
options.rationale: Dawn is a morning rise from overnight growth hormone and cortisol, with no preceding low. The 0300 reading of 48 is what separates them.

questions.takeaway: Somogyi has an overnight low that rebounds. Dawn rises without a low. The 0200 to 0300 check is what distinguishes them.
questions.strategy: Both produce a high morning glucose, and the overnight reading is the only thing that separates them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: One predicts a steady rise, one dismisses real data.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: Somogyi phenomenon.

questions.stem: A patient with type 1 diabetes has influenza and is vomiting. Which sick-day instructions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Keep taking the insulin, even when not eating normally
options.rationale: Illness raises glucose through stress hormones. Stopping insulin during illness is how patients arrive in ketoacidosis.

options.text: Check the glucose every three to four hours
options.rationale: More often than usual, because illness makes the glucose unpredictable.

options.text: Test for ketones when the glucose stays above 240
options.rationale: Ketones signal that fat is being broken down for fuel and that ketoacidosis may be developing.

options.text: Take small sips of fluid frequently
options.rationale: Vomiting plus a rising glucose dehydrates quickly, and dehydration accelerates the whole process.

options.text: Stop the insulin until eating normally again
options.rationale: The single most dangerous sick-day error. Insulin need usually rises during illness.

options.text: Wait until the fever settles before contacting the provider
options.rationale: Persistent vomiting, ketones, or a glucose that will not come down need reporting rather than waiting.

questions.takeaway: Sick days: never stop insulin, check glucose every three to four hours, test ketones above 240, and keep fluids going.
questions.strategy: Two options tell the patient to wait or to stop. Ask what illness does to the insulin requirement.

strategies: Test each option on its own

steps.detail: The need goes up, not down.
Vomiting with ketones is what needs reporting.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A patient using an insulin pump reports the glucose has risen from 140 to 310 mg/dL over four hours and ketones are now present. Which does the nurse suspect first?

options.text: A faulty glucose meter
options.rationale: The ketones corroborate the reading. Two findings agreeing is not a meter fault.

options.text: The pump is delivering too much basal insulin
options.rationale: Too much would lower the glucose, not raise it, and would not produce ketones.

options.text: An expected rise after a high-carbohydrate meal
options.rationale: A meal does not produce ketones, and the rise would not continue over four hours.

options.text: An interruption in insulin delivery at the site or in the tubing
options.rationale: A pump delivers only rapid-acting insulin, with no long-acting reserve. An occlusion or dislodged cannula leaves the patient with no insulin at all within hours.

questions.takeaway: Pump patients have no long-acting insulin on board. An interruption produces hyperglycemia and ketones within hours.
questions.strategy: Ask what a pump does and does not deliver. The ketones are the finding that rules out a simple meal-related rise.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: They indicate no insulin is reaching the patient.

steps.action: Cut the meal and meter options

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: an interruption in delivery.

skills.title: The Endocrine System
skills.subtitle: Hormones, feedback, and the major glands: pituitary, thyroid, parathyroid, adrenal, and pancreas

questions.stem: A patient with hyperthyroidism reports fatigue. Over the next two hours her heart rate rises from 96 to 138 and her temperature from 37.4 C to 38.9 C. Which finding is the priority?

options.text: Neither finding, since tachycardia and warmth are both expected features of hyperthyroidism
options.rationale: Tachycardia is expected; a rise of this size with fever is not.

options.text: The fatigue, since it is the symptom the patient reported herself and reflects her own experience
options.rationale: Real and it is not the finding that can deteriorate rapidly.

options.text: The temperature alone, since a fever of this size most likely indicates a developing infection
options.rationale: Separating the two loses the pattern. Together they point at thyroid storm.

options.text: The rising heart rate and temperature, which may signal thyroid storm
options.rationale: Cardiovascular status and temperature are the monitoring priorities, and this trend is the emergency this condition produces.

questions.takeaway: In hyperthyroidism, monitor cardiovascular status and temperature closely and watch for thyroid storm. In hyperthyroidism, monitor cardiovascular status and temperature closely, watch for thyroid storm, promote rest, and reduce environmental stimulation.
questions.strategy: Fatigue is what the patient reports and the vital sign trend is what will kill her. When a stem gives you a symptom and a trend, the trend usually wins.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: Heart rate and temperature both climbing over two hours.
One normalizes the trend, one splits the pattern.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: cardiovascular status and temperature are the monitoring priorities, and this trend is the emergency this condition produces.

questions.concept: In hyperthyroidism, monitor cardiovascular status and temperature closely, watch for thyroid storm, promote rest, and reduce environmental stimulation.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews the major endocrine glands with a student before a shift on a medical unit where three patients have endocrine disorders. She asks the student to pair each gland with what it regulates, since the symptoms follow from the function. Which pairings are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pituitary: the master gland that regulates other endocrine glands
options.rationale: It also controls growth hormone and regulates water balance through ADH.

options.text: Thyroid: controls metabolism, energy, and body temperature
options.rationale: Which is why symptoms cluster around rate and temperature.

options.text: Parathyroids: regulate calcium and phosphate in blood and bone
options.rationale: And calcium is essential for nerve conduction, muscle contraction, and cardiac rhythm.

options.text: Hypothalamus: produces reproductive hormones
options.rationale: The ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones. The hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems.

options.text: Thymus: regulates blood glucose
options.rationale: The pancreas regulates blood glucose. The thymus is lymphatic.

options.text: Adrenal glands: produce insulin and glucagon
options.rationale: The pancreas produces insulin and glucagon. The adrenals manage stress response and fluid balance.

questions.takeaway: Hypothalamus links the systems, pituitary directs, thyroid sets the pace, parathyroids manage calcium, adrenals handle stress and fluid, pancreas handles glucose. Hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and regulates pituitary output. Pituitary is the master gland. Thyroid controls metabolism, energy, and temperature. Parathyroids regulate calcium and phosphate. Adrenals manage stress, fluid balance, and blood pressure. Pancreas regulates glucose. Ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones.
questions.strategy: Disorders affect the whole body, not just the gland. Once you know what a gland regulates, its dysfunction predicts which systems will show symptoms.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Reproductive hormones come from the ovaries and testes.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Hypothalamus links the nervous and endocrine systems and regulates pituitary output. Pituitary is the master gland. Thyroid controls metabolism, energy, and temperature. Parathyroids regulate calcium and phosphate. Adrenals manage stress, fluid balance, and blood pressure. Pancreas regulates glucose. Ovaries and testes produce reproductive hormones.

questions.stem: A student asks the nurse how the body keeps blood glucose within such a narrow range after eating. The nurse describes the sequence: glucose rises, the pancreas releases insulin, cells absorb glucose, blood glucose falls, and insulin secretion decreases. Which mechanism does this describe?

options.text: Osmotic diuresis, the mechanism by which elevated blood glucose produces increased urine output
options.rationale: The mechanism by which high glucose produces polyuria.

options.text: Receptor specificity, which determines which tissues are able to respond to the circulating hormone
options.rationale: Explains which tissues respond, not how secretion is regulated.

options.text: Negative feedback, where the response counteracts the original change and then stops
options.rationale: The body detects a change, adjusts secretion to counteract it, restores balance, and signaling stops. It is what prevents dangerous extremes.

options.text: Positive feedback, where the response amplifies the original change until an endpoint is reached
options.rationale: Amplification would drive glucose further from normal rather than back toward it.

questions.takeaway: Negative feedback detects a change, counteracts it, restores balance, and switches off. It prevents dangerous extremes, and diabetes is a broken glucose feedback loop. Negative feedback: the body detects a change in hormone or substance level, glands adjust secretion to counteract it, balance is restored, and signaling stops.
questions.strategy: When feedback fails, disorders emerge. Framing diabetes that way makes the complications follow logically rather than needing separate memorization.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The response opposes the change rather than amplifying it.
A targeting principle and a fluid mechanism.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the body detects a change, adjusts secretion to counteract it, restores balance, and signaling stops.

questions.concept: Negative feedback: the body detects a change in hormone or substance level, glands adjust secretion to counteract it, balance is restored, and signaling stops. It prevents dangerous extremes, and diabetes is a broken glucose feedback loop.

questions.stem: A 44-year-old is admitted with symptoms her provider suspects are thyroid-related. She reports feeling constantly warm, has lost weight over three months despite eating well, and her hands are visibly tremulous. Which findings are consistent with hyperthyroidism? Select all that apply.

options.text: Weight loss despite normal or increased appetite
options.rationale: Thyroid hormone drives metabolism, so an excess burns through calories faster than he can eat them.

options.text: Heat intolerance and excessive sweating
options.rationale: The thyroid controls body temperature regulation.

options.text: Restlessness, anxiety, and tremors
options.rationale: Everything speeds up, including the nervous system.

options.text: Increased heart rate and blood pressure
options.rationale: Correct, and it is the reason cardiovascular monitoring is a nursing priority.

options.text: Cold intolerance and dry skin
options.rationale: Cold intolerance and dry skin come from a slowed metabolism, which is the opposite problem.

options.text: Constipation and slowed reflexes
options.rationale: Constipation and slow reflexes also point to an underactive thyroid, where everything runs slower.

questions.takeaway: Hyper speeds everything up: weight loss, heat intolerance, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia. Hypo slows everything down. Hyperthyroidism speeds metabolism: weight loss despite appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, restlessness, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, raised blood pressure. Hypothyroidism slows it: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, slowed reflexes, bradycardia.
questions.strategy: You do not need to memorize two lists. Decide whether metabolism is fast or slow, then predict what each system does.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weight, temperature, mood, and heart rate all speed up.
Cold intolerance and constipation are the slow picture.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Hyperthyroidism speeds metabolism: weight loss despite appetite, heat intolerance, sweating, restlessness, anxiety, tremor, tachycardia, raised blood pressure. Hypothyroidism slows it: fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance, dry skin, constipation, slowed reflexes, bradycardia.

questions.stem: A patient with adrenal dysfunction has an unstable blood pressure, a serum sodium of 128 mEq/L, and reports profound fatigue. Which hormone's action best explains the blood pressure and sodium findings?

options.text: Aldosterone, which controls sodium and water retention to maintain blood pressure
options.rationale: Aldosterone regulates sodium and potassium, and disruption produces both the electrolyte abnormality and the unstable pressure.

options.text: Insulin, which moves glucose from the bloodstream into cells and lowers the blood glucose level
options.rationale: A pancreatic hormone affecting glucose, not sodium.

options.text: Antidiuretic hormone released from the thyroid gland, which governs water retention by the kidney
options.rationale: ADH is pituitary, not thyroid, and the option misattributes it.

options.text: Parathyroid hormone, which raises blood calcium when circulating levels begin to fall
options.rationale: Calcium regulation rather than sodium and pressure.

questions.takeaway: The adrenal glands manage stress response, blood pressure through aldosterone, fluid and electrolyte balance, and glucose metabolism through cortisol. The adrenal glands release cortisol and epinephrine in the stress response, regulate blood pressure through aldosterone's control of sodium and water retention, manage sodium and potassium balance, and influence glucose metabolism through cortisol.
questions.strategy: Adrenal dysfunction shows up as unstable blood pressure, electrolyte imbalance, fatigue, and an impaired stress response. Those four together are the pattern.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves A: aldosterone.

questions.concept: The adrenal glands release cortisol and epinephrine in the stress response, regulate blood pressure through aldosterone's control of sodium and water retention, manage sodium and potassium balance, and influence glucose metabolism through cortisol.

questions.stem: A patient with a pituitary disorder has a urine output of 4,200 mL over eight hours with a specific gravity of 1.002, and reports constant thirst. Which assessment is the priority?

options.text: Serum calcium and phosphate
options.rationale: Parathyroid concerns rather than pituitary.

options.text: Serum sodium and fluid balance
options.rationale: Pituitary dysfunction disrupts water balance through ADH, and dilute polyuria with thirst fits diabetes insipidus.

options.text: Blood glucose and serum ketones
options.rationale: Osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus produces urine loaded with glucose. Urine this dilute points elsewhere.

options.text: Thyroid function and temperature tolerance
options.rationale: Fits a thyroid disorder and does not explain dilute polyuria.

questions.takeaway: The pituitary regulates water balance through ADH. Monitor urine output, fluid balance, and serum sodium.
questions.strategy: Diabetes insipidus and diabetes mellitus both cause polyuria and thirst. The urine tells you which: very dilute points at ADH, glucose-laden points at osmotic diuresis.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Fits a thyroid disorder and does not explain dilute polyuria.
Osmotic diuresis in diabetes mellitus produces glucose-laden urine, not urine this dilute.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: pituitary dysfunction disrupts water balance through ADH, and dilute polyuria with thirst fits diabetes insipidus.

questions.concept: The pituitary regulates water balance through ADH. Nursing focus includes monitoring urine output and fluid balance, assessing serum sodium, and recognizing diabetes insipidus, which presents with excess dilute urine and thirst.

questions.stem: A patient's serum calcium is 7.4 mg/dL on the first day after a thyroidectomy. She reports tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips. Which nursing actions are indicated? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess for Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs
options.rationale: Neuromuscular indicators of hypocalcemia, and they are the assessments.

options.text: Monitor cardiac rhythm
options.rationale: Calcium is essential for cardiac rhythm, and imbalance produces arrhythmias.

options.text: Watch for muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones
options.rationale: The picture of hypercalcemia, which is the opposite imbalance.

options.text: Encourage a high-phosphate diet
options.rationale: Phosphate and calcium move inversely. Raising phosphate lowers calcium further.

options.text: Restrict dietary calcium
options.rationale: Calcium is already low. Restricting it worsens the problem.

options.text: Implement fall prevention measures
options.rationale: Safety is a priority given the neuromuscular effects.

questions.takeaway: Hypocalcemia produces tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias. Hypercalcemia causes muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones. PTH raises blood calcium when levels drop; calcitonin lowers it when levels are high. Hypocalcemia causes tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias, assessed through Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs.
questions.strategy: PTH raises calcium when it drops; calcitonin lowers it when it is high. Knowing which hormone is missing predicts which direction the calcium moves.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Weakness and kidney stones describe hypercalcemia.

elimination.verdict: A, B and F are selected.

questions.concept: PTH raises blood calcium when levels drop; calcitonin lowers it when levels are high. Hypocalcemia causes tetany, seizures, and arrhythmias, assessed through Trousseau's and Chvostek's signs. Hypercalcemia causes muscle weakness, confusion, and kidney stones.

questions.stem: A nursing instructor reviews endocrine physiology with a student before a clinical shift, asking her to explain how hormones reach their targets and what happens when regulation fails. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "A hormone only reaches the tissues it is meant to affect."
options.rationale: Hormones are released into the bloodstream and reach every tissue. Only cells with matching receptors detect and respond, which is why the same hormone produces different effects in different places.

options.text: "Hypocalcemia causes tetany and seizures; hypercalcemia causes weakness and confusion."
options.rationale: Accurate. The direction of the calcium determines the presentation.

options.text: "Negative feedback counteracts a change and then switches off."
options.rationale: Accurate, and diabetes is a broken glucose feedback loop.

options.text: "Hyperthyroidism speeds everything up, so I would expect weight loss and heat intolerance."
options.rationale: Accurate. Setting the direction predicts what each system does.

questions.takeaway: Hormones reach every tissue. Receptors decide which ones respond.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement sounds like targeting and describes delivery. The targeting happens at the receptor, not in the bloodstream.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Circulation is universal; response is selective.
Feedback, thyroid direction, and calcium are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: hormones reach everywhere, receptors decide.

questions.stem: A student asks why insulin circulates through the entire body but does not affect every tissue in the same way. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: Hormones are broken down before reaching most tissues
options.rationale: Hormones do reach nearly every tissue. Whether a tissue responds depends on whether it has receptors for that hormone.

options.text: Every cell reached responds equally
options.rationale: Would make targeted hormonal regulation impossible.

options.text: Only cells with matching receptors respond
options.rationale: Receptor specificity determines which tissues are affected, which is why the same hormone produces different responses in different places.

options.text: Hormones reach only the organ that produced them
options.rationale: Hormones are released into the bloodstream and travel to distant targets.

questions.takeaway: Hormones reach every tissue. Only cells with matching receptors respond, which is why one hormone produces different effects in different places. Hormones are chemical messengers released directly into the bloodstream and travel to distant target cells. Only cells with matching receptors detect and respond, so the same hormone produces different responses in different tissues.
questions.strategy: Receptor specificity explains a great deal at once: why insulin resistance affects some tissues more than others, and why a single gland disorder produces symptoms across several systems.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Why circulation is universal and effect is not.
Hormones are released into the bloodstream and travel to distant targets.
Circulation to all tissues is the point; the response depends on receptors.
Would make targeted hormonal regulation impossible.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: receptor specificity determines which tissues are affected, which is why the same hormone produces different responses in different places.

questions.concept: Hormones are chemical messengers released directly into the bloodstream and travel to distant target cells. Only cells with matching receptors detect and respond, so the same hormone produces different responses in different tissues.

questions.stem: A nurse is assigned four patients with endocrine disorders at the start of a shift and must decide what to assess first on each. Two have laboratory results pending and one has been increasingly drowsy overnight. Which questions guide her priorities? Select all that apply.

options.text: Are the ABCs affected, with a patent airway, adequate breathing, and stable circulation?
options.rationale: The first priority-setting question in any acute situation.

options.text: Are vital signs within a safe range, including blood pressure and temperature extremes?
options.rationale: Endocrine disorders produce hypertension, hypotension, tachycardia, and temperature extremes.

options.text: Is there altered mental status, confusion, or decreased level of consciousness?
options.rationale: A specified priority, and mental status change is often the first sign of a critical glucose or electrolyte value.

options.text: Determine how long the endocrine diagnosis has been present
options.rationale: Duration of a diagnosis does not determine acute priority. What is happening now does.

options.text: Confirm the patient has a follow-up appointment booked
options.rationale: A discharge consideration rather than a question that sets priority at the bedside.

options.text: Has the patient's gland disorder been present for more than a year?
options.rationale: Duration of the diagnosis does not determine acute priority. What is happening now does.

questions.takeaway: ABCs, vital signs, mental status, fluid and electrolytes, and glucose. Endocrine emergencies deteriorate rapidly. Endocrine priority questions: are the ABCs affected, are vital signs in a safe range, is there altered mental status, is there a fluid or electrolyte imbalance in sodium, potassium, or calcium, and is blood glucose at a critical level.
questions.strategy: Every question on this list asks what is happening now. The wrong option asks about history, which never sets acute priority.

strategies: Apply the ABCs
Priority key word

steps.detail: History does not determine acute priority.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Endocrine priority questions: are the ABCs affected, are vital signs in a safe range, is there altered mental status, is there a fluid or electrolyte imbalance in sodium, potassium, or calcium, and is blood glucose at a critical level.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old newly prescribed levothyroxine for hypothyroidism tells the nurse he plans to take it only on the days he feels sluggish, since he does not want to take medication he does not need. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Document that he is non-adherent with his prescribed regimen and notify the provider of his intent
options.rationale: Labels a misunderstanding as non-adherence before teaching has occurred.

options.text: Explain that consistent daily dosing is essential for symptom control and preventing complications
options.rationale: Adherence is the nursing priority, and intermittent dosing leaves the deficiency untreated.

options.text: Tell him to take a double dose on the days he feels sluggish to compensate for the missed doses
options.rationale: Improvises a dose and risks overtreatment.

options.text: Agree with his plan, since the dose can reasonably be adjusted according to how he feels each day
options.rationale: Self-titrating a hormone replacement by symptom leaves the level unstable.

questions.takeaway: Levothyroxine requires consistent daily dosing. Symptoms are not a guide to whether the dose is needed. Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine, and consistent daily dosing is essential for symptom control and preventing complications. Myxedema coma is a rare but life-threatening complication of severe untreated hypothyroidism.
questions.strategy: Untreated severe hypothyroidism can progress to myxedema coma, which is why adherence is a safety issue rather than a compliance one.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: Both let symptoms set the dose.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: adherence is the nursing priority, and intermittent dosing leaves the deficiency untreated.

questions.concept: Hypothyroidism is treated with levothyroxine, and consistent daily dosing is essential for symptom control and preventing complications. Myxedema coma is a rare but life-threatening complication of severe untreated hypothyroidism.

skills.title: Donning and Doffing PPE
skills.subtitle: Standard, contact, droplet, and airborne precautions and the sequences that keep them working

questions.stem: A nurse is leaving the room of a patient on contact and droplet precautions. She is wearing a gown, gloves, a surgical mask, and a face shield. Which item does she remove FIRST?

options.text: The mask
options.rationale: Removed last of the PPE items, before the final hand hygiene.

options.text: The gloves
options.rationale: The outside of the gloves is the most contaminated surface, so they come off first using a glove-in-glove or pinch-pull method.

options.text: The gown
options.rationale: Removed after the gloves, touching only the inside.

options.text: The face shield
options.rationale: Removed after the gown, by the headband or earpieces.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews four handwritten orders during a system downtime. Which is written correctly and safely?

questions.stem: A nurse reviews abnormal lung sounds with a student before a clinical shift on a respiratory unit, where four patients have different presentations. The student asks how to tell the sounds apart at the bedside. Which descriptions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Crackles result from sudden reinflation of groups of alveoli and are not cleared by coughing
