options.rationale: Massage is avoided after several injections, including anticoagulants, and it is not a comfort measure.

options.text: Insert the needle slowly to reduce the sensation
options.rationale: The needle is inserted smoothly and quickly. Slow insertion prolongs the discomfort.

questions.takeaway: Shortest, smallest, sharpest needle. Change it if coated. Relax the limb, divert attention, and numb the site. Insert quickly, inject slowly. To minimize discomfort: use a sharp, beveled needle of the shortest length and smallest gauge, change the needle if medication coats the shaft, position and flex the limb to reduce muscular tension, divert the patient's attention, and apply a vapocoolant spray, topical anesthetic, or wrapped ice before injection. Insert the needle smoothly and quickly and inject the medication slowly.
questions.strategy: Insert quickly and inject slowly is the pairing to remember. Reversing either one increases pain, and students frequently reverse both.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Insertion is smooth and quick; the injection is what goes slowly.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: To minimize discomfort: use a sharp, beveled needle of the shortest length and smallest gauge, change the needle if medication coats the shaft, position and flex the limb to reduce muscular tension, divert the patient's attention, and apply a vapocoolant spray, topical anesthetic, or wrapped ice before injection. Insert the needle smoothly and quickly and inject the medication slowly.

questions.stem: A nurse precepts a student who is preparing several injections for the morning round and describes her technique for each as she works. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I do not expel the air bubble from a low-molecular-weight heparin prefilled syringe."
options.rationale: Accurate. The bubble is part of the dose.

options.text: "I aspirate before every subcutaneous injection to make sure I am not in a vessel."
options.rationale: Aspiration is not required for subcutaneous injection. It is a step imported from intramuscular technique.

options.text: "I insert the needle quickly and inject the medication slowly."
options.rationale: Accurate, and reversing either one increases pain.

options.text: "I withdraw an ampule dose through a filter needle and change it before injecting."
options.rationale: Accurate. The filter prevents glass fragments being drawn up and is used in one direction only.

questions.takeaway: Do not aspirate for subcutaneous injection. Insert quickly, inject slowly, withdraw at the insertion angle.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is careful and belongs to a different route. That is what makes it convincing.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Match the step to the route

steps.detail: LMWH bubble, speed, and filter needle are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: subcutaneous injection does not require aspiration.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares an intramuscular vaccine for an 11-month-old using the vastus lateralis. Which syringe volume is appropriate?

options.text: 3 to 5 mL
options.rationale: Above the adult range and far beyond an infant's.

options.text: 0.1 mL
options.rationale: An intradermal volume, and this order is intramuscular.

options.text: 0.5 to 1 mL
options.rationale: Infants and small children receive smaller intramuscular volumes because the available muscle mass is limited.

options.text: 2 to 3 mL
options.rationale: The adult range, and it exceeds what an infant's muscle can accommodate.

questions.takeaway: Intramuscular syringe volume is 2 to 3 mL for adults and 0.5 to 1 mL for infants and small children.
questions.strategy: Muscle mass sets the ceiling. The same principle changes needle length by site and by patient size, which is why the intramuscular figures are given as ranges.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An intradermal volume, and this order is intramuscular.
The adult range, and it exceeds what an infant's muscle can accommodate.
Above the adult range and far beyond an infant's.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: infants and small children receive smaller intramuscular volumes because the available muscle mass is limited.

questions.concept: Intramuscular syringe volume is 2 to 3 mL for adults and 0.5 to 1 mL for infants and small children.

questions.stem: A thick intramuscular antibiotic is ordered for an adult using the ventrogluteal site. The patient is of average build and the ordered volume is 2 mL. Which needle and angle are correct?

options.text: A 27 gauge, 3/8 inch needle inserted at 15 degrees, which limits discomfort during administration
options.rationale: Intradermal equipment and angle.

options.text: A 20 gauge, 1.5 inch needle inserted at 45 degrees, which reduces the depth of tissue penetration
options.rationale: The needle is right and the angle is not. Intramuscular is 90 degrees.

options.text: A 20 to 25 gauge, 1 to 1.5 inch needle at 90 degrees
options.rationale: Intramuscular injection requires enough length to reach muscle and a large enough bore for thicker medications.

options.text: A 30 gauge, 5/8 inch needle inserted at 45 degrees, which is the finest needle available
options.rationale: Subcutaneous equipment and angle.

questions.takeaway: Intramuscular: 90 degrees, 2 to 3 mL syringe for adults, 20 to 25 gauge, 1 to 1.5 inch. Used for most vaccines, antibiotics, and thicker medications. Intramuscular: angle 90 degrees, 2 to 3 mL syringe for adults and 0.5 to 1 mL for infants and small children, 20 to 25 gauge needle, 1 to 1.5 inch depending on site and patient size.
questions.strategy: Option B is the closest wrong answer. Correct equipment at the wrong angle deposits an intramuscular dose into subcutaneous tissue, where it absorbs differently and hurts more.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves C: intramuscular injection requires enough length to reach muscle and a large enough bore for thicker medications.

questions.concept: Intramuscular: angle 90 degrees, 2 to 3 mL syringe for adults and 0.5 to 1 mL for infants and small children, 20 to 25 gauge needle, 1 to 1.5 inch depending on site and patient size. Used for most vaccines, antibiotics, and thicker medications.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares a medication supplied in a single-dose glass ampule with a pre-scored neck. She has gathered her supplies and is working at the medication preparation area. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Tap or flick the top of the ampule to move fluid out of the neck before opening
options.rationale: Medication trapped above the neck is lost when the top is snapped off.

options.text: Protect the fingers with gauze or an alcohol pad when snapping the top
options.rationale: The glass breaks at the scored neck and the edges are sharp.

options.text: Use a filter needle to withdraw the medication
options.rationale: Snapping the neck can release glass fragments into the solution, and the filter prevents them being drawn up.

options.text: Change to a regular needle before administering the dose
options.rationale: A filter needle is used to withdraw and never to inject.

options.text: Dispose of the ampule in the regular waste bin
options.rationale: Broken glass goes into the sharps container.

questions.takeaway: Clear the neck, protect your fingers, withdraw through a filter needle, change the needle before injecting, and dispose of the glass in sharps.
questions.strategy: The filter needle is the step most often missed, and it is used in one direction only: withdraw through it, then change it before the dose goes anywhere near a patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.stem: A nurse is to give NPH and regular insulin together in one syringe for a patient's morning dose. She has rolled the NPH vial and injected air into both vials. Which medication does she withdraw first?

options.text: The regular insulin, because it is clear and clear is drawn before cloudy
options.rationale: Drawing the clear insulin first prevents the cloudy suspension contaminating the clear vial.

options.text: Neither, because regular and NPH insulin cannot be combined in the same syringe
options.rationale: Regular and NPH may be mixed. Long-acting insulins such as glargine and detemir may not.

options.text: Either insulin may be drawn first, as long as the total volume in the syringe is correct
options.rationale: Order matters because contamination runs one way.

options.text: The NPH, because the cloudy suspension must be resuspended and drawn before the clear insulin
options.rationale: The NPH is rolled before drawing and it is still withdrawn second.

questions.takeaway: Clear before cloudy. Regular is drawn before NPH, and long-acting insulins are never mixed at all. Clear before cloudy: regular insulin is withdrawn before NPH when the two are mixed in one syringe. Long-acting insulins such as glargine and detemir are never mixed with any other insulin.
questions.strategy: The rule protects the clear vial. If cloudy suspension enters it, every subsequent dose drawn from that vial is altered.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Regular is clear, NPH is cloudy.
Rolling happens before drawing; the order is unchanged.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: regular first.

questions.concept: Clear before cloudy: regular insulin is withdrawn before NPH when the two are mixed in one syringe. Long-acting insulins such as glargine and detemir are never mixed with any other insulin.

questions.stem: A nurse must combine a medication supplied in a vial with a medication supplied in a glass ampule, giving both in one syringe. Both are ordered at the same time and are compatible. Which sequence is correct?

options.text: Withdraw from the ampule first, then inject air into the vial and withdraw the second medication
options.rationale: Injecting air into the vial with ampule medication already in the syringe risks pushing it into the vial.

options.text: Draw both medications without a filter needle, since they are being combined in one syringe anyway
options.rationale: The ampule still requires a filter needle regardless of what else is in the syringe.

options.text: Prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule
options.rationale: The vial requires air injection before withdrawal, and doing it first avoids introducing the ampule medication into the vial.

options.text: Use separate syringes for each medication and combine the two doses immediately before injecting
options.rationale: Adds a transfer step and a contamination opportunity.

questions.takeaway: Vial first, then the ampule, using the same syringe and filter needle. When mixing medications from a vial and an ampule, prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule.
questions.strategy: The order follows from the mechanics: vials need air injected in, ampules do not. Whatever needs air pushed into it goes first.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: The vial, because it is sealed.
Air injection with medication already drawn risks contaminating the vial.
The ampule always needs a filter needle.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: the vial requires air injection before withdrawal, and doing it first avoids introducing the ampule medication into the vial.

questions.concept: When mixing medications from a vial and an ampule, prepare the medication from the vial first, then use the same syringe and filter needle to withdraw from the ampule.

questions.stem: A nurse reviews needlestick prevention with a student after a colleague on another unit sustained an injury while disposing of a used syringe. Which statements and actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers
options.rationale: Which is why the prevention measures are federally mandated.

options.text: Injuries occur when workers recap needles, mishandle lines and needles, or leave needles at the bedside
options.rationale: Recapping, mishandling lines, and leaving sharps loose are where most needlesticks happen, and all three are avoidable.

options.text: Use sharps with engineered sharps injury protection, such as safety syringes and blunt-end cannulas
options.rationale: Required under the Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act.

options.text: Dispose of sharps in a puncture-proof, leak-proof container that stands upright and is labeled with the biohazard symbol
options.rationale: And the container is never overfilled.

options.text: Recap the needle carefully with one hand before disposal
options.rationale: Recapping is a cause of needlestick injury. The needle goes straight into the container.

questions.takeaway: Never recap. Use engineered safety devices, and dispose into an upright, puncture-proof container that is not overfilled. Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers and occur through recapping, mishandling lines and needles, and leaving needles at the bedside. The Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act mandates sharps with engineered sharps injury protection. Sharps containers are puncture-proof, leak-proof, upright, labeled with the biohazard symbol, and never overfilled.
questions.strategy: The wrong option describes a technique taught as safer recapping. It is still recapping, which is one of the three causes.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Recapping, mishandling, leaving needles at the bedside.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Needlestick injuries are the most frequent route of exposure to bloodborne disease for health care workers and occur through recapping, mishandling lines and needles, and leaving needles at the bedside. The Needlestick Safety and Prevention Act mandates sharps with engineered sharps injury protection. Sharps containers are puncture-proof, leak-proof, upright, labeled with the biohazard symbol, and never overfilled.

questions.stem: A nurse uses the Z-track method to administer an intramuscular medication known to be irritating to subcutaneous tissue. A student asks why she displaces the skin before inserting the needle. What is the purpose of this technique?

options.text: To reduce the depth the needle must travel before reaching the muscle tissue beneath
options.rationale: The needle still enters at 90 degrees to reach muscle.

options.text: To eliminate the need to rotate injection sites between doses of the same medication
options.rationale: Sites are rotated regardless, to prevent induration and abscess formation.

options.text: To allow a larger volume of medication to be given safely in one injection site
options.rationale: Volume limits are set by the muscle mass, not by the technique.

options.text: To keep the medication in the muscle and prevent it tracking back into subcutaneous tissue
options.rationale: Displacing the skin before injection means the tissue layers no longer line up when released, sealing the medication in the muscle.

questions.takeaway: The Z-track method keeps intramuscular medication in the muscle and prevents it tracking back into the subcutaneous tissue layer above.
questions.strategy: Medication that tracks back into subcutaneous tissue irritates it and absorbs at the wrong rate, so the technique protects both comfort and the intended action.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
elimination.verdict: That leaves D: displacing the skin before injection means the tissue layers no longer line up when released, sealing the medication in the muscle.

questions.concept: The Z-track method keeps intramuscular medication in the muscle and prevents it tracking back into the subcutaneous tissue layer above.

questions.stem: A student notices that an intramuscular antibiotic is drawn with a 21 gauge needle while an insulin dose uses a 29 gauge, and asks whether the larger number means a larger needle. Which explanation is accurate?

options.text: A smaller gauge number means a finer needle, which is gentler on the dense tissue of a muscle
options.rationale: Reverses the relationship.

options.text: Gauge is selected according to the patient's body weight rather than the medication being given
options.rationale: Needle length may vary with body size; the gauge follows the medication and the route.

options.text: Gauge describes the length of the needle rather than the width of its bore or lumen
options.rationale: Length is stated separately in inches.

options.text: A smaller gauge number means a larger bore, which thicker medications require
options.rationale: Gauge runs inversely to diameter. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.

questions.takeaway: Needle gauge runs inversely to bore: the smaller the number, the wider the needle. IM 20 to 25, SQ 25 to 30, ID 25 to 27. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25 gauge, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.
questions.strategy: This one relationship makes the three tables coherent. The route needing the thickest medication has the lowest numbers.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Length and body size are separate considerations.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: gauge runs inversely to diameter.

questions.concept: Needle gauge runs inversely to bore: the smaller the number, the wider the needle. Intramuscular uses 20 to 25 gauge, subcutaneous 25 to 30, and intradermal 25 to 27.

skills.title: Medication Administration and Safety
skills.subtitle: Legal responsibility, the ten rights, assessment before the dose, error response, and patient education

questions.stem: A nurse finishes teaching a 66-year-old about a newly prescribed medication before discharge. He nodded throughout the explanation and said it made sense, and she now wants to confirm he actually understood. Which question is most effective?

options.text: "Do you have any questions about what we covered today?"
options.rationale: Useful and it confirms nothing about what he retained.

options.text: "Do you understand everything I have explained to you?"
options.rationale: A yes tells you nothing, and a patient who does not know what he does not know will say yes.

options.text: "I have gone through everything, so let me know if anything comes up."
options.rationale: Closes the exchange without checking anything.

options.text: "Can you tell me how you will take this when you get home?"
options.rationale: Teach-back asks the patient to describe the plan, and phrasing it as a check on the nurse's explanation removes the sense of.

questions.takeaway: Do not ask whether they understand. Ask them to tell you how they will take it. Teach-back asks the patient to explain how they will take the medication rather than whether they understand. Cover what the medication is, why they are taking it, how and when to take it, what to expect, and when to call.
questions.strategy: The phrasing matters as much as the technique. Framing it as checking your own explanation makes it easier for a patient to admit he is unsure.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.detail: One returns a description; three return yes or nothing.
Both can be answered without understanding.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: teach-back asks the patient to describe the plan, and phrasing it as a check on the nurse's explanation removes the sense of.

questions.concept: Teach-back asks the patient to explain how they will take the medication rather than whether they understand. Cover what the medication is, why they are taking it, how and when to take it, what to expect, and when to call.

questions.stem: A scheduled morning medication is due for a patient admitted two days ago with a changing clinical picture. Before she goes into the room she considers what she needs to know. Which assessments come before administration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Allergies
options.rationale: Checked before every medication, every time.

options.text: Vital signs and relevant laboratory values
options.rationale: Both may contain a parameter that decides whether the dose goes ahead.

options.text: Level of consciousness and ability to swallow
options.rationale: Both determine whether the route is safe for this patient right now.

options.text: Confirm the patient's insurance covers the medication
options.rationale: An access consideration at discharge rather than an assessment before this dose.

options.text: Verify the medication was dispensed by the hospital pharmacy
options.rationale: Dispensing source is not among the assessments made before administration.

options.text: Whether the medication is on the unit's formulary
options.rationale: An availability question rather than a clinical assessment of this patient.

questions.takeaway: Before you give: allergies, vital signs, relevant labs, pain, level of consciousness, swallowing, current medications, indication, and previous response. Assess before administration: allergies, vital signs, relevant laboratory values, pain level, level of consciousness, swallowing ability, relevant physical assessment, current medications, the indication, and the previous response.
questions.strategy: Each of these can stop the dose. That is what makes it an assessment rather than a formality.

strategies: Assessment before intervention

steps.action: Ask what could stop the dose

steps.detail: Coverage matters at discharge, not before this dose.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Assess before administration: allergies, vital signs, relevant laboratory values, pain level, level of consciousness, swallowing ability, relevant physical assessment, current medications, the indication, and the previous response.

questions.stem: A nurse realizes she has administered a scheduled medication to the wrong patient during the morning round. The patient is alert, has no symptoms, and the drug is not one he takes. Which action does she take FIRST?

options.text: Assess the patient
options.rationale: Assessment comes before notification, documentation, and reporting, because it establishes whether the patient needs immediate protection.

options.text: Notify the provider and the charge nurse
options.rationale: Required, and it follows the assessment that tells you what to report.

options.text: Document the error in the patient's record
options.rationale: Documentation follows the assessment and the immediate response.

options.text: Complete the facility's safety report
options.rationale: Required, and it is not the first action.

questions.takeaway: Assess the patient, protect the patient, notify, follow policy, document, complete safety reporting, continue monitoring. After a medication error: assess the patient, protect the patient, notify the appropriate persons, follow facility policy, document appropriately, complete required safety reporting, and continue monitoring.
questions.strategy: Three of these four options are genuinely required. The key word FIRST separates sequence from content, and the patient comes before the paperwork every time.

strategies: Priority key word
Assessment before intervention

steps.detail: Seven steps, beginning with the patient.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: assess the patient.

questions.concept: After a medication error: assess the patient, protect the patient, notify the appropriate persons, follow facility policy, document appropriately, complete required safety reporting, and continue monitoring.

questions.stem: A nurse orients to a medical unit and reviews the medications that require additional safeguards, including those stored in the controlled substance cabinet. The unit stocks insulin, opioids, and anticoagulants. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes are high-alert medications
options.rationale: Errors with these may cause significant patient harm.

options.text: The DEA regulates controlled substances including opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, and certain sedatives
options.rationale: Under the Controlled Substances Act.

options.text: Nursing responsibilities for controlled substances include secure storage and accurate counts
options.rationale: Along with accurate documentation and waste procedures.

options.text: Nurses are responsible for recognizing and preventing diversion
options.rationale: Nurses are the ones close enough to notice discrepancies in counts, wastage, or a colleague's behavior, so recognizing diversion falls to them.

options.text: High-alert medications are those most frequently prescribed on the unit
options.rationale: Frequency is not the criterion. The criterion is the severity of harm when an error occurs.

questions.takeaway: High alert means the harm is severe when an error occurs, not that the drug is dangerous or common. High-alert medications include insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes. The DEA regulates controlled substances including opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, and certain sedatives, and nursing responsibilities include secure storage, accurate counts, accurate documentation and waste procedures, and recognizing and preventing diversion.
questions.strategy: Insulin appears on both lists: high-alert here, and the medication with its own safety checks in the glucose material. That is not a coincidence.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Severity of harm, not frequency of use.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: High-alert medications include insulin, opioids, anticoagulants, and concentrated electrolytes. The DEA regulates controlled substances including opioids, stimulants, benzodiazepines, and certain sedatives, and nursing responsibilities include secure storage, accurate counts, accurate documentation and waste procedures, and recognizing and preventing diversion.

questions.stem: One month into practice, a new graduate is asked by her manager to describe how she decides whether a dose is safe to give. Which statement by the new graduate indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "If all ten rights match, the dose is safe to give."
options.rationale: The ten rights check the order. Right medication plus wrong patient condition is unsafe administration, and the nurse integrates assessment, labs, vital signs, and clinical condition alongside the rights.

options.text: "Errors can occur at prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring."
options.rationale: Accurate. All six are points in the medication use process.

options.text: "I ask a patient to tell me how he will take it rather than whether he understands."
options.rationale: Accurate. Teach-back confirms understanding rather than agreement.

options.text: "After an error I assess the patient before I notify anyone."
options.rationale: Accurate. Assessment establishes whether the patient needs immediate protection.

questions.takeaway: The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. They check the order, not the patient.
questions.strategy: This is the central claim of the whole lecture, and the wrong statement is exactly what students conclude from learning the rights.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: The rights verify the order against the record.
Error response, error points, and teach-back are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: matching the rights does not make a dose safe.

questions.stem: A nurse receives an order she believes is inconsistent with the patient's current condition. A colleague tells her the provider wrote it, so the responsibility is his. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: The nurse may administer any order that is legible, complete, and signed
options.rationale: Legible and complete are two of six considerations, and appropriateness and safety are among the others.

options.text: The nurse determines whether the order is complete, appropriate, safe, and in scope
options.rationale: An order does not transfer responsibility. The nurse who administers answers for the administration.

options.text: The provider carries sole responsibility once the order is written
options.rationale: Prescribing and administering are separate acts and each carries its own accountability.

options.text: The nurse should administer the dose and document her concern afterward
options.rationale: Documents a concern about a dose she has already given.

questions.takeaway: An order is not a substitute for nursing judgment. Check that it is complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the condition, and within your scope.
questions.strategy: Six tests, and the two that catch most unsafe orders are appropriate and consistent with the patient's condition. The other four can all be satisfied by an order that should not be given.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Each act carries its own accountability.
One stops at legibility, one acts before questioning.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: an order does not transfer responsibility.

questions.concept: An order is not a substitute for nursing judgment. The nurse determines whether the order is complete, clear, appropriate, safe, consistent with the patient's condition, and within the nurse's scope.

questions.stem: A student tells the nurse she has learned the five traditional rights of medication administration and asks what the remaining rights cover. Which are among the additional rights? Select all that apply.

options.text: Right documentation
options.rationale: Covers what was given, when, and how the patient responded.

options.text: Right reason
options.rationale: Why this patient is receiving this drug, which is what makes the order make sense.

options.text: Right to refuse
options.rationale: The patient's right, and it belongs to the patient rather than the nurse.

options.text: Right prescriber
options.rationale: Verifying the prescriber's authority matters and is not one of the ten rights.

options.text: Right cost
options.rationale: Affordability affects adherence and is not one of the ten rights.

options.text: Right pharmacy
options.rationale: Where the drug was dispensed is not among the rights.

questions.takeaway: Ten rights: patient, medication, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response, education, and the right to refuse.
questions.strategy: Three distractors are real considerations that are not rights. The additional five describe what happens around the dose, plus one that belongs to the patient.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.action: Recall the five beyond the traditional

steps.detail: Cost affects adherence rather than being a right.

elimination.verdict: A, B, and C are selected.

questions.concept: The ten rights: right patient, medication, dose, route, time, documentation, reason, response, education, and the right to refuse.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old has a scheduled order for metoprolol 50 mg orally daily. At the time the dose is due his blood pressure is 88/52 and his apical rate is 54. The order is complete and all ten rights match. Which action does the nurse take?

options.text: Administer half of the ordered dose to reduce the effect on his heart rate
options.rationale: Altering a prescribed dose is outside nursing scope and improvises a decision that belongs to the prescriber.

options.text: Document that the patient refused the medication and notify the provider
options.rationale: The patient has not refused. Recording a refusal that did not occur falsifies the record.

options.text: Hold the dose, notify the provider, and document the assessment
options.rationale: The right medication given to a patient in the wrong condition is unsafe administration. Metoprolol lowers both blood pressure and heart rate, and both are already low.

options.text: Administer the dose, since all ten rights have been verified
options.rationale: The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. Matching every right does not make a dose safe.

questions.takeaway: Right medication plus wrong patient condition equals unsafe administration. The ten rights do not replace assessment. The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. The nurse integrates assessment, medication knowledge, labs, vital signs, clinical condition, provider orders, and nursing judgment.
questions.strategy: This is the scenario the whole lecture is built around. Every right can match and the dose can still be wrong, because the rights check the order rather than the patient.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Both already low, and the drug lowers both further.
Rights verified does not equal safe.
One alters the dose, one falsifies the record.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: hold, notify, document.

questions.concept: The ten rights are not a substitute for assessment. Right medication plus wrong patient condition equals unsafe administration. The nurse integrates assessment, medication knowledge, labs, vital signs, clinical condition, provider orders, and nursing judgment.

questions.stem: A quality committee maps every point in the medication use process where an error can occur, from the moment an order is written to the follow-up after a dose is given. Which set is correct?

options.text: Administering only, since that is the final step
options.rationale: The final step is where errors become visible, not where they all originate.

options.text: Prescribing and administering only, since those are the two clinical decisions
options.rationale: Omits four points where errors regularly originate.

options.text: Prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring
options.rationale: Six points, and the nurse is involved in the last three as well as in verifying the first.

options.text: Dispensing and administering only, since those involve the pharmacy and nurse
options.rationale: Two of the six points, and errors at prescribing, transcribing, or monitoring reach the patient just as easily.

questions.takeaway: Medication errors can occur at six points: prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring.
questions.strategy: Monitoring is the one people forget. An error can occur after the dose is given, by failing to watch for the response the drug required.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false
Global or umbrella option

steps.detail: Each omits points where errors originate.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: six points, and the nurse is involved in the last three as well as in verifying the first.

questions.concept: Medication errors can occur at six points: prescribing, transcribing, dispensing, preparing, administering, and monitoring.

questions.stem: A 67-year-old declines his scheduled antihypertensive, saying it makes him dizzy and he would rather manage without it today. He is alert and understands he has high blood pressure. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Determine why he is refusing
options.rationale: The reason is clinically useful and often solvable.

options.text: Assess his understanding of the medication
options.rationale: A refusal frequently reflects a gap in what he has been told.

options.text: Provide education and respect his right to refuse
options.rationale: The right to refuse is one of the ten rights.

options.text: Notify the provider when indicated and document according to policy
options.rationale: The prescriber needs to know, and the record needs the refusal and the reason.

options.text: Conceal the medication in food so the dose is not missed
options.rationale: Covert administration removes his decision entirely.

options.text: Document that the patient is non-compliant
options.rationale: Automatically recording non-compliance labels a decision rather than describing it, and it discards the reason he gave.

questions.takeaway: Do not force, hide, shame, or automatically label. Determine why, assess understanding, educate, respect the right, notify, and document. If a patient refuses: do not force the medication, hide it in food, shame the patient, or automatically document non-compliant. Determine why, assess understanding, educate, respect the right to refuse, notify the provider when indicated, and document according to policy.
questions.strategy: Non-compliant is the entry to avoid. It converts a reason you could have acted on into a judgment about the patient.

strategies: Patient-centered option

steps.action: Read the four things not to do

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: If a patient refuses: do not force the medication, hide it in food, shame the patient, or automatically document non-compliant. Determine why, assess understanding, educate, respect the right to refuse, notify the provider when indicated, and document according to policy.

questions.stem: A patient taking an antihistamine for allergic rhinitis reports his sneezing and congestion have improved and that he feels drowsy every afternoon. Which terms describe these two outcomes?

options.text: Side effect and toxic effect
options.rationale: Symptom relief is the intended response rather than a side effect.

options.text: Therapeutic effect and side effect
options.rationale: The therapeutic effect is the desired response. A side effect is an expected secondary effect.

options.text: Therapeutic effect and adverse effect
options.rationale: An adverse effect is harmful or unwanted. Expected drowsiness from an antihistamine is a side effect.

options.text: Adverse effect and toxic effect
options.rationale: Neither describes the symptom relief, which is what was intended.

questions.takeaway: Therapeutic effect is the desired response. A side effect is an expected secondary effect. Adverse is harmful. A toxic effect is an excessive drug effect or toxicity. An adverse effect is a harmful or unwanted response.
questions.strategy: Side and adverse are the pair students blur. Expectedness separates them: a known secondary effect is a side effect, and a harmful unwanted response is adverse.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: An adverse effect is harmful or unwanted.
Symptom relief is the intended response rather than a side effect.
Neither describes the symptom relief, which is what was intended.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: the therapeutic effect is the desired response.

questions.concept: Therapeutic effect is the desired response. A side effect is an expected secondary effect. An adverse effect is a harmful or unwanted response. A toxic effect is an excessive drug effect or toxicity.

skills.title: Personal Hygiene, Perineal Care, and Bedmaking
skills.subtitle: Bathing and CHG, oral and hair care, catheter care, enemas, and occupied and unoccupied beds

questions.stem: A nurse performs catheter care for a 53-year-old with an indwelling urinary catheter inserted three days ago. The meatus is intact with no discharge and the patient reports no discomfort. In which direction does she clean the catheter?

options.text: From the drainage tubing back toward the meatus, in one continuous motion
options.rationale: Moves organisms along the catheter toward the urinary tract.

options.text: From the meatus outward for about four inches, without pulling or creating friction
options.rationale: Cleaning away from the meatus moves organisms away from the entry point rather than toward it, which is the cleanest-to-dirtiest principle applied to this site.

options.text: Only at the meatus itself, leaving the catheter surface untouched
options.rationale: The first few inches of catheter carry organisms toward the meatus and are cleaned.

options.text: In a back-and-forth motion along the length of the catheter
options.rationale: Returns the cloth to the meatus after it has been soiled, and the friction irritates the tissue.

questions.takeaway: Clean from the meatus outward for about four inches. Cleanest to dirtiest, always moving away from the entry point. Catheter care: assess the meatus and surrounding skin for redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, or discomfort, perform perineal hygiene with 2% chlorhexidine cloth or mild soap and warm water, and clean the catheter from the meatus outward for about four inches without pulling or friction.
questions.strategy: The whole of hygiene runs on one principle: cleanest to dirtiest. Catheter care is that principle applied to the shortest route into the bladder.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Cleanest to dirtiest means away from the meatus.
Both return organisms toward the meatus.
The proximal catheter is cleaned too.

elimination.verdict: That leaves B: cleaning away from the meatus moves organisms away from the entry point rather than toward it, which is the cleanest-to-dirtiest principle applied to this site.

questions.concept: Catheter care: assess the meatus and surrounding skin for redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, or discomfort, perform perineal hygiene with 2% chlorhexidine cloth or mild soap and warm water, and clean the catheter from the meatus outward for about four inches without pulling or friction.

questions.stem: A nurse gives a bed bath to a 90-year-old who tires quickly and has fragile skin over her shoulders and sacrum. She has been in bed for four days and her daughter is visiting. Which principles apply? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use lukewarm water and mild cleansers to prevent irritation
options.rationale: Hot water and harsh cleansers dry and damage skin.

options.text: Avoid excessive force and friction
options.rationale: Both damage skin that is already fragile in a dependent patient.

options.text: Bathe the patient at the same time each day regardless of tolerance
options.rationale: Timing is matched to the patient rather than to the routine.

options.text: Encourage normal range of motion during bathing
options.rationale: Movement that would otherwise require a separate intervention.

options.text: Use hot water to improve circulation during the bath
options.rationale: Lukewarm water is used. Hot water damages fragile skin and is unsafe.

options.text: Use a single basin of water for the whole bath
options.rationale: Water contaminated early in the bath is carried to every later area, including the perineum.

questions.takeaway: Lukewarm water, mild cleanser, minimal friction, assess while you bathe, encourage movement, and match the bath to the patient's tolerance. Bathing principles: clean skin when soiled and at regular intervals, use lukewarm water and mild cleansers, avoid excessive force and friction, minimize factors that dry the skin, use the bath to interact with and assess the patient, encourage range of motion, and consider a partial bath for a patient who fatigues easily.
questions.strategy: Three separate things happen during a bath: hygiene, skin assessment, and range of motion. That is why it is worth doing well rather than quickly.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A full bath regardless of tolerance ignores what the stem tells you.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: Bathing principles: clean skin when soiled and at regular intervals, use lukewarm water and mild cleansers, avoid excessive force and friction, minimize factors that dry the skin, use the bath to interact with and assess the patient, encourage range of motion, and consider a partial bath for a patient who fatigues easily.

questions.stem: A patient is being transferred from the emergency department by stretcher after a fall and will arrive on the unit within the hour. The bed is empty and the linen has been changed. How does the nurse prepare the bed?

options.text: As an occupied bed, with the patient already lying in it
options.rationale: An occupied bed is made with a patient already in it.

options.text: It does not matter, as long as the linen is clean
options.rationale: The preparation determines how easily and safely the transfer can be made.

options.text: As a closed bed, with the top sheets pulled up to the head of the bed
options.rationale: A closed bed is usually made by housekeeping after discharge and is not prepared for an arriving patient.

options.text: As an open bed, with the top sheets fanfolded lengthwise and not tucked in
options.rationale: An open bed is prepared for immediate use, and fanfolding the linen allows transfer from a stretcher without fighting tucked bedding.

questions.takeaway: Open bed: fanfolded, untucked, ready for immediate use. Closed bed: top sheets up, made after discharge. An open bed is prepared for immediate use with the top sheets fanfolded lengthwise and not tucked in, to ease transfer from a stretcher. A closed bed has the top sheets pulled up to the head and is usually made after discharge.
questions.strategy: The distinction is about the next few minutes. An open bed says someone is arriving now; a closed bed says the room is waiting.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A patient arriving by stretcher within the hour.
A closed bed is for an empty room.
One requires a patient present, one ignores the transfer.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: an open bed.

questions.concept: An open bed is prepared for immediate use with the top sheets fanfolded lengthwise and not tucked in, to ease transfer from a stretcher. A closed bed has the top sheets pulled up to the head and is usually made after discharge.

questions.stem: A nurse changes the linen for a 51-year-old who cannot tolerate being out of bed after hip surgery. The bed is at its lowest position and one other staff member is available to help. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Identify how many additional people are needed before starting
options.rationale: Work out how many people you need before you start. Discovering it halfway through leaves the patient unsupported.

options.text: Tell the patient what you are going to do before moving him
options.rationale: Communication before movement is specified, and it is what allows him to help rather than resist.

options.text: Lower the bed fully before beginning the linen change
options.rationale: The bed is raised to a comfortable working height while working, then lowered before leaving.

options.text: Keep the back straight, bend the knees, and avoid twisting
options.rationale: A straight back with bent knees puts the load through your legs, and twisting under load is what injures backs.

options.text: Remove the pillow so the sheet lies flat
options.rationale: Removing support after hip surgery adds discomfort without helping the linen change.

options.text: Work quickly without involving the patient, to shorten the procedure
options.rationale: Patient self-help is encouraged as much as possible, and it preserves both function and dignity.

questions.takeaway: Plan the help, raise the bed, communicate before you move him, keep him covered, and let him help. For an occupied bed: identify how many additional people are needed, encourage patient self-help, raise the bed to a comfortable working height, keep the back straight and knees bent while avoiding twisting, keep the patient covered as much as possible, and communicate before moving the patient.
questions.strategy: Every one of these protects something different: the nurse's back, the patient's dignity, his warmth, and his sense of control over what is happening to him.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: People, height, and what you will say.
Self-help is encouraged rather than bypassed.

elimination.verdict: A, B and D are selected.

questions.concept: For an occupied bed: identify how many additional people are needed, encourage patient self-help, raise the bed to a comfortable working height, keep the back straight and knees bent while avoiding twisting, keep the patient covered as much as possible, and communicate before moving the patient.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old reports a hard, painful stool he has been unable to pass for two days despite a stool softener. Which type of enema is indicated?

options.text: Mineral oil
options.rationale: Its action is lubrication rather than volume, which is what a hard impacted stool requires.

options.text: Medicated
options.rationale: Delivers a drug rather than addressing the consistency of the stool.

options.text: Tap water
options.rationale: Uses volume to stimulate peristalsis and does not soften a hard stool already in place.

options.text: Soapsuds
options.rationale: Also acts by volume and irritation rather than by lubricating the stool.

questions.takeaway: Enemas promote defecation by stimulating peristalsis. Tap water flushes with volume; mineral oil coats and lubricates hard stool. An enema instills solution into the rectum and sigmoid colon and promotes defecation by stimulating peristalsis. A tap water enema flushes the colon with a large volume of plain water. A mineral oil enema coats and lubricates a hard, painful stool. Medicated enemas must be administered by a nurse.
questions.strategy: Match the mechanism to the problem. Volume moves stool that can move; lubrication is for stool that cannot.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Hard, painful stool that will not pass.
Uses volume to stimulate peristalsis and does not soften a hard stool already in place.
Also acts by volume and irritation rather than by lubricating the stool.
Delivers a drug rather than addressing the consistency of the stool.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: its action is lubrication rather than volume, which is what a hard impacted stool requires.

questions.concept: An enema instills solution into the rectum and sigmoid colon and promotes defecation by stimulating peristalsis. A tap water enema flushes the colon with a large volume of plain water. A mineral oil enema coats and lubricates a hard, painful stool. Medicated enemas must be administered by a nurse.

questions.stem: Assistive personnel describe their plan for hygiene and catheter care on a unit where several patients have indwelling catheters. The AP describes how she plans to manage the drainage systems during the shift. Which statement by the assistive personnel indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I will empty the bag when it is about half full."
options.rationale: Accurate. A full bag becomes heavy and may rise or pull.

options.text: "I will hang the drainage bag on the side rail so it is easy to reach."
options.rationale: A side rail moves with position changes, which can lift the bag above bladder level or pull on the catheter. The bag is kept below the bladder and off the floor.

options.text: "I will tell the nurse if the patient's skin around the catheter looks red."
options.rationale: Accurate. Redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, and discomfort are all reported.

options.text: "I will clean from the meatus outward, not back toward it."
options.rationale: Accurate. Cleanest to dirtiest means moving away from the entry point.

questions.takeaway: Below the bladder, off the floor, and not on anything that moves.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement optimizes for convenience, and the side rail is the one surface in the room designed to move.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A side rail is raised and lowered.
Cleaning direction, emptying, and reporting are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: never hang the bag on a side rail.

questions.stem: A unit introduces daily 2% chlorhexidine gluconate bathing after a rise in central line infections. Staff ask how it differs from a standard soap and water bath and what it is expected to achieve. Which statements about this practice are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: It reduces skin bacteria and health care-associated infections
options.rationale: The purpose of the practice.

options.text: Chlorhexidine is effective against a broad range of bacteria
options.rationale: It works against a wide range of bacteria, which is why it is used before surgery rather than plain soap.

options.text: Preoperative chlorhexidine bathing can reduce surgical site infections
options.rationale: Bathing with it before an operation lowers the bacterial load on the skin, which is where surgical site infections start.

options.text: Rinse the chlorhexidine off with clear water after bathing
options.rationale: The residual chlorhexidine is what provides the continuing antimicrobial effect.

options.text: Apply chlorhexidine to the face and mucous membranes
options.rationale: Chlorhexidine is kept away from the face, the eyes, and mucous membranes, where it causes irritation and can damage the eye.

options.text: Chlorhexidine cloths must be used alongside a full soap and water bath each day
options.rationale: Disposable washcloths impregnated with chlorhexidine replace soap and water baths rather than supplementing them.

questions.takeaway: Daily 2% CHG bathing reduces skin bacteria, HAIs, surgical site infections, and CLABSIs, and it replaces the soap and water bath. Daily 2% chlorhexidine gluconate bathing reduces skin bacteria and health care-associated infections, is effective against a broad range of bacteria, reduces surgical site infections when used preoperatively, reduces central line-associated bloodstream infections, and reduces exposure from infected or colonized roommates and previous room occupants. CHG-impregnated disposable cloths replace soap and water baths.
questions.strategy: The roommate and previous occupant finding is the one worth carrying. It says the risk is not only what the patient brought with them.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Skin flora, HAIs, SSIs, CLABSIs, environmental exposure.
CHG cloths replace the soap and water bath.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Daily 2% chlorhexidine gluconate bathing reduces skin bacteria and health care-associated infections, is effective against a broad range of bacteria, reduces surgical site infections when used preoperatively, reduces central line-associated bloodstream infections, and reduces exposure from infected or colonized roommates and previous room occupants. CHG-impregnated disposable cloths replace soap and water baths.

questions.stem: A 72-year-old receiving anticoagulation therapy for a deep vein thrombosis asks the nurse to help him shave before his family visits. His platelet count is low and he has bruising on both forearms. Which action is correct?

options.text: Use an electric razor, because he is at risk for bleeding
options.rationale: An electric razor is used for any patient with bleeding tendencies. A blade razor risks a cut that will not stop readily.

options.text: Use a blade razor carefully with generous lather to soften the skin
options.rationale: Care and lather do not remove the risk of a cut in an anticoagulated patient.

options.text: Ask assistive personnel to shave him with a blade razor
options.rationale: Handing the task to someone else does not make the razor safer. The bleeding risk comes from the blade, whoever holds it.

options.text: Decline to shave him until the anticoagulant has been discontinued
options.rationale: Withholds routine hygiene when a safe alternative exists.

questions.takeaway: Use an electric razor for any patient at risk for bleeding tendencies. Review coagulation status and bleeding risk before oral care as well. Use an electric razor for any patient at risk for bleeding tendencies, and obtain consent before cutting or shaving hair.
questions.strategy: Bleeding risk changes the equipment for two hygiene tasks: shaving and oral care. Both involve tissue that bleeds readily and is easy to nick.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Technique does not remove the risk.
One withholds care, one transfers the same risk.

elimination.verdict: That leaves A: electric razor.

questions.concept: Use an electric razor for any patient at risk for bleeding tendencies, and obtain consent before cutting or shaving hair. Review coagulation status and bleeding risk before providing oral care.

questions.stem: A nurse prepares oral hygiene for a patient four days after a stroke who has a reduced gag reflex and a saturation of 94%. He is currently lying supine. Which position is appropriate?

options.text: Flat supine, with the head turned to one side
options.rationale: Flat positioning allows fluid to pool at the back of the throat.

options.text: Prone, to protect the airway
options.rationale: Not a workable position for oral care and does not protect the airway here.

options.text: Head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees
options.rationale: Elevating the head of the bed positions the patient so that fluid drains away from the airway rather than toward it.

options.text: Trendelenburg, so secretions drain out
options.rationale: Head-down positioning directs fluid toward the airway.

questions.takeaway: During oral hygiene, position the patient to avoid aspiration by keeping the head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees. Observe for bleeding of the oral mucosa or gums, reported pain, and changes in the oral mucosa.
questions.strategy: Oral care puts fluid in the mouth of someone who may not be able to protect the airway. Position is the intervention that makes the rest of it safe.

strategies: Apply the ABCs

steps.detail: Weakness plus a reduced gag reflex.
Both let fluid reach the airway.
Not a position for oral care.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: 30 to 45 degrees.

questions.concept: During oral hygiene, position the patient to avoid aspiration by keeping the head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees. Observe for bleeding of the oral mucosa or gums, reported pain, and changes in the oral mucosa.

questions.stem: A nurse checks a patient's indwelling catheter at 0700. The drainage bag holds 900 mL, is resting on the floor, and the tubing loops below the bag. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Assess the meatus and surrounding skin for redness, swelling, discharge, trauma, or discomfort
options.rationale: The five specified findings, and each is an early sign of a problem at the entry point.

options.text: Check the tubing for kinks, loops, and clamps and maintain unobstructed flow
options.rationale: Obstructed drainage backs urine up toward the bladder.

options.text: Keep the drainage bag below bladder level and off the floor
options.rationale: Below the bladder prevents backflow; off the floor prevents contamination.

options.text: Clamp the tubing when the patient ambulates
options.rationale: Clamping obstructs drainage. The bag is carried below bladder level instead.

options.text: Change the drainage bag daily to reduce infection
options.rationale: Routine bag changes break the closed system, which raises infection risk rather than lowering it.

options.text: Hang the drainage bag on the side rail for easy access
options.rationale: A side rail moves, which can lift the bag above the bladder or pull on the catheter.

questions.takeaway: Below the bladder, off the floor, no kinks, emptied at about half full, closed system maintained. Keep the drainage bag below bladder level and off the floor, check tubing for kinks, loops, and clamps, maintain unobstructed flow, empty the bag when about half full, and maintain the closed drainage system.
questions.strategy: Every rule here manages one of two risks: urine flowing back toward the bladder, or organisms entering a system that should stay closed.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: A moving rail can lift the bag above the bladder.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: Keep the drainage bag below bladder level and off the floor, check tubing for kinks, loops, and clamps, maintain unobstructed flow, empty the bag when about half full, and maintain the closed drainage system.

questions.stem: A nurse plans hygiene for four patients. Which patient requires perineal care more frequently than routine bathing provides?

options.text: A patient receiving oral antibiotics for a chest infection this week
options.rationale: Not among the indications.

options.text: A patient who is ambulatory, continent, and independent with hygiene
options.rationale: Routine hygiene is sufficient.

options.text: A patient with an indwelling urinary catheter and incontinence-associated dermatitis
options.rationale: Both are indications for more frequent perineal care, and they compound each other.

options.text: A patient with a well-healed abdominal scar from surgery ten years ago
options.rationale: An old, healed scar is not an indication.

questions.takeaway: Perineal care cleans the external genitalia and surrounding skin and is provided more frequently for patients with incontinence-associated dermatitis, an indwelling urinary catheter, or recovery from rectal or genital surgery.
questions.strategy: The three indications share one thing: skin in that area is either already damaged or has something passing through it that organisms can travel along.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Dermatitis, catheter, rectal or genital surgery.
An old scar and an unrelated infection.

elimination.verdict: That leaves C: two indications in one patient.

questions.concept: Perineal care cleans the external genitalia and surrounding skin and is provided more frequently for patients with incontinence-associated dermatitis, an indwelling urinary catheter, or recovery from rectal or genital surgery.

skills.title: Vital Signs
skills.subtitle: Temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, pulse oximetry, pain, and reading the trend

questions.stem: A nursing instructor reviews vital sign technique with a student after observing her assess two patients on a medical unit. She asks the student to describe how she obtained each measurement. Which student statement indicates a need for further teaching?

options.text: "I tell the patient I am counting respirations so he breathes normally for me."
options.rationale: Respiration is the one vital sign a patient can change voluntarily. Announcing it makes the breathing conscious and the count unreliable, which is why the fingers stay on the wrist.

options.text: "Nail polish, cold hands, and movement can all make pulse oximetry inaccurate."
options.rationale: Accurate, and poor perfusion will do the same thing.

options.text: "I compare a value to the patient's own baseline, not just to the normal range."
options.rationale: Accurate, and a trend is more valuable than a single reading.

options.text: "A cuff that is too small reads falsely high."
options.rationale: Accurate, and one that is too large reads falsely low.

questions.takeaway: Count respirations without the patient's awareness, for a full 60 seconds or 30 doubled if regular.
questions.strategy: The wrong statement is polite and it is the thing that invalidates the measurement.

strategies: Negative polarity
Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Only respiration can be altered voluntarily.
Cuff size, oximetry, and baseline comparison are correct.

elimination.verdict: A is the statement needing correction: do not announce a respiratory count.

questions.stem: Blood pressure is due on a patient who has just walked from the waiting room and is talking about his journey. Several cuff sizes are available and his sleeve is rolled tightly above the elbow. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: Have the patient seated and resting for five minutes beforehand
options.rationale: Recent activity raises the reading.

options.text: Support the arm at heart level
options.rationale: An arm above heart level reads low; below it reads high.

options.text: Have the patient sit with feet flat on the floor and legs uncrossed
options.rationale: Crossed legs raise the reading.

options.text: Have the patient hold the arm above heart level
options.rationale: An arm above heart level produces a falsely low reading. It is supported at heart level.

options.text: Inflate the cuff rapidly to 200 mm Hg for every patient
options.rationale: Inflating to a fixed high pressure is unnecessary and uncomfortable.

options.text: Take the reading over the patient's sleeve to save time
options.rationale: Constricting clothing is removed, because it alters the reading and interferes with the cuff.

questions.takeaway: Resting five minutes, arm at heart level, feet flat, legs uncrossed, no talking, no constricting clothing, and the right arm chosen. For accurate blood pressure: correct cuff size, arm supported at heart level, patient seated and resting five minutes, comfortable position, no talking, feet flat and legs uncrossed, constricting clothing removed. Avoid an arm with mastectomy, dialysis access, an intravenous line, or injury, and use a lower extremity when upper extremities are unavailable.
questions.strategy: Every item on this list moves the number in a predictable direction. A blood pressure obtained through a sleeve on a patient who has just walked in and is talking is not a measurement.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: Position, rest, clothing, and arm selection.

elimination.verdict: A, B and C are selected.

questions.concept: For accurate blood pressure: correct cuff size, arm supported at heart level, patient seated and resting five minutes, comfortable position, no talking, feet flat and legs uncrossed, constricting clothing removed. Avoid an arm with mastectomy, dialysis access, an intravenous line, or injury, and use a lower extremity when upper extremities are unavailable.

questions.stem: Over four hours a patient's pulse rises from 78 to 116 and his blood pressure falls from 128/76 to 96/58. His temperature is 37.1 C and he is alert. Which interpretation is correct?

options.text: Each reading is acceptable
options.rationale: Interpreting vital signs in isolation is what this pattern is designed to catch.

options.text: This reflects daily variation
options.rationale: Normal daily variation is a few beats and a few points. A 38 beat rise with a 32 point fall in four hours is a change, not variation.

options.text: The findings are unrelated
options.rationale: The two move together for a reason, and separating them loses the pattern.

options.text: The trend suggests shock
options.rationale: A rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure is the pattern of possible shock, and a trend is more valuable than any single reading.

questions.takeaway: Trends matter more than single readings. A rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure suggests possible shock. Compare vital signs to the patient's own baseline rather than to normal ranges alone, and identify trends suggesting deterioration. When a patient's condition worsens, monitor as often as every 5 to 15 minutes.
questions.strategy: Compare to the patient's own baseline rather than to a textbook range. Every value here could be called acceptable, and the direction of travel is what matters.

strategies: Priority key word

steps.detail: Heart rate up, blood pressure down, over four hours.
Interpreting vital signs in isolation is what this pattern is designed to catch.
The two move together for a reason, and separating them loses the pattern.
Daily variation does not produce a 38 beat rise alongside a 32 point systolic fall in four hours.

elimination.verdict: That leaves D: A rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure is the pattern of possible shock, and a trend is more valuable than any single reading.

questions.concept: Compare vital signs to the patient's own baseline rather than to normal ranges alone, and identify trends suggesting deterioration. A rising heart rate with a falling blood pressure suggests possible shock. When a patient's condition worsens, monitor as often as every 5 to 15 minutes.

questions.stem: A patient's pulse oximetry reads 84% while his respiratory rate is 16 and he is conversing comfortably. His hands are cold and his nails are painted. Which factors could explain an inaccurate reading? Select all that apply.

options.text: Nail polish on the finger being used
options.rationale: Interferes with light transmission through the nail bed.

options.text: Poor peripheral perfusion
options.rationale: The sensor needs pulsatile flow to read.

options.text: A cold extremity
options.rationale: A cold finger has less blood flowing through it, and the probe needs that flow to read a signal.

options.text: Motion artifact
options.rationale: Movement disrupts the waveform the sensor depends on.

options.text: The patient's alert and comfortable appearance
options.rationale: His appearance is a reason to question the reading rather than a cause of the inaccuracy.

questions.takeaway: Factors causing inaccurate pulse oximetry readings include nail polish, poor perfusion, cold extremities, and motion artifact. For a low reading: reposition, reassess, apply oxygen per order, and notify the provider.
questions.strategy: The reading and the patient disagree here. Reposition and reassess before acting, and do not dismiss the number either: apply oxygen per order and notify the provider if it persists.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: His appearance is the reason to check, not the cause.

elimination.verdict: A, B, C, and D are selected.

questions.concept: Factors causing inaccurate pulse oximetry readings include nail polish, poor perfusion, cold extremities, and motion artifact. For a low reading: reposition, reassess, apply oxygen per order, and notify the provider.

questions.stem: A nurse assesses a 74-year-old before ambulation. Lying: 132/78, pulse 72. After three minutes standing: 108/70, pulse 96. He reports feeling lightheaded. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: The findings are within expected limits
options.rationale: A drop of this size is not expected and carries a fall risk.

options.text: Further readings are needed to decide
options.rationale: The measurement has already been taken at the interval.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension is present
options.rationale: A drop of 20 mm Hg or more systolic, or 10 or more diastolic, within three minutes of standing. The systolic fell 24 points.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension is absent
options.rationale: The systolic criterion alone is sufficient and it has been met.

questions.takeaway: Orthostatic or postural hypotension is a drop of 20 mm Hg or more systolic, or 10 mm Hg or more diastolic, within three minutes of standing.
questions.strategy: Either number alone qualifies. Students look for both and conclude the criteria are not met when one of them is.

strategies: Treat each option as true or false

steps.detail: 132 to 108 is a 24 point systolic drop.
The systolic criterion alone is sufficient and it has been met.
A drop of this size is not expected and carries a fall risk.
The measurement has already been taken at the interval.
